docs.title: AWC — Agent Workspace Cache
docs.text:
AWC is an object-storage-backed, content-addressed workspace system for Linux coding-agent fleets. A platform prepares one development environment, forks thousands of private workspaces from it without copying data, and mounts each one as a normal directory. Agents keep using ordinary tools. Shared content is cached once per host. Writes stay private until they are checkpointed.

Prepare once, fork many, fetch common bytes once, and store only unique changes.

The first release exposes five user-level primitives:

snapshot → fork → mount → checkpoint → diff/export

AWC is deliberately not a general distributed filesystem, a sandbox, an agent orchestrator, or a shared multi-writer filesystem (scope discipline).

Tutorial Your first workspace

Import a snapshot, fork, mount, edit, checkpoint, and export. End to end, in one sitting.

Tutorial See the economics

Fan out 100 workspaces from one base and watch the backend reads collapse to one.

How-to Solve a goal

Import, fork, mount, checkpoint, deploy, operate, and develop. Step-by-step answers.

Reference Look it up

CLI flags, configuration, environment variables, metrics, APIs, and on-disk formats.

Explanation Understand the design

Why content addressing, caching, singleflight, leases, and explicit durability.

Explanation What AWC is not

The guardrails that keep the product narrow and the wedge sharp.

docs.title: Why AWC
docs.text:
Coding-agent fleets clone the same repositories, install the same dependencies, and read many of the same files, hundreds of times over. The number of agent hypotheses scales linearly; the underlying data does not. AWC makes the physical system match that workload:

  • One shared base for many logical workspaces.
  • One host-level fetch for correlated reads across many agents (singleflight).
  • Constant-time forks — forking creates metadata, not a copy (no hidden copy on fork).
  • Explicit durability — only checkpoints survive host loss, not every write (the durability model).
  • Pricing on unique bytes and real materialization, not logical volume count (economics).

docs.title: Who it is for
docs.text:
The first user is the infrastructure team behind a coding-agent, code-review, security-analysis, migration, evaluation, or internal developer-AI platform. The best first workloads have 50 to 500 concurrent agents, 20 or more agents per prepared base, environments of 5 to 50 GB, correlated reads, private deltas below roughly 5 percent of the base, and task lifetimes of minutes to hours.

AWC is not intended for small fleets, large per-agent datasets, continuously active workspaces, shared multi-writer POSIX workloads, or applications that need remote durability on every write.

docs.title: Get started
docs.text: The fastest way to see AWC work on a laptop is the local-dev smoke, which stands up PostgreSQL and an S3-compatible store in containers and runs the binaries on the host. Walk through it in Your first workspace, or read the architecture overview first.

Explanation answers why. These pages are discursive and opinionated: they make the design choices and the rejected alternatives visible. They do not teach a procedure (use the tutorials) and they do not list the facts (use the reference).

  • The durability model — explicit durability versus fsync, and what survives host loss.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text: AWC splits into three planes. A stateless control plane owns mutable metadata. A privileged data plane on each host serves bytes and builds checkpoints. A durable object store holds immutable content. The split exists because the system handles two different kinds of truth, and they scale differently (spec §7.2, §17.1).

docs.title: Two stores of truth
docs.text:
AWC keeps mutable state and immutable bytes apart. PostgreSQL is the source of truth for mutable metadata: workspace heads, leases, states, and retention (spec §7.2, §8.7). The object store is the source of truth for immutable content: blobs, trees, files, and snapshots (spec §8.8). The store is content-addressed (a CAS), scoped per tenant (spec §9.2, §16.3).

These two stores do different work. A workspace head must move atomically and linearizably, so it advances in one PostgreSQL transaction (spec §14.3). File bytes are immutable, so they live in the object store, where they deduplicate and fetch by range (spec §8.8). Folding both into one system forces a bad choice. The transactional store would carry every byte, or the byte store would have to do transactions. AWC refuses both.

Host-local state is disposable, not truth (spec §3.2, §6.7). The local cache and the writable upper directory are acceleration and scratch space. Losing the cache costs performance, not correctness. Only an acknowledged checkpoint survives host loss (spec §6.8).

docs.title: Why the control plane is off the read path
docs.text:
The control plane owns identities, authorization, leases, publication, and retention (spec §7.2, §8.1). It does not touch ordinary file reads. That choice is what lets a mounted workspace keep serving reads during a control-plane outage (spec §17.5).

A warm read stays in the kernel and on the host:

agent process
  → Linux VFS
  → shared read-only FUSE base
  → host-local CAS file
  → page cache / local NVMe

It needs no control-plane request, no database query, no object-store request, and no per-workspace FUSE process (spec §7.3). A cold read adds the parts that cost a round trip:

→ host cache lookup
→ singleflight coordinator
→ object storage
→ streaming digest verification
→ atomic cache install

Concurrent cold reads for the same (tenant, digest) on one host share one fetch (spec §7.4, §10.4). A singleflight coordinator sits over the one shared host cache. A hundred readers that miss the same object produce one remote fetch, not a hundred.

The object store, not the control plane, is the data dependency for reads. The control plane must not proxy file reads or writes (spec §8.1). Hosts fetch objects directly from the tenant-scoped CAS.

docs.title: Why one daemon owns the host
docs.text:
awcd is one privileged Linux service per compute host (spec §8.3). It holds the shared read-only FUSE base mount, the host-local cache, the singleflight table, the OverlayFS mount manager, and the checkpoint builder. There is one multiplexed base filesystem for the whole host, not one FUSE daemon per workspace (spec §8.4).

The privilege is narrow and forced. The daemon needs capabilities for FUSE, OverlayFS, bind mounts, cgroup freeze, and namespace operations (spec §15.3). Nothing else needs those powers. So the control plane and the worker are kept stateless, unprivileged, and horizontally replaceable instead.

awc-control runs as stateless replicas behind a load balancer, with PostgreSQL as the only coordination dependency (spec §8.1, §21.2). awc-worker drains a PostgreSQL job queue with bounded, idempotent workers (spec §8.2). Neither mounts a filesystem or talks to the kernel. If a replica dies, another takes over with no host-local state to recover.

The spec also asks awcd to split its own privilege internally: a small privileged mount helper, an unprivileged cache and FUSE service, and hashing workers with no mount rights (spec §15.3). The current build runs awcd as one process, as the spec permits for the initial implementation. That is a scope decision for now, not a departure from the model.

docs.title: How the planes connect
docs.text:
Mount authorization crosses the planes by capability, not by trust. The control plane issues a short-lived, signed mount ticket (spec §9.11, §13.8). awcd verifies the ticket without a synchronous control-plane call and fails closed if verification or host authorization fails (spec §8.3, §13.9). Internal host-to-control traffic uses gRPC over mutual TLS (spec §13.1).

On checkpoint, the data plane does the byte work and the control plane does the metadata work. awcd quiesces the writer, scans the upper delta, hashes and uploads new objects directly to the CAS, then asks the control plane to advance the workspace head in one transaction (spec §11.6, §13.12). Bytes go to the object store. The head moves in PostgreSQL. The two stores of truth stay on their own sides.

docs.title: Known limits
docs.text:
These are architecture-relevant gaps between the spec and the committed build.

  • Control-plane REST surface. awc-control serves the core lifecycle over REST today: import sessions, snapshots with :diff, workspace create/fork/get, and mount-ticket issuance (T112, done). The internal gRPC LeaseService and CheckpointService are wired. Authentication is narrower than spec §13.2: service-account tokens verify, but OIDC discovery still resolves to an empty verifier, so id tokens do not yet authenticate.
  • Singleflight concurrency bounds. The singleflight coordinator is wired onto the read path, but the remote-read admission limiter and object-store circuit breakers are not attached yet. Coalescing works. A global fetch bound does not (spec §10.10, §10.11).
  • Worker job coverage. awc-worker runs snapshot validation, a decay scrub, workspace expiry, snapshot retention, and durable GC. Several job types in spec §8.2 are not yet separate handlers.
  • Cross-host evidence. The fan-out gate (spec §20.7) is defined for one host cache domain (100 workspaces on one host), and it is measured there: 100 concurrent readers fetch about 1.00878 times the remote bytes of one reader, under the 1.25 gate. On loopback that flat-byte result is the host object cache and the Linux page cache, not singleflight: the follower path stays idle on a single host, and coalescing is proven only by the regression gate. The cross-host economic case for singleflight — the reason the coordinator exists — is not yet measured; it needs a second host.

docs.title: Content addressing
docs.text: AWC names every immutable object by a digest computed from its bytes, not by where the bytes live. The address is the content. This single choice is why a fork costs nothing, why storage grows with distinct bytes rather than with workspace count, and why the cache can serve the same object to many readers.

docs.title: Identity comes from the bytes
docs.text:
A content-addressed object is named by a digest derived from a canonical encoding of its own content. For the structured objects (file, tree, snapshot) that encoding is deterministic canonical CBOR; for a raw blob it is the bytes themselves. The digest domain folds in the object kind:

SHA256("awc:v1:" || object_kind || 0x00 || canonical_payload)

Mixing the kind into the domain means the same byte payload cannot be read as two different object types. The implementation computes this in one streaming pass, so an object is hashed without ever holding its full payload.

Immutability follows from the addressing scheme. If the address is the content, then changing the content changes the address. The spec therefore states that a published object MUST never change in place, and that a second upload under an existing digest MUST either be byte-identical or fail. The object store enforces this with conditional writes that refuse to overwrite an existing key.

docs.title: Why forks cost nothing
docs.text:
A location-addressed store names bytes by where they sit: a volume, an inode, a path. Forking such a store means either copying the bytes, or maintaining a growing table of references from each workspace to each location. You pay per workspace, and the cost grows with the size of the base.

Content addressing inverts this. The address does not depend on location, so a workspace refers to a base snapshot by a single digest. Fork creates only a metadata record that points at that digest. The spec is explicit that fork work MUST stay independent of snapshot size, and that any work proportional to file count is import or checkpoint work, not fork work.

The dedup property is the same mechanism viewed from storage. Because the address is the bytes, two uploads of identical bytes in one tenant produce one key. A conditional create turns the second upload into a no-op. Durable storage therefore tracks distinct content, not workspace count. The acceptance scenario makes the shape concrete: 1000 forks of a 20 GiB base, each changing 50 MiB, must retain roughly 20 GiB plus 50 GiB plus overhead, not approach 20 TiB merely because 1000 branches exist.

The same shape applies to fetch. The in-flight request table is keyed by (tenant, digest), so many concurrent reads of one absent object share a single remote fetch. The fan-out gate restates this: 100 simultaneous reads of one object MUST produce one underlying fetch per host and tenant.

docs.title: The tenant is part of the address
docs.text:
Dedup stops at the tenant boundary. The cache key MUST include the tenant, the hash algorithm, and the digest:

tenant_id + hash_algorithm + object_digest

The durable key carries the same tenant, in path form:

cas/v1/tenants/<tenant-id>/<algorithm>/<first-2>/<next-2>/<digest>

Identical bytes uploaded by two different tenants therefore produce two objects, two cache entries, and two fetches. The spec is deliberate about this: a digest collision across tenants does not imply a shared object or a shared cache key, and the system MUST NOT perform cross-tenant existence checks or deduplication.

The on-disk cache layout mirrors the same boundary, nesting objects under a tenant directory. In the implementation, the tenant scope is not an optional string; it is a mandatory argument to every CAS operation.

The reason is isolation. If a tenant could learn that bytes it never uploaded already exist in another tenant's namespace, that fact would be a side channel: an adversary who guesses content could probe for its presence, its size, or its cache warmth. Scoping every key, every existence check, and every fetch to a tenant closes that channel at the addressing layer rather than at a policy layer that might be bypassed.

A future deployment MAY deduplicate across an explicitly configured trust domain, but only with a separate security review. The MVP does not.

docs.title: What is specified versus what is measured
docs.text:
The digest domain, the tenant-scoped namespace, the mandatory tenant scope, and the singleflight key are committed code, not just spec text. The dedup and fork-independence properties are structural consequences of that code path.

The cache-key composition has one wrinkle worth naming. The cache key lists three components: tenant, algorithm, digest. The singleflight key carries two fields, tenant and digest, because a digest compares equal only when both its algorithm and its raw bytes match. Two fields, three components, same identity.

The economic gates are a separate matter. The fan-out gate is defined for one host cache domain — 100 workspaces on one host — and the delta-storage gate is durable-storage accounting over many forks; neither is a multi-host test. The dedup ratio on a single warm host is a structural fact, and the measurements recorded in this repo so far are single-host. The cross-host storage and I/O case is not yet measured. See measuring AWC for what has and has not been demonstrated.

docs.title: Design decisions
docs.text:
AWC fixes twelve architecture decisions in spec Appendix F. They are not preferences. The spec labels them "architecture decisions fixed by this specification." This page walks the ones that carry a real trade-off: the choice, the alternative that was rejected, what the choice costs, and the risk that remains (spec §26). For the mechanism behind any one decision, read the deeper page this one links to.

The decisions are not independent. Most of them follow from one root choice: durable data is immutable and content-addressed (spec Appendix F.1). Once the truth is a set of immutable, hash-named objects, the rest of the shape falls out of it. Local writes become a private delta. Fork becomes a metadata pointer. Dedup becomes a key lookup. Publication becomes an atomic pointer swap. The sections below make those consequences explicit.

docs.title: Immutable, content-addressed durable data
docs.text:
The first decision is that every durable object is immutable and addressed by the SHA-256 digest of its content (spec Appendix F.1, §9.3). The alternative is a mutable or block-addressed filesystem, where bytes live at a location and change in place.

Immutability is what makes the rest of the design cheap. Two snapshots that contain the same file share one object, so deduplication is a key lookup, not a scan (spec §3.1). A cached object is verified once, by recomputing its digest, and then trusted forever, because it cannot change (spec §6.2). A snapshot reaches READY only when every object reachable from its root is present and valid, and that closure never needs rechecking (spec §6.4).

The cost is that there is no in-place edit. Changing one byte of a file writes a new blob and a new chain of manifests up to the root. That is the trade the system makes on purpose. The risk it leaves behind is object count: a tree of millions of small files becomes millions of small objects, which stresses the object store and the garbage collector. Spec §26.5 names this directly, and small-object packing is deferred, not solved (spec §27.2). The MVP keeps the format simple until traces justify packing (spec §26.5).

For how content addressing works in detail, read Content addressing.

docs.title: Local writes, explicit durability
docs.text:
Ordinary writes are local, and remote durability is an explicit checkpoint (spec Appendix F.4, §6.8). The rejected alternative is synchronous remote durability, where fsync(2) means the byte is safe off-host.

This choice exists to keep the writer cheap. A mounted workspace is an immutable lower plus a private local upper (spec Appendix F.5, §11.3). The agent writes to the upper with normal OverlayFS copy-on-write semantics. No write crosses the network, so no write waits on a quorum. That is what makes the writer disposable: lose the host, and you lose only work that was never checkpointed (spec §6.8).

The cost is a sharp split between what the agent sees and what survives. Inside a mount, fsync and fdatasync touch the local upper only (spec §14.8). They do not imply remote durability. A user who treats fsync as durability will be wrong. Spec §26.9 names this as a first-class risk, and the mitigation is documentation and CLI language, not a different design: the product must state the distinction in the CLI, the APIs, the mount metadata, and the dashboards (spec §26.9).

The consequence is that checkpointing is on the critical path of recoverability, not of correctness. An uncheckpointed workspace can be lost at any time. Only an acknowledged checkpoint is guaranteed to survive host loss (spec §6.8). For the full model, read The durability model.

docs.title: One writer, single-authority publication
docs.text:
Each workspace has at most one active writer, and publication is single-authority (spec Appendix F.3, F.10). The rejected alternative is concurrent writers, where several processes or hosts publish to one workspace through a distributed-coherence protocol.

Concurrent writers would force the very thing the cache model exists to avoid. Two writers on one workspace need distributed locking, coherence, and conflict resolution. That is a shared mutable filesystem, which the spec refuses as a non-goal (spec §4.2). Picking one writer lets AWC drop all of that machinery.

Publication still has to be safe against a paused or partitioned old host. The spec solves this with a monotonically increasing fencing generation and an optimistic workspace version, not with distributed consensus (spec Appendix F.10, §14.4). A checkpoint commits only inside one PostgreSQL transaction that checks version, head, lease.generation, and mount_session together (spec §14.3). A stale host may keep writing to its local upper, but those bytes can never become the canonical head, because its generation fails the check (spec §14.4).

The residual risk is operational. A partitioned writer keeps mutating local state that will be discarded. An operator may need to recover that work through an explicit path, or accept its loss (spec §14.4, §17.11). For the full fencing model, read Fencing and split-brain.

docs.title: PostgreSQL as the metadata authority
docs.text:
Mutable metadata lives in PostgreSQL, and the workspace head advances in one transaction (spec §7.2, §8.7, §14.3). The rejected alternative is a purpose-built consensus service, or a per-workspace Raft group.

PostgreSQL is on the publication path and the lease path. It is not on the read path (spec Appendix F.7, §7.2). That separation is what lets the control plane fail without stalling mounted workspaces: once a mount is established, reads and writes continue during a control-plane outage, subject to the local lease (spec §17.5). The database only has to be strongly consistent for the one operation that needs linearizability, which is moving a head.

The cost is a single metadata dependency and a scaling ceiling. Spec §26.10 names the risk that large workspace fan-out overloads PostgreSQL. The mitigation is to keep reads off the database hot path, batch forks, use compact rows, and partition the audit tables (spec §26.10). A specialized metadata service is deferred until measured need (spec §26.10). For how the planes split, read Architecture.

docs.title: FUSE and OverlayFS, not a custom filesystem
docs.text:
The active Linux view is an immutable lower plus a private upper, built on FUSE and kernel OverlayFS (spec Appendix F.5, §15.6, §15.8). The rejected alternative is a custom filesystem, or a custom kernel module. The spec forbids a custom kernel module outright (spec §4.2).

Using the kernel OverlayFS for the writable composition avoids a second copy of overlay semantics inside FUSE. The immutable lower is served by one shared read-only FUSE mount per host, not one FUSE process per workspace (spec §8.4, Appendix F.7). That keeps the fast path in the kernel and on local NVMe (spec §7.3).

The cost is dependence on kernel behavior that the project does not control. OverlayFS stacked over FUSE is kernel-version-sensitive, and spec §26.1 names it as the first-listed risk. The mitigation is a certified kernel matrix, host admission probes, and a held-in-reserve fallback such as a merged writable FUSE path or eager lower materialization (spec §26.1, §28). The spec does not claim universal Linux compatibility.

The performance risk is real and measured. A cold read of many small files through FUSE is expensive: one pilot measurement reads 300 source files at 75.6x native time, because each file pays a cold-fetch cost. The feared tax on synchronous builds did not appear: a cold build measures 1.99x native and a warm build 1.06x, because compile compute dilutes the read cost. Spec §26.2 keeps the risk open and points at virtio-fs or a specialized kernel path only after traces show FUSE is the dominant cost. For the read and write model, read Overlay, cache, and singleflight.

docs.title: Tenant-scoped deduplication
docs.text:
Deduplication is scoped to a tenant (spec Appendix F.2, §6.3, §16.3). The rejected alternative is a global content-addressed store that deduplicates across all tenants.

Global dedup would save storage when two tenants hold the same public base. It would also create a cross-tenant side channel. An attacker who controls upload timing can learn whether a digest already exists for another tenant, and so leak information about what that tenant stores (spec §16.3). The MVP refuses that trade. Every object-store request is scoped to a tenant prefix (spec §9.2, §16.3), and a digest collision across tenants does not imply a shared object (spec §9.2).

The cost is duplicate storage for identical content held by different tenants. The spec accepts that cost as the price of isolation. A future deployment may deduplicate across an explicitly configured organization trust domain, but only after a separate security review (spec §16.3). For the trust model, read Security model.

docs.title: A shared, disposable host cache
docs.text:
The host-local cache is disposable and shared across all mounts on that host (spec Appendix F.8, §6.7). The rejected alternative is a rigid per-workspace cache partition.

A shared cache is what makes cross-workspace dedup pay off locally. Two workspaces from the same tenant that read the same object share one cache file, with no per-workspace copy (spec §4.1). Losing the entire cache costs performance only, never correctness (spec §6.7). Recovery is trivial, because there is nothing to recover.

The cost is contention. One scan-heavy workload can evict another tenant's hot set, which spec §26.7 names as a risk. The mitigation is segmented admission, per-tenant concurrency limits, optional reservations, and scheduling locality, and the spec explicitly avoids rigid per-workspace partitions (spec §26.7). The cache admission policy is the place where that tension is managed. For how singleflight and eviction fit together, read Overlay, cache, and singleflight.

docs.title: Fork is metadata-only
docs.text:
Fork creates a logical workspace without copying file content (spec Appendix F.6, §6.10). The rejected alternative is a copy, however fast.

This decision is a direct consequence of immutability. Because the base is immutable and content-addressed, a new workspace only needs a metadata row that points at the base snapshot (spec §6.10). Fork cost stays independent of snapshot size. Any work proportional to the number or size of files is classified as import, mount warmup, or checkpoint work, not fork work (spec §6.10).

There is no real residual risk here. The invariant is a guard against drift. If a future change made fork proportional to size, it would break the economic premise of the product (spec §3.1). The invariant exists to make that regression visible.

docs.title: The five operations are the whole surface
docs.text: The product surface is exactly snapshot, fork, mount, checkpoint, and diff/export (spec Appendix F.12). Cross-host shared mutable POSIX semantics are out of scope (spec Appendix F.11, §4.2). These two are treated together in Scope discipline, because the refusal is the point. Each neighbor the product refuses (orchestration, sandboxing, a build system, a memory database) would widen the correctness kernel and blur the economic wedge. Read that page for the full argument and for the deferred capabilities in spec §27.

docs.title: Known limits
docs.text:
Appendix F is normative. These are decisions fixed by the specification, not a description of a finished system. The current build does not yet match the spec everywhere. Treat each decision as a design commitment, and check the deeper page for what is implemented today.

  • Cross-host evidence is local so far. The fan-out acceptance target (spec §20.7) is itself a one-host test: 100 workspaces on one host cache domain. Measured evidence in this repo is single-host, too. The build-tax and read-tax numbers cited above come from one pilot host. The cross-host economic edge that motivates singleflight (coalescing the same read across hosts) needs a second host with a real network path to the object store, which the repo does not yet have.
  • The overlay fallback is a held design, not a built path. Spec §26.1 names a merged writable FUSE path or eager lower materialization as the fallback if OverlayFS-over-FUSE proves unreliable. That fallback is specified, not implemented.
  • Deferred capabilities stay deferred. Small-object packing (§27.2), live rebase (§27.5), virtio-fs (§27.8), and the other items in §27 are candidates that need economic evidence before they enter the surface (spec §26.12).

docs.title: The durability model
docs.text: AWC makes durability an explicit act. A process calls checkpoint, or it does not. There is no middle state. Ordinary writes land on a host-local upper filesystem and stay there until a checkpoint publishes them. This is the opposite of a shared filesystem, where every write chases the network and fsync is the durability boundary.

docs.title: Why durability is explicit, not fsync-based
docs.text:
The workload is agents that compile, install packages, and generate files at high rates. If every write had to reach shared storage, the data plane would pay round-trip and consistency costs on the hot path. AWC keeps the hot path local. The host overlays a private upper directory on an immutable snapshot, and tools see a normal local filesystem. Read-your-writes is the OverlayFS view, not a remote round-trip.

The cost of that speed is honesty about what is durable. fsync inside a writable mount touches the local upper filesystem only. It is not a remote guarantee.

fsync is local

fsync and fdatasync apply to the host-local upper filesystem. They do not imply a remote checkpoint.

So the product asks you to say when a state is worth keeping. That act is the checkpoint.

docs.title: Two stores of durable truth
docs.text:
Durable state lives in two places, and they do different jobs.

The object store holds immutable content. Blobs, file manifests, tree manifests, and snapshot manifests are content-addressed and written once. Once an object is accepted, it does not change.

PostgreSQL holds the authoritative mutable pointer: the workspace head_snapshot_id and version. The object store can hold many candidate snapshots for one workspace. PostgreSQL decides which one is the head.

This split is why the system is safe. The object store is a set of immutable candidates. The database is the single arbiter of which candidate counts. See architecture for how the planes divide this work.

docs.title: The atomic head advance
docs.text:
A checkpoint ends in one database transaction. That transaction either advances the head, or it changes nothing. There is no partial head.

The publisher uploads objects, confirms they are durable, and only then advances the head. A reader of an acknowledged head can always find every object the head references.

docs.title: Why no head is ever reconstructed
docs.text:
If PostgreSQL is lost, you do not rebuild workspace heads by scanning the object store. The object store holds immutable candidate snapshots, many of them orphans from failed or superseded checkpoints. Without the database, there is no way to know which candidate a workspace last acknowledged. PostgreSQL determines the head.

PostgreSQL itself must run with automated failover and point-in-time recovery. That is a deployment duty, not something the daemon provides.

docs.title: What is ephemeral
docs.text:
The upper directory is ephemeral by design. Writes a process makes to its writable mount live on one host. No other host sees them. No remote client sees them. They are not durable until a checkpoint commits.

This is where the distinction between acknowledged and unacknowledged matters. An acknowledged state is one whose publication transaction committed. The response came back, the head moved, and the version incremented. Everything else is unacknowledged. Unacknowledged writes survive a process crash and a daemon restart, because the upper directory and the kernel mount persist. They do not survive host loss.

Host loss is the sharp boundary

Host loss destroys the uncheckpointed upper delta. Only what the acknowledged head references survives. Everything that lived only in host-local files is gone.

docs.title: Recovery
docs.text:
Each failure mode has a recovery procedure. The boundary to remember is the one above: host loss loses only un-checkpointed work.

  • Recover from host loss
  • Recover from a control-plane outage
  • Recover from an object-store outage
  • Recover from a PostgreSQL failover
  • Recover from an interrupted checkpoint

docs.title: The lease is the gate on publication
docs.text:
Durability is not just "the transaction committed." The transaction also fences the writer. Only the holder of the current lease generation may advance the head. A host that is paused, partitioned, or superseded holds a stale generation. Its publication fails even if it resumes later, because the generation it presents no longer equals the lease's.

This protects the head from split-brain. A stale host may keep writing to its own upper directory. But those bytes cannot become the canonical head through any normal path. They leave only through an explicit, operator-assisted recovery that never advances the head automatically. See fencing and split-brain and handle a stale writer.

docs.title: Lost responses are safe
docs.text:
A checkpoint can fail after the transaction commits but before the response arrives. The client retries with the same idempotency key. The publication path treats the candidate snapshot as content-addressed. A retry that presents the same manifest either creates the snapshot row or reuses the existing one, then returns the already-committed result. The head advances exactly once. The audit event records whether the row was created or reused.

Objects uploaded before a failed or cancelled checkpoint are not wasted and not harmful. They are immutable orphans. Garbage collection reclaims them later.

docs.title: Limits and what is not proven here
docs.text:
Be precise about what this model guarantees and what it does not.

  • PostgreSQL high availability is a deployment responsibility. The system expects automated failover and point-in-time recovery, but the daemon does not provide it. A single-node database is a single point of failure for publication.
  • Object-store durability is deployment-dependent. The system detects a missing object and marks the snapshot degraded rather than return wrong bytes. It cannot manufacture bytes the store has lost.
  • The properties on this page are design facts, not measured guarantees. They describe specified behavior confirmed against the code, not results from a chaos test.

docs.title: Economics and cost model
docs.text:
AWC is an agent workspace cache. Its bet is that the physical bill can track new bytes and cold reads, not the workspace count. This page explains why the design is shaped that way, what the three flattening mechanisms buy you, and where the measured evidence stops.

For the hand-held version, read see the economics. That tutorial fans out many forks and shows the remote-fetch count collapsing. This page is the why behind it.

docs.title: Why fork count is free
docs.text:
A conventional fleet gives each agent its own clone, volume, or sandbox snapshot. The bill then scales with the agent count, because each workspace is priced as a full physical copy. AWC rejects that model. The design holds that charging each branch as a full volume contradicts the economic thesis. Fork operations should be free or nearly free.

Fork can be free because a fork creates only metadata. A workspace begins as a reference to an existing immutable snapshot and an empty private delta. The base bytes already live in the tenant content store, keyed by digest. A new fork points at them. It does not copy them. Fork work stays independent of snapshot size. Any work proportional to file count is import, mount, or checkpoint work, not fork work.

The bill tracks new content and cold reads, not how many workspaces exist. Branch count is reporting only, not a primary charge. That is the central design choice. The rest of this page is about what makes it true, and what it costs.

docs.title: The three mechanisms that flatten the bill
docs.text:
Three mechanisms turn "many workspaces, one base" into "about one remote fetch, not N". Each has an honest limit.

Tenant-scoped content addressing. Each distinct object lives once per tenant. Identical bytes share one object, whether they appear in one fork or in a hundred. All forks of one base under one tenant resolve a shared file to the same object. The limit is the tenant boundary. Cross-tenant deduplication is prohibited, to avoid content-presence side channels. The dedup ceiling is per-tenant commonality, not global. For how content identity works, read content addressing.

The cache hierarchy. A read walks the Linux page cache and the host-local object cache before it touches object storage. Once an object is cached, repeated reads cost zero remote bytes. The limit is that the cache is per host and disposable. A second cold host pays again. Loss of the host cache affects performance only, never correctness.

Singleflight. The daemon keeps an in-memory map of active fetches keyed by cache key. When several readers miss the same object at the same instant, one becomes the leader and fetches. The rest become followers and share the result. The read path routes through the fetch coordinator. The leader and follower counters publish at /metrics (awc_singleflight_leader_fetches_total, awc_singleflight_follower_requests_total). The limit is timing. Singleflight only helps when concurrent readers contend on one digest while the leader is still in flight. On one loopback host the leader tends to install the cache entry before the other readers arrive. They then take the cache fast path, and the follower path stays idle. Singleflight's value is the cross-host regime, where network round trips widen the contention window. That regime is not yet measured. For the design choices behind this path, read overlay, cache, and singleflight.

docs.title: The measured shape
docs.text:
The evidence comes from two places. The regression gates are deterministic checks over the software data path. The pilot run is one end-to-end measurement on a single loopback host.

On the pilot, a fan-out of many agents over a common base reads about the same remote bytes as one agent. Local FUSE and CPU work scale with concurrency. Remote bytes do not. The fan-out property holds on loopback.

For storage, physical unique bytes come out at the base plus the sum of unique deltas, not forks times base. Storage amplification (logical retained divided by physical unique) is greater than one. The economic meaning is direct. Forking a large snapshot many times costs the base plus the unique deltas, not one full copy per fork.

For reads, the cache effect is the cold-versus-warm gap. A cold read costs one remote fetch plus verify-and-install. The same read warm is a pure local-cache read. On a real object store the cold cost widens by the store round trip, while the warm cost stays local. So the gap, and the egress savings, grows.

docs.title: What it costs you
docs.text:
The same measurements expose the local cost. AWC is slower than a plain OverlayFS or ext4 view for local storage and for cold access. This is the price of routing reads through a FUSE content cache.

Cold reads are taxed. A cold build costs more than a warm one, because each first-touch file pays a remote fetch plus verify-and-install. The per-file cold-fetch cost dominates when the working set is small. Workloads that read or transform many files cold pay the most.

Editing a base file pays copy-up. Editing a file that lives in the lower overlay triggers a full data copy-up through FUSE. The first cold edit of each base file is the expensive one.

Publishing a snapshot costs bandwidth. Ingest does more byte work than a bare checksum pass, because it verifies and installs each object. This is a one-time cost per snapshot, not a per-read cost.

These are local taxes. The economic bet is that cross-host byte reuse pays them back.

docs.title: Where the evidence stops
docs.text:
The pilot is one loopback host with a local object store. The flat-bytes result is real, but on loopback it is explained by the object cache plus the Linux page cache. The singleflight follower path is idle there. So the pilot proves the byte-amplification property, not the singleflight mechanism. The regression gates prove the coalescing property directly in the software data path, with no page cache in the loop.

The cross-host regime is where the economic case has to hold. A cross-host run needs a second host, a real network, the fetch coordinator on the read path, and its counters published. That run is not yet measured.

Until that cross-host run exists, the cross-host economic edge stays an open thesis. That edge is the whole reason the local tax is worth paying. It is not a proven result.

Read this before you reuse a claim

The pilot fan-out result is a local loopback measurement, not a cross-host proof. The cross-host economic edge is unmeasured. Singleflight's follower path is idle on loopback; the loopback win is the caches. Locally, AWC is slower than plain OverlayFS for cold reads and for editing base files.

For the boundary that keeps the write side cheap, read the durability model. For how shared bytes survive the deletion of one fork, read run garbage collection.

docs.title: Fencing and split-brain
docs.text:
A workspace has one writer at a time. That rule is easy to state and hard to enforce when a host can be paused, partitioned, or simply slow. The writer may believe it still owns the workspace long after the control plane has moved on. Fencing is how AWC keeps that confused writer from corrupting the head.

The mechanism is one number: a fencing generation on each writer lease. This page explains why that number exists, what a stale writer sees, and why the obvious alternatives do not work.

docs.title: The problem a generation solves
docs.text:
A read-write mount holds an exclusive writer lease. The lease lets one host publish checkpoints that advance the workspace head. "Exclusive" must survive failure. Consider what happens when host A freezes for a minute, or loses its network link.

While A is unreachable, the control plane cannot tell whether A is gone or merely paused. A new mount request may arrive for the same workspace. The control plane issues a fresh lease to host B. Now two hosts believe they can write. This is the split-brain window. If both can publish, the head can advance along two divergent histories, and the workspace has no single canonical state.

The lease cannot solve this by time alone. A's lease may still read as unexpired on A's own clock. Even if the control plane marks A's lease as expired, A may resume a second later, still convinced it is the active writer. Something must let B win and make A's attempt fail, no matter when A wakes up.

That thing is the generation.

docs.title: Why a generation, not just a timer
docs.text:
Every new writer lease for a workspace gets a monotonically increasing generation. B's lease carries a generation strictly higher than A's. Publication is allowed only when the host presents the one generation the control plane granted for that lease. A host cannot invent a token. A writer that presents a stale generation is fenced off, and a writer that presents a higher generation than its lease holds is also rejected.

The decision does not depend on the writer's wall clock. Correctness rests on the generation and one database transaction, not on synchronized time. Wall clocks drive expiry and observability. They do not fence.

This is why lease expiration alone is not enough. A partitioned host holding an older generation is rejected even if it resumes later. The token it holds is now permanently behind.

docs.title: The lease lifecycle
docs.text:
A lease moves through a small set of states, from ISSUED to ACTIVE and on to RELEASED, with a timeout path to EXPIRED and an admin path to REVOKED.

Only two states may publish: ACTIVE and RELEASING. RELEASING exists so a final checkpoint can publish during a clean unmount. The other states cannot advance the head.

The host drives the lifecycle. It activates its lease when the kernel mount succeeds, renews it in the background, and then releases or is fenced. Renewal is a control-plane RPC. The reply is one of four verdicts: extend the lease, remount read-only, revoke, or report the workspace gone. The last three demote the cached lease to a non-authorizing state. The host then fences on the next reconcile.

docs.title: What publication checks
docs.text:
A checkpoint ends in one transaction that advances the head. Before it advances anything, that transaction checks that the writer is still the writer. It confirms the lease, its generation, its state, and the head the caller expected. If the check fails, the transaction rolls back and the head is unchanged.

The caller gets a distinct rejection, not a vague failure. The stable error codes include STALE_LEASE_GENERATION and WORKSPACE_VERSION_CONFLICT. A stale writer learns precisely that it no longer holds the workspace.

docs.title: What a stale writer keeps and what it loses
docs.text:
Fencing stops publication. It does not delete the writer's work in progress. A stale host may keep modifying its local upper directory. Those bytes remain useful to the agent that wrote them. The merged mount is still a correct local view.

What those bytes cannot do is become the canonical head through any normal path. They leave only through an explicit, operator-assisted recovery that never advances the head automatically. The stale generation is fenced at the control plane. The host daemon also fences itself on restart: its reconciler detects a non-authorizing lease and refuses to publish from that generation.

This split is deliberate. The agent's local work is not destroyed from under it. But the single durable history is protected from a confused writer.

docs.title: The rejected alternative: last writer wins
docs.text:
A simpler design would let any host that can reach the database publish. The last publication wins. The head converges on whoever wrote last. This is the "last writer wins" model.

It fails the workload contract. Two hosts that checkpoint the same workspace would clobber each other. A host partitioned for an hour could resume, publish its stale view, and silently overwrite hours of newer work. There is no durable history, only a race. AWC forbids this. At most one unexpired writer lease generation may publish, and every publication must carry that generation.

A second rejected design fences by time alone. The lease has an expiry. On expiry, the old host is presumed dead. This is the naive timer model. It fails because time is not authoritative across a partition. The frozen host's clock may disagree, or it may wake at the boundary and race. A monotonic token has no such failure mode. Once B's generation is higher, A's token can never catch up, no matter when A resumes.

docs.title: How this connects to the rest of the model
docs.text:
Fencing is the publication half of a larger promise about durability. The other half is that the head advances atomically, or not at all, in one transaction. See the durability model for that side of the contract.

The lease state machine sits inside the wider workspace and mount-session lifecycle. See lifecycle states. When a host finds itself fenced, the operator recovery path is in handle a stale writer. The broader outage behavior is in recover from a control-plane outage.

docs.title: Limits and what is not proven here
docs.text:
Be precise about what the evidence supports.

  • The fence is enforced in code and covered by unit tests. The tests reject a stale generation, a higher presented generation, a moved head, a moved version, a non-publishable state, an expired lease, a foreign workspace's lease, and a mismatched mount session.
  • The behavior is exercised beyond the unit tests. Fault-injection tests model a superseded lease and assert that a stale generation is rejected at publish and is not retried. Security and soak tests cover the stale-lease publication fence and credential rotation. The transactional path also has a database-gated integration test.
  • A live two-host split-brain has not been demonstrated in a recorded chaos test. Recorded measurements cover economics, cold-start, and amplification. They do not measure partition recovery or fencing under a real network split. Treat split-brain prevention as specified behavior confirmed against the code, not as a measured result.
  • Fencing protects the head. It does not reclaim the stale host's local disk usage. Those bytes persist on the host until the daemon fences the session, or until an operator exports and removes them.

docs.title: Lifecycle states
docs.text:
AWC holds state that outlives any single process. A snapshot, once published, is an immutable root that other workspaces fork from. A workspace head is one durable pointer that many readers trust. A writer lease decides who may advance that pointer. When a host crashes and returns, the daemon must rebuild a correct view from disk and one database. There is no operator in that loop to disambiguate.

That is the case for explicit state machines. A snapshot is not "uploaded and maybe validated and maybe deleted." It sits in one named state, and only a fixed set of edges leave that state. The same holds for workspaces, mount sessions, and leases. This page explains why those machines are shaped the way they are, and what the daemon does with them on restart.

docs.title: Why states, not flags
docs.text:
The rejected alternative is a handful of booleans. A snapshot could carry uploaded, validated, deleting. Six booleans compose into dozens of combinations, and most of them are impossible. Recovery code would have to test each one. The head pointer would depend on a convention nobody enforced.

A state collapses that space. "The snapshot is READY" is one fact. The legal exits are enumerable, and the illegal exits are rejectable in code. The workspace, mount-session, and lease enums each ship a transition predicate. The snapshot enum does not — its transitions are validated separately by the control plane. For a mount-session move, the store consults the predicate before it persists the record, and a transition that skips a state, loops on itself, or leaves a terminal state returns IllegalTransition. For the enums that carry the predicate, the diagram in the spec is the same graph the daemon or control plane enforces.

The payoff is deterministic recovery. On restart the daemon does not ask "what combination of flags did the dead process leave?" It asks "what state is this record in, and what edges are legal from here?"

docs.title: Snapshots: gate usability behind validation
docs.text:
A snapshot moves through a fixed path:

UPLOADING → VALIDATING → READY
                       └──► FAILED
READY → DELETING → DELETED

The shape answers two questions.

Why is READY gated behind VALIDATING? Because a snapshot becomes a workspace base only after two things are true. Its object closure must be complete and content-addressed. Its backing objects must be durably readable before the metadata record commits. The publisher sequences the work as upload, verify, publish record, advance head, and must never publish metadata first. VALIDATING is the state where that ordering is checked. A snapshot that fails closure becomes FAILED, and only READY snapshots may serve as a new workspace base. FAILED means "never usable," not "was usable and broke."

Why is DELETING distinct from DELETED? Because logical deletion and garbage collection are two transactions. A snapshot may be DELETING while its immutable objects remain on disk, and retained references must keep reading until the deletion transaction proves the snapshot is unreachable. Conflating the two would either delete objects under live readers or never reclaim them at all.

The code adds one state the spec §12.1 diagram does not draw: DEGRADED. The spec §12.1 diagram omits it; the runbooks treat it as an operational mark set when a published snapshot references a missing object. The system returns a distinct integrity error and starts the repair runbook rather than rewriting history. DEGRADED means "readable, but some backing objects are unavailable." It is an operator condition, not a base a new workspace forks from. (The control-plane transition validator does model edges to and from it — see the caveat in Limits and what is not proven here.)

docs.title: Workspaces: separate the writer from the head
docs.text:
A workspace is mutable; its head snapshot is not. The workspace state machine keeps the two apart:

CREATING → IDLE → MOUNTED → CHECKPOINTING → MOUNTED → IDLE → EXPIRING → DELETED

CHECKPOINTING exists as its own state so a crash mid-publish has an unambiguous resume target. On restart the daemon sees the record in CHECKPOINTING and knows the publish transaction may not have committed. It does not guess. It retries the publication with the same expected version and idempotency key. The head advances only if the precondition conjunction still holds. If it does not, the workspace stays where it was. See recover an interrupted checkpoint.

EXPIRING waits rather than deletes. An expired workspace that still has an active lease enters EXPIRING and stays there until the lease resolves. Deleting a workspace under a live writer would discard uncommitted upper bytes the agent might still need. The TTL is a statement about logical retention, not an order to tear down a data path.

FAILED is recoverable, not terminal. A workspace whose creation failed may be retried or torn down according to the failure reason. The code makes Failed → Creating, Failed → Idle, Failed → Expiring, and Failed → Deleted legal edges. Expiration is reversible for the same reason: a configurable grace period lets an operator undo a mistaken expiry, so Expiring → Idle is legal. Deleted alone is terminal.

docs.title: Leases: terminal means terminal
docs.text:
A writer lease carries the fencing generation. Its lifecycle is small:

ISSUED → ACTIVE → RELEASING → RELEASED
           ├── timeout ──► EXPIRED
           └── admin ────► REVOKED

Two design choices matter here.

RELEASING exists so a clean unmount can publish a final checkpoint. Publication is gated by a publication predicate, and only ACTIVE and RELEASING pass it. Without RELEASING, the last checkpoint of a session would have to publish from a state the predicate rejects. The alternative is to leave the lease ACTIVE and rely on a timer, which gives publication no defined endpoint.

The three terminal states — RELEASED, EXPIRED, REVOKED — never leave. A new writer does not resurrect a released lease. It is a fresh lease row at a strictly higher generation. The transition predicate encodes this: there is no edge out of a terminal state. This is what makes fencing monotonic. Once host B holds a higher generation, host A's token is permanently behind, no matter when A resumes. What a stale writer keeps and loses is in fencing and split-brain.

docs.title: Guarded transitions
docs.text:
The states are only useful if the edges are enforced. The workspace, mount-session, and lease enums each carry a transition predicate that rejects three classes of move: skipping a state, looping on the same state, and leaving a terminal state. The session store calls that predicate before it persists any mount-session move and returns IllegalTransition otherwise. Workspace transitions are checked the same way at the control-plane database; snapshot transitions go through a separate validator.

Guarding transitions turns the spec diagrams into a machine the daemon enforces, not a convention it hopes to honor. The atomic-publication rule depends on it. A checkpoint advances the head in one transaction, or not at all. If the transaction rolls back, the workspace state rolls back with it. A reader never observes a workspace stuck in CHECKPOINTING with a head that already moved.

Recovery is the one path allowed to skip. A stale mount may need to move straight to CLOSED, and the normal "must unmount first" edge does not apply. The store exposes a separate forced-state path for that, used only by reconciliation. The rule is that recovery is the authoritative unmount, not a second front door.

docs.title: Restart reconciliation
docs.text:
On restart the daemon scans its durable session store and reconciles each local session against the authoritative lease the control plane holds. The recovery classifier assigns each session one verdict:

  • Active lease valid — the lease is live, unexpired, and its generation matches. Renew it and resume serving. This is the only verdict that permits publishing.
  • Control plane unknown — the mount is live but the control plane holds no matching lease. Preserve the session and its upper. Do not delete, fence, or publish.
  • Stale generation — the lease exists but the generation is wrong, the lease is expired, or it is revoked. Fence the session to CLOSED. Never publish.
  • Preserved delta — the session is torn down but its upper holds uncommitted data. Preserve it for a bounded host-local recovery window.

The classifier also handles two more checkpoint precedence cases — cleanup incomplete (a checkpoint committed but local cleanup remained) and checkpoint interrupted (a checkpoint was in flight when the host died) — and a final fallthrough, safe to delete (torn down, no delta).

The order is deliberate. Interrupted durable operations take precedence over lease status. The classifier checks for pending checkpoint cleanup and an in-flight checkpoint before it looks at the lease. A half-finished durable checkpoint is more dangerous to abandon than a stale lease, so it is preserved for resume regardless of what the control plane says. Only after those cases does the classifier ask whether the lease still authorizes the session.

The control-plane-unknown verdict carries the strongest invariant. The spec forbids deleting an upper directory merely because the control plane is unreachable. The code enforces it twice. The classifier routes an unknown live mount to a preserve-and-mark-unknown verdict. The live executor then refuses to delete any session whose upper still holds uncommitted data, even if it were routed there. See handle a stale writer and recover from a control-plane outage.

docs.title: Limits and what is not proven here
docs.text:
Be precise about what the evidence supports.

  • The state machines and their transition predicates are unit-tested. The tests cover every legal edge and the rejected skips, self-loops, and terminal exits.
  • The recovery classifier is pure policy and is unit-tested for all seven verdicts, including the precedence of interrupted checkpoints over lease status.
  • Restart reconciliation is wired into daemon startup. Startup calls the reconcile path against a control-plane lease cache that consults authoritative leases and returns None when the control plane is unreachable.
  • Two limits are real. First, the mount path does not yet issue control-plane leases, so no durable session carries a lease_id. On restart every live session resolves to the control-plane-unknown verdict and is preserved. The active-lease and stale-generation paths are exercised in tests, not yet by a live mount. Second, the recovery executor updates durable records, the in-memory session registry, and health counters, but the privileged kernel effects — remount read-only and real OverlayFS teardown — are layered on by the mount component when wired.
  • The DEGRADED snapshot state is defined in the code and described in the spec runbooks. It is not drawn in the spec §12.1 diagram, but the control-plane transition validator does model edges to and from it (Ready → Degraded, Degraded → Ready, Degraded → Deleting). Treat it as a repair-driven condition, not a base a new workspace forks from.
  • No recorded chaos test restarts a live two-host deployment and observes the stale-generation verdict under a real partition. The recorded measurements cover economics and amplification, not multi-host restart recovery.

docs.title: Measuring AWC
docs.text: AWC is a cache. That makes it easy to benchmark badly. Warm the cache, compare against a naive full copy, and report one headline number. That run will flatter AWC, cheat AWC, or both. This page explains why the measurement discipline is the way it is, and where the measured evidence stops.

docs.title: Why a naive benchmark lies
docs.text:
The AWC win is a fan-out win. One agent reading one base pays a local tax for routing reads through a FUSE content cache. Ten agents reading the same base, or one agent forking a base it already paid for, get the reuse. The economic bet is that physical storage is approximately base plus unique deltas, not workspace count times complete size. Many agents requesting the same object on one cache domain collapse to one remote fetch.

Two bad baselines follow from misunderstanding that shape. The first is a plain cp -a or a full eager download as the comparison. Both pay the whole base for every workspace. Against them, AWC looks like a large win at fan-out even when it does nothing clever. At a fan-out of one, AWC loses to a plain copy, because it pays a FUSE tax a plain copy does not.

The second bad baseline is the opposite error. A local OverlayFS mount gives base amortization away for free. If you compare AWC to OverlayFS on one host, AWC loses, because it pays a FUSE tax OverlayFS does not. The apparent amplification is generic base amortization, not an AWC feature. OverlayFS delivers it with no FUSE cost.

A fair measurement needs both baselines, and it needs to say which regime each applies to. The naive full copy is the cross-host baseline, where OverlayFS structurally cannot follow because the bytes must cross a network. OverlayFS is the honest local baseline, and locally AWC is candid about being slower.

docs.title: Cache state is the variable you are not measuring
docs.text:
A warm read and a cold read of the same object differ by orders of magnitude. A number that does not say which state produced it says nothing.

AWC stacks three caches: the Linux page cache, the daemon in-memory manifest cache, and the host-local object cache on disk, in front of the object store. A cold result must name which of these were cleared. No single headline result may mix cold and warm states. A run must also report the environment that sets those states: kernel, NVMe model, object-store region, network bandwidth, snapshot file count, and read pattern.

On a live pilot you usually cannot clear the on-disk object cache while the daemon runs. So a trial is often page-cache cold but object-cache warm. That understates the true first-command cost. The coldest trial, not the median, is the honest first-command number.

This is the discipline: fix the variables you are not testing. Same host, same repository, same agent, same model, same prompts, same evaluator. Fix concurrency, and report queue time separately from service time so a saturated scheduler does not masquerade as a slow read. Use unique idempotency keys per trial so a fork does not replay a prior workspace. Drop the page cache before every cold trial, and verify it actually ran. Each control removes one alternative explanation for the number.

docs.title: Correctness is absolute, performance is conditional, economics is open
docs.text:
The targets fall into three classes, and a fair measurement treats them differently.

Correctness gates are absolute and must never regress. Fork work must be independent of snapshot logical size. A ready snapshot must never reference a missing object. Injected corruption must be detected before bytes are returned. Every failure injection must yield either the old head or the complete new head. A stale lease generation must fail to publish. These are not latency questions. They hold on any hardware. The failure-injection and recovery suites exercise the integrity gates: snapshot closure, digest correctness, checkpoint atomicity, and fencing. The count-based invariants — fork invariance, delta storage, fan-out coalescing, and singleflight suppression — are asserted as counts and ratios, not wall clock.

Performance targets are conditional on a published reference host. Fork latency has a budget. A batch of forks has a budget. Warm mount has a budget, excluding sandbox startup. Cold metadata mount for a large snapshot has a budget, with no full materialization. Many simultaneous reads of one absent object must produce one underlying fetch per host and tenant. These are service targets measured on a named environment. They are not guarantees across arbitrary customer networks.

Economic gates are the open ones. The fan-out test bounds the remote bytes many workspaces pull when they scan one base. The delta-storage test asks that many forks, each changing a little, cost about base plus unique deltas in physical storage, not the total that workspace count times base would imply. The launch gate asks for a clear improvement on at least one real design-partner workload. The last is not measured.

docs.title: The validation ladder
docs.text:
You cannot interpret an economic number unless the rungs below it hold. The specification orders its own evidence that way, from absolute correctness up to contingent economics. The measurement follows the same ladder.

The contract rung is the correctness set: fork invariance, snapshot closure, digest correctness, checkpoint atomicity, and fencing. If these fail, no latency number matters. The lifecycle rung is the set of state machines: snapshot, workspace, mount session, and lease. Measuring here means showing transitions are clean, and that a ready snapshot, an active lease, and a mounted writer behave as defined.

The crash-matrix rung is the failure matrix. Every failure path must preserve the last acknowledged workspace head. With the control plane down past its grace and expiry windows, durability writes complete with zero errors, and reads and writes continue during the outage. New mounts and checkpoints fail as expected, because both need the control plane. A checkpoint that crosses the expiry window is rejected after recovery. You can work through a long outage, but you cannot publish that work until the lease is re-established.

The sparse-scale rung is the delta-storage test. The workload and economics rung is the fan-out test and the launch gate. The attribution rung is the set of product ratios, backed by the storage accounting. Attribution is what stops a headline from crediting the wrong mechanism.

docs.title: Attribute the win to the right mechanism
docs.text:
A flat-remote-bytes result has at least three causes on one host: the object cache, the Linux page cache, and singleflight. They are not interchangeable. The measurement gives you the ratios to tell them apart. Storage amplification is logical retained divided by tenant-unique durable bytes. The I/O suppression ratio is one minus actual remote bytes over logical immutable bytes requested. Singleflight efficiency is follower requests served over total cold-miss requesters. Delta efficiency is checkpoint unique uploaded bytes over logical workspace bytes.

Attribution matters because a flat-bytes result on one host can be explained by the caches alone. The deterministic gates prove coalescing directly in the software data path, with no page cache in the loop. Many concurrent readers of one absent object produce exactly one remote fetch, and warm repeated reads make no remote requests. When you report a number, say which mechanism produced it.

docs.title: Measure the first useful command, not the fork
docs.text:
Fork latency is metadata work. It is the wrong headline. The metric that matters is the time from a fork request to the successful completion of a command that represents useful readiness, such as git status, rg, pytest --collect-only, or cargo metadata.

This matters because the local taxes show up here, not in the fork. A cold build costs more than native, and warm collapses toward native. A read- or transform-heavy cold build costs more than a build-heavy one. The pure-read tax is larger and less stable, because the per-file cold-fetch cost dominates when the native work is small. Editing a base file pays copy-up. metacopy=off is forced, so the first cold edit of a base file is expensive. The fork is instant. The command after it is not.

For how these local taxes stack against the cross-host reuse that pays them back, read economics and cost model. For the read and write path that sets the cold-versus-warm gap, read overlay, cache, and singleflight.

docs.title: Report what you actually proved
docs.text:
The honest measurement states its scope. Three layers carry different weight.

The regression gates are deterministic and hold on any host. They assert the ratios and counts a release rates on: singleflight suppression, warm cache hit rate, remote requests equal to distinct objects, fan-out coalescing, delta storage as base plus unique deltas, fork invariance, and checkpoint scaling with changes rather than base.

The reference-host wall clock is conditional on a named environment. The runner measures the software path against an in-memory store. It isolates FUSE, NVMe, and the object-store network. It is not the same as the service targets, and it must not be compared to those targets. Absolute latency needs the published reference environment.

The cross-host claim is open. The economic launch gate needs a second host, a real network, the coordinator on the read path, and its counters published. Until a real cross-host run exists, the cross-host edge stays a thesis.

Read this before you quote an AWC number

State the cache. Name the baseline. Pick the rung. One-host numbers are candid, and locally AWC is slower than plain OverlayFS for cold reads and for editing base files. The fan-out and delta-storage properties are proven in the software data path. The cross-host economic launch gate is not yet measured.

For what survives the loss of a host, which any cross-host measurement assumes, read the durability model.

docs.title: Metadata normalization
docs.text: AWC identifies a snapshot by a digest computed over its content. For two imports of the "same" tree to share storage, they must produce the same digest. Filesystems attach incidental metadata to every file: a modification time, an owner, a mode that drifts between checkouts. Left in, that metadata leaks into the digest and breaks deduplication. Normalization is the step that removes it before the manifests are hashed.

docs.title: The digest depends on metadata, not just bytes
docs.text:
A FILE manifest hashes more than file content. Its canonical payload carries the POSIX mode and the optional mtime. A TREE manifest hashes the mode of every entry. So two files with identical bytes but different modes or timestamps get different FILE digests, and two otherwise equal directories then differ at the tree above them.

This is deliberate. Mode and timestamp are part of what a filesystem is, and a snapshot that ignored them could not reproduce a working tree at mount time. But it creates a problem. A fresh git clone of the same revision gives every file a new mtime. Without normalization, every clone would become a distinct snapshot, and the economic premise — that most agents share the same bytes — would not hold.

docs.title: What normalization does
docs.text:
At import time, the builder captures each file's metadata, rewrites it according to a declared policy, and only then hashes the manifests. AWC ships two policies.

source-normalized rewrites metadata to the smallest set that still describes a usable source tree:

  • A regular file collapses to 0o755 if any execute bit is set, else 0o644.
  • A directory becomes 0o755. A symlink becomes 0o777.
  • File mtime is discarded.
  • setuid and setgid bits are dropped by the mode collapse.

This is the default for source repositories, where the only metadata that matters is whether a file runs. Two checkouts of the same revision — different mtimes, umask drift, a stray 0o600 — collapse to the same manifests and the same digest.

environment-preserving keeps what source-normalized throws away:

  • Mode bits are kept as captured, with setuid and setgid cleared by default.
  • File mtime is kept.

This policy exists for prepared dependency and build trees, where tools such as make and compilers read mtimes to decide what to rebuild. You trade some deduplication for metadata fidelity.

docs.title: What is normalized and what is preserved
docs.text:
Normalization touches metadata. It does not touch content or structure.

Normalized: mode (under source-normalized), mtime (under source-normalized), and ownership. Owner and group normalize to zero under both policies. In the MVP this holds by omission: the FILE manifest schema has no owner field, so UID and GID are never recorded. Ownership reappears only at mount time, through the host UID and GID mapping, not from the snapshot.

Preserved: the file content bytes, the file type, the executable decision (under source-normalized) or the full mode (under environment-preserving), the symlink target bytes, and the filenames and directory shape. Filenames are kept as raw bytes and the tree entries are sorted lexicographically, so the path structure is deterministic without any rewriting of names.

docs.title: The policy is part of the digest
docs.text:
The SNAPSHOT manifest carries the normalization_policy field inside its canonical bytes. The policy is therefore part of the snapshot digest. Two imports of the same tree under different policies produce different snapshot digests, on purpose.

This prevents an accidental cross-policy match. A source-normalized tree and an environment-preserving tree of the same files describe different logical states, because one has discarded mtimes. Deduplicating them would be wrong. Folding the policy into the digest keeps the two namespaces disjoint.

docs.title: Choosing a policy
docs.text:
You pick the policy at import time with the --normalization flag:

awcctl snapshot create --from-dir /opt/prepared/backend \
  --normalization source-normalized

The accepted values are source-normalized (the default) and environment-preserving. The control plane defaults an unspecified policy to source-normalized.

docs.title: The cost: provenance you cannot recover from metadata
docs.text:
Normalization buys determinism by discarding metadata. Once an import collapses a file to 0o644 and drops its mtime, the original mode and timestamp are gone. You cannot reconstruct who owned a file or when it was last touched by reading the snapshot.

AWC compensates by recording provenance that the metadata can no longer carry. The SNAPSHOT manifest has a source block (source type, locator, immutable revision) and a free-form labels map. The importer MUST record the normalization policy, the principal, and the source locator in provenance. The convention is to put the things normalization erases — a git revision, a build id, a base image digest — into labels, where they survive the collapse.

The split is the point. Content identity comes from normalized, deterministic metadata. Where the bytes came from comes from explicit labels. Mixing the two back into the digest would reintroduce the very drift normalization exists to remove.

docs.title: Limits and what is not implemented
docs.text:
• xattrs are not preserved in either policy. The spec says source-normalized removes unsupported xattrs and environment-preserving preserves only an allow-list. The MVP manifest schema has no xattr field, so xattrs are dropped by omission under both policies. ACLs and arbitrary xattrs are deferred. An environment-preserving import in the current build does not preserve xattrs.
  • UID and GID normalization is by omission. The spec normalizes owner to zero. The manifest carries no owner field, so this is satisfied trivially. Owner is not stored and cannot be recovered. It is applied fresh at mount time.
  • Determinism is unit-tested, not measured at scale. One test imports two directories whose files carry different modes (0o600 and 0o640) and asserts the snapshot digests are equal. There is no published measurement of deduplication ratios across real cross-host workloads.
  • Hard-link identity is not preserved. The spec permits hard links as independent entries. Link identity is not required.

docs.title: Overlay, cache, and singleflight
docs.text: AWC serves a mounted workspace from an immutable base plus a private writable delta. The read path behind that view is layered, and the layers share one purpose. They keep the common case local, and they make many readers of one cold object pay for a single remote fetch. This page explains why the layers are arranged as they are, why OverlayFS carries the writes, and what the singleflight coordinator is worth today.

docs.title: A read walks four layers
docs.text:
A read for an immutable object descends through four caches, cheapest first:

Linux page cache
  → awcd in-memory manifest cache
  → host-local object cache (NVMe)
  → object storage

Each layer answers a different question. The Linux page cache answers "did some process on this host already read these bytes?" The kernel owns it. The manifest cache answers "do I already know the structure for this path?" It holds decoded SNAPSHOT, TREE, and FILE manifests in memory, with a byte budget and a bounded negative cache. A storm of stat and readdir calls therefore never reaches the bytes. The host-local object cache answers "is the verified blob on local disk yet?" Object storage, last, is the durable source of truth.

The control plane is absent from this list on purpose. A read must not depend on PostgreSQL, on a lease check, or on an API call. Once a mount is authorized, reads and writes continue through a control-plane outage. Putting the database on the read path would make every fleet read share one scaling limit.

The layers are disposable by design. Losing every host-local cache affects performance only. It cannot lose an acknowledged snapshot. That license is what lets the cache serve an object without re-verifying it on every read. Verification happens once, at install. The daemon streams the object into a temporary file, computes SHA-256, and rejects any digest or length mismatch. Then it atomically renames the file into place. Every later read trusts that one check.

docs.title: One shared FUSE base, one writable upper
docs.text:
All workspace lower directories on a host point into one read-only FUSE filesystem mounted at /var/lib/awc/basefs. Snapshots appear under digest-qualified paths:

/var/lib/awc/basefs/tenants/<tenant-id>/snapshots/<root-digest>/

There is one FUSE daemon per host, not one per workspace. A per-workspace FUSE process would multiply daemons and file descriptors with fan-out. That is the cost AWC exists to avoid. The base is read-only. A write attempt returns EROFS. All mutation happens above it.

The writable layer is OverlayFS. A mounted workspace is the kernel's merge of the read-only lower, the snapshot inside basefs, and a private upper directory:

merged = immutable lower snapshot + private local upper

OverlayFS is the native kernel mechanism for stacking a writable tree over a read-only one. The agent therefore sees an ordinary filesystem with local read-your-writes semantics. Writes land on the local upper only. They never synchronously reach object storage. Durability comes later, at checkpoint.

The initial OverlayFS configuration disables redirect_dir, metacopy, index, and xino. The choice trades performance for simplicity. With metacopy=off, a copy-up is a full data copy, not a metadata stub. Every changed file is then fully present in the upper, which keeps checkpoint delta interpretation simple and unambiguous. The price is local. On the pilot, editing one byte of a base file cost 13 to 23 times a native edit when cold. The kernel pulls the whole file up through the FUSE lower. That tax is the cost of a delta a checkpoint can read back without reconstructing kernel metadata.

docs.title: Why singleflight
docs.text:
