The motive is the thundering-herd problem. When many agents on one host all miss the same cold object, each would open its own fetch. The object store would see N times the load for one logical read. The spec states the inverse as the goal. Many readers of one object become a single remote fetch.

The fetch coordinator is the mechanism. It keeps an in-memory table of in-flight fetches keyed by (tenant, digest). The first miss for a key becomes the leader and runs the fetch. Every later miss for the same key, while the leader is still in flight, becomes a follower. The follower awaits the leader's result.

Three design choices matter, and each answers a failure mode.

The leader runs in a detached task, not on the requester's future. A follower that cancels, or a requester that became leader and then aborted, cannot strand the fetch while other followers wait. A drop guard removes the in-flight entry on every exit, success or failure. A dead leader is detected, and a follower takes over.

Followers share one outcome through a single-slot channel. They all observe the same verified bytes, or the same error. A failed fetch retries with bounded, jittered backoff while the failure is transient. A permanent failure is negatively cached for a short, bounded interval, so a broken object does not trigger a fresh fetch on every reader.

The coordinator bounds concurrent fetches, globally and per tenant, and trips a circuit breaker when the object store is unhealthy. The daemon attaches both through the remote-control hooks. A leader must obtain an admission permit before it contacts the store. When the queued-miss ceiling is reached, the permit request is retried with the same bounded, jittered backoff as a failed fetch, and a refusal after those retries is returned to the waiting readers but is never negatively cached: the next read of that digest may spawn a fresh leader at once. This keeps a large cold fan-out from poisoning digests. A backpressure refusal is transient by contract, so caching it would fail reads across the host for the negative-cache interval. The intended effect is that one slow tenant cannot consume the host fetch budget, and a down store is failed fast rather than hammered.

docs.title: What is proven, and what is not
docs.text:
The coordinator is on the read path. Both the manifest source and the byte source route every read through it. The daemon builds both sources over one shared coordinator. This wiring is committed, not a working-tree change. A sampler folds the leader and follower counters into /metrics every five seconds.

On a single loopback host, however, the follower path is typically idle. The pilot staged 16 concurrent reads of identical content, released together by a pthread_barrier. Across six repeats the counters showed two leader fetches and zero followers. The cause is in the code. The read path checks the verified cache first. On loopback the leader's fetch finishes in roughly five to ten milliseconds. It installs the cache entry before the other readers reach the singleflight check, so they take the cache fast-path instead.

The follower path itself is proven, but by a regression test, not by live traffic. The test holds the leader's fetch open with a gated remote. That widens the window so a follower arrives while the leader is still in flight. Without that artificial gate, loopback is too fast for the window to open.

The value of singleflight is therefore cross-host. Real network round-trip widens the fetch window to tens of milliseconds, and many readers can land in it at once. That regime is not measured. The cross-host emulation with netem failed its methodology, and the pilot has no second host. The byte-amplification property itself holds on loopback, but there it is explained by the object cache plus the page cache, not by the follower path. The cross-host economic edge remains open.

docs.title: Reference-path correctness
docs.text: A mounted AWC workspace is a real Linux filesystem, not a simulation. A build or an agent that walks the tree sees a directory served by the kernel. The choice is deliberate, and it is the reason standard tools behave correctly inside a workspace (spec §6.9, §14.1).

docs.title: The kernel resolves paths
docs.text:
AWC mounts a workspace as a kernel OverlayFS. The lower layer is the shared, read-only FUSE filesystem at /var/lib/awc/basefs. The upper layer is a private writable directory. The merged view is what the agent sees (spec §8.4, §11.1, §11.3):

merged view = immutable lower snapshot + private local upper

Path resolution is the kernel's job, not the daemon's. The Linux VFS walks a path one component at a time. For each component it sends a single lookup to the filesystem that owns the parent. It handles ., .., trailing slashes, and symlink-following rules itself. AWC does not reimplement any of that.

This matters because path resolution is full of edge cases. Symlink loops, .. across mount boundaries, O_NOFOLLOW, and magic links all have defined Linux semantics. A custom virtual filesystem that took a whole path string and resolved it itself would have to reimplement every rule, and would get some of them wrong. Routing through the VFS inherits the kernel's implementation, which tools already depend on.

docs.title: The lower layer is read-only and content-addressed
docs.text:
Every snapshot lives at a digest-qualified path (spec §8.4):

/var/lib/awc/basefs/tenants/<tenant-id>/snapshots/<root-digest>/

Two properties follow from that address.

The content cannot change. A snapshot is an immutable Merkle tree (spec §6.1, §9.7). A read is strongly snapshot-consistent: every path resolves against one root digest, and the bytes cannot shift after publication (spec §14.1). The daemon returns generous entry and attribute TTLs to the kernel, because the answer is fixed for the life of the mount (spec §15.7).

The daemon answers one component at a time. The FUSE lookup takes a parent inode and a single name. It never parses a path string, and it rejects a name that contains / or NUL. To resolve a name inside a snapshot, it walks the immutable TREE manifests (spec §10.1). Symlinks are data, not directions: the stored target is returned by readlink, and the kernel decides whether to follow it (spec §9.6, §10.1).

docs.title: Writes are isolated to the upper layer
docs.text:
The basefs rejects every mutation. The FUSE layer replies EROFS to write, create, mkdir, unlink, rename, setattr, setxattr, and every other mutator. open refuses anything that is not O_RDONLY. Reported permission bits have the write bits stripped, so a stat agrees with the read-only truth. The spec requires exactly this: unsupported writes on the base filesystem MUST return EROFS, and all mutations occur in the private upper through OverlayFS (spec §8.4, §11.1).

The overlay does the write work. Copy-up, whiteouts, and directory opacity are OverlayFS semantics, interpreted by the checkpoint builder (spec §11.7). A tool that writes a file is talking to a normal writable filesystem. It does not know that some bytes came from an immutable snapshot underneath.

docs.title: The caches must agree with this path
docs.text:
Spec §6.9 defines the invariant. Every optimized read path — the page cache, the manifest cache, prefetch, singleflight — MUST be observationally equivalent to resolving the path from the immutable snapshot manifests and fetching the verified objects.

The design makes the invariant easier to keep. The kernel drives resolution, and the daemon answers each lookup from the same manifests a cold, unoptimized read would walk. A cache that served a different answer for the same path would be visible to any tool that re-stat the file. There is no second, private resolution path to drift out of agreement. For how those caches are layered, see overlay, cache, and singleflight.

docs.title: Safe traversal on ingest
docs.text: Path safety runs in the other direction too, when content is ingested. Import, checkpoint, and export open files relative to directory descriptors, not by concatenating paths. They prefer openat2 with RESOLVE_BENEATH and RESOLVE_NO_MAGICLINKS, and fall back to openat with O_NOFOLLOW where the kernel lacks openat2 (spec §8.6, §15.10). Symlinks are reported, never followed (spec §9.6). Containment is never left to the caller: where openat2 exists the kernel enforces the authorized root, and on the openat fallback the crate rechecks each component itself.

docs.title: Where the evidence stops
docs.text:
The kernel-VFS resolution just described is a local property of one host. The spec also requires that a read-only mount of the same snapshot on different hosts resolves to identical logical bytes (spec §14.1). That cross-host equivalence is specified, not yet measured. The AWC pilot is a single host, and the recorded micro-measurements are loopback-only.

The read-only basefs is exposed to root and to the awcd mount owner through FUSE AllowRoot. That grant exists so the kernel OverlayFS can resolve its lowerdir with the credentials it needs. Without it the overlay mount fails with EACCES. The grant does not widen write access, because the mutators still reply EROFS.

Spec §6.9 is a property the optimized paths must maintain, not a claim the code can prove on its own. It is checked by the digest-correctness and tool-compatibility gates, which compare mounted behaviour against the verified objects (spec §20.2).

docs.title: Scope discipline
docs.text:
AWC is narrow on purpose. The whole user surface is five operations:

snapshot → fork → mount → checkpoint → diff/export

Everything outside that list is someone else's job, or a deferred idea. This page explains why the fence sits where it does, and what changes if you move it. For the product thesis, read What is AWC. For the composition contract with the systems around it, read on.

docs.title: The narrowness is the product
docs.text:
The MVP is positioned as an agent workspace cache (spec §3.2). The word cache is the point, not a hedge:

"The object store contains durable immutable truth, while host-local state is disposable acceleration. The mounted workspace is a generated local view consisting of an immutable base and a private local delta." (spec §3.2)

That sentence rules out a family of neighbors. Spec §3.2 names them directly. The MVP is not:

  • a general distributed POSIX filesystem;
  • a block-storage service;
  • an agent orchestration framework;
  • an agent memory database;
  • a vector database;
  • a source-control replacement;
  • a build system;
  • a sandbox provider.

The design principle behind this is explicit. The system prefers "a small correct reference path over a broad feature set" and "measured workload traces over speculative optimization" (spec §3.3). A small path can be proven correct and measured. A broad feature set cannot, and it hides the economic wedge.

docs.title: Scope creep is a tracked risk
docs.text:
The spec does not treat breadth as an accident. It lists it as a first-class risk:

"Risk: The team expands into sandboxing, orchestration, build caching, semantic memory, or a general filesystem before proving the wedge." (spec §26.12)

The mitigation is operational, not aspirational:

"maintain the five-operation product surface, require economic evidence for adjacent work, and reject features that do not improve fork, first use, shared read suppression, checkpoint, or recoverability." (spec §26.12)

Read those five verbs carefully. They are the test for any new work. A feature must move one of fork, first use, shared read suppression, checkpoint, or recoverability. Otherwise it does not belong in AWC.

The launch criteria repeat the same discipline. "No launch dependency exists on semantic memory, vector retrieval, agent orchestration, shared writes, or multi-region active-active operation" (spec §29.6). Any deferred feature that ships before launch must show "a measured direct effect on the core economic gate" (spec §29.6).

docs.title: The non-goals are a contract
docs.text:
Section 4.2 is written as a MUST NOT list, not a wish (spec §4.2). The MVP MUST NOT attempt to provide:

  • concurrent writers to one workspace;
  • shared mutable POSIX semantics across hosts;
  • distributed file locking;
  • remote durability after every ordinary write(2) or fsync(2);
  • live migration of an actively writable workspace between hosts;
  • multi-region active-active writes;
  • arbitrary block-device semantics;
  • database-consistent snapshots of running database engines;
  • semantic code merging;
  • conflict-free replicated data types;
  • cross-tenant deduplication;
  • a custom Linux kernel module;
  • complete support for every POSIX filesystem feature;
  • Windows or macOS mounts;
  • a package registry, build system, or remote execution engine;
  • an agent scheduler or model gateway;
  • persistent process, memory, or VM snapshots.

Each refusal protects the cache model. Remote durability after every write would force distributed locking and coherence. That turns a disposable local view into a shared mutable filesystem. The two ideas do not compose. Picking one means rejecting the other, and AWC picks the cache.

docs.title: Why a job broker is a composition
docs.text:
Consider what a caller actually wants. It wants a durable Linux job that runs an agent, records evidence, and returns an accepted result. No single subsystem does all of that. A durable Linux-job broker is a composition of four systems:

caller -> job broker -> fleet scheduler -> sandbox
                       \-> AWC workspace

The caller owns intent and acceptance. The broker owns job reconciliation. The scheduler owns placement. The sandbox owns processes and isolation. AWC owns workspace data and publication.

AWC's job in that chain is the smallest one. It hands an agent a private directory, fetches the shared bytes once, and publishes an immutable checkpoint when the agent is done. Reconciliation, placement, process isolation, and acceptance all live outside AWC. The composition contract turns each boundary into a named requirement, from idempotency keys to read-only evaluator mounts.

The temptation is to pull the neighbors in. An agent scheduler looks close to a workspace lease. A sandbox looks close to a mount. They are not the same problem. The spec states this directly: "AWC is not itself a complete sandbox. The agent platform remains responsible for process, network, syscall, and resource isolation" (spec §16.9). A mount is not an execution boundary.

Absorbing the scheduler or the sandbox would import cgroups, command policy, network limits, and placement heuristics into the correctness kernel. The kernel would stop being small. The five verbs above would stop being the whole test.

docs.title: Deferred is not abandoned
docs.text:
Section 27 keeps a separate shelf for ideas that are real but not committed (spec §27). These are future directions, not MVP features:

  • content-defined chunking (§27.1);
  • small-object packing (§27.2);
  • learned prefetch and cache admission (§27.3);
  • package and build-cache views (§27.4);
  • live rebase (§27.5);
  • a shared mutable handoff directory (§27.6);
  • multi-region replication (§27.7);
  • virtio-fs and microVM integration (§27.8);
  • a persistent world graph, the long-term memory-substrate vision (§27.9);
  • generated storage policies (§27.10);
  • semantic diff and merge (§27.11).

The distinction between §4.2 and §27 matters. A non-goal is a refusal that defines the product. A deferred capability is a candidate that needs economic evidence before it earns a place. Content-defined chunking ships only "after fixed-chunk traces show meaningful wasted upload or storage" (spec §27.1). Package and build-cache views carry a trust boundary. "Do not mix untrusted agent artifacts with production-trusted build caches" (spec §27.4).

The persistent world graph is the clearest case. It is "the long-term memory-substrate vision, not the initial wedge" (spec §27.9). AWC stores filesystem trees. It does not store agent memory. The launch criteria forbid depending on it (spec §29.6).

docs.title: What changes if the fence moves
docs.text:
Run the counterfactual for any one guardrail.

If AWC provided shared mutable POSIX across hosts, every write(2) would need cross-host agreement. That brings distributed locks, coherence, and failure modes that disposable local state exists to avoid (spec §4.2). The cache stops being a cache.

If AWC absorbed the sandbox, it would own process isolation and command policy. A workspace bug would then become a sandbox escape. A mount would become an execution boundary. The two must stay separate, so each can be correct on its own terms (spec §4.2, §16.9).

If AWC absorbed orchestration, it would schedule agents and gate models. That work has its own correctness demands. None of it improves fork, first use, shared read suppression, checkpoint, or recoverability. The §26.12 test fails on day one.

The pattern is consistent. Each guardrail exists because the thing it forbids would widen the correctness kernel and blur the economic wedge. The fence is what keeps the five operations the whole story.

docs.title: Where this is firm and where it is open
docs.text:
The scope guardrails are normative spec text. They bind design decisions now, and the launch criteria in §29.6 enforce them at launch. They are not a description of a finished system. The current build still has gaps against the spec.

The composition boundary is a design, not a proven integration. It is a target contract, not a claim that every requirement is implemented or proven. The cross-host economic claim remains unmeasured. A second host and real shared storage are still required to turn the composition into evidence.

The deferred capabilities in §27 are specified but not implemented. Naming them here is not a commitment to build them. Each one must clear the §26.12 test on measured data before it enters the surface.

For the economic wedge that scope exists to protect, read Economics. For how AWC measures up against that wedge today, read Measuring AWC.

docs.title: Security model
docs.text:
AWC caches content that comes from repositories, generated code, and agent processes. None of that is trusted. The security model draws one line and then makes every other decision follow from it: the agent and everything it produces sit on the untrusted side; the daemon, the control plane, the signing keys, and the object-store credentials sit on the trusted side. Tenant isolation, mount tickets, mTLS, and the audit log are consequences of where that line falls, not independent features.

This page explains the why behind the design. For the exact field list of a mount ticket, see the reference; for the procedure to enroll a host, see the how-to.

docs.title: One boundary, not many
docs.text:
The spec names the two sides explicitly. The untrusted side is the agent process, repository content, generated code, filenames and symlinks, and workspace upper contents. The trusted computing base is awcd, its cache and manifest verifier, the control-plane authorization and publication path, the PostgreSQL metadata transaction, the tenant content-addressed storage (CAS) credentials, and the signing keys and host identity.

The assumption that matters is this: agent code is capable of intentionally producing adversarial directory trees, symlink ladders, deep paths, large sparse files, inode churn, and resource-exhaustion workloads. A design that treats the agent as cooperative will be wrong in the cases where being right costs the most. So awcd treats every tree as hostile before it verifies it.

docs.title: Tenant isolation by construction, not by query
docs.text:
AWC does not deduplicate content across tenants. Every object-store request is scoped to a tenant prefix, and the host cache key is the pair (tenant_id, digest), not the digest alone. A digest collision across tenants is two distinct rows. A snapshot that belongs to another tenant is reported as NotFound, never as a hit, so the store does not leak object existence, timing, size, or cache state across the boundary.

The rejected alternative is cross-tenant deduplication for the storage savings. The spec is explicit about why it is rejected: dedup creates a content-presence side channel, leaks cache state, and confuses trust domains. An attacker who can observe whether a digest already exists can infer what another tenant stored. The cost of saying no is duplicate bytes. The benefit is that no query path can accidentally cross tenants, because no such path exists.

A future deployment MAY deduplicate inside an explicitly configured organization trust domain, but only after a separate security review. The MVP does not.

docs.title: Four principals, one decision
docs.text:
Every caller reduces to the same principal shape before authorization runs. There are four kinds:

  • User — a human authenticated through OIDC.
  • ServiceAccount — a machine authenticated by a scoped, revocable signed token.
  • Host — a registered host authenticated by mutual TLS.
  • MountTicket — a short-lived signed capability, not an account.

The reason to collapse these into one type is that the authorization engine then reasons about a single question: does this principal have this permission on this project? The engine is pure logic over project role memberships, and the control plane calls it on every external request. Project roles — Viewer, Developer, Operator, Admin, Billing viewer — are project-scoped, so a principal who is an Admin in one project is nothing in another.

Capability principals (hosts, mount tickets) deliberately do not go through project RBAC. They carry a narrow delegated capability instead. A signed mount ticket grants the right to mount one snapshot on one host. It does not replace project authorization for anything else.

docs.title: Capabilities, not credentials in the sandbox
docs.text:
The model keeps long-lived secrets on the trusted side of the line. Long-lived object-store credentials MUST NOT enter agent sandboxes. What crosses the boundary is a short-lived, signed capability that the trusted side can verify on its own.

A mount ticket is the clearest example. The control plane signs it; awcd verifies it without a synchronous control-plane call. It is Ed25519-signed, audience-bound to one host, nonce-protected, and carries an expiry. It binds the tenant, the workspace, the sealed snapshot and root digest, the access mode, the fencing lease generation for a writable mount, and an allow-list of target roots. awcd refuses to mount anywhere outside those roots, and it MUST NOT accept an arbitrary host path from an untrusted sandbox.

Two implementation details matter because they remove whole classes of attack.

The signature covers the literal transmitted claim bytes, not a re-canonicalized form. Verification recomputes the signature over the exact bytes received. There is no JSON-canonicalization step to get wrong, so a sender cannot exploit parser disagreement between signer and verifier.

The signing key's debug representation is redacted. The same is true of the tenant-scoped object credential. A leaked log line must not hand over a working capability.

The object credential is the same idea applied to storage. It is a short-lived, Ed25519-signed capability scoped to one tenant prefix and a closed set of operations (get, put, delete, list), audience-bound to one host where practical. A deployment exchanges it for concrete short-lived STS or SigV4 material at the object-store gateway; that exchange is out of scope for the auth layer and lives with the CAS adapter.

docs.title: mTLS is the identity root for hosts
docs.text:
A host proves who it is with a client certificate. Internal gRPC is mutually authenticated with TLS outside AWC_DEV_MODE=1. The daemon requires an https:// endpoint and a client identity, and the control plane mirrors the rule on the server side. Host credentials are short-lived where supported and restricted by tenant prefix and operation. Renewal provisions a new credential with a fresh fingerprint while the prior one stays valid until its own expiry, so rotation is overlap-safe. A credential can be revoked before its natural expiry.

AWC_DEV_MODE=1 is the single escape hatch. In that mode the daemon and control plane relax the requirements for the service-token key, the mount-ticket seed, the ticket public key, and TLS. The switch exists for local development and tests, not for deployment. Nothing else disables mTLS.

docs.title: Why awcd is privileged but not a sandbox
docs.text:
AWC is not a complete sandbox. The agent platform keeps responsibility for process, network, syscall, and resource isolation. AWC's job is narrower: ensure a workspace mount exposes only the authorized snapshot and its private upper, that bind targets stay inside allow-listed roots, that symlinks cannot cause privileged host traversal by awcd, that agent code cannot write the shared base FUSE mount or the host CAS cache, and that one workspace cannot reach another workspace's upper directory.

awcd is privileged because it must. It performs OverlayFS and FUSE mounts and writes cgroup files to pause and resume execution for checkpointing. The systemd unit runs it as the unprivileged awc user and bounds it to a minimal capability set: CAP_SYS_ADMIN, CAP_DAC_READ_SEARCH, CAP_DAC_OVERRIDE, CAP_CHOWN, and CAP_FOWNER (the awcd.service unit). NoNewPrivileges, a @system-service plus @mount syscall filter, MemoryDenyWriteExecute, and a closed device policy that admits only /dev/fuse round out the hardening.

Be honest about what that hardening is not. awcd is not network-isolated. The unit sets RestrictAddressFamilies=AF_UNIX AF_INET, because the daemon must reach the control plane and the object store. If you need egress restrictions, enforce them at the network layer around the host, not in the unit.

The unit also deliberately omits the systemd directives that create a private mount namespace (ProtectSystem=, ProtectHome=, PrivateTmp= and related). awcd publishes its FUSE and OverlayFS mounts into the host namespace so that clients, the worker, and the acceptance checks can see them. A private namespace hid awcd's own mounts from the host during the pilot, so the directives were removed. The trade is real: awcd runs in the host mount namespace by design, and the capability set above is what bounds it there.

docs.title: The threat: one compromised agent
docs.text:
Walk through what an attacker who compromises one agent process can and cannot do.

They hold that workspace's writer lease, if it is mounted READ_WRITE. They can write the private upper. They cannot read another tenant. Object-store requests are tenant-prefixed, the cache key includes the tenant, and a cross-tenant snapshot is NotFound. They cannot reach another workspace's upper directory.

They cannot forge a checkpoint for a workspace they do not hold the lease for. Checkpoint publication MUST include the current lease generation and the expected workspace version, and at most one unexpired lease generation may publish for a workspace. The mount ticket stamps the fencing generation into the signed claims, so a stale writer's generation is rejected at publication. See fencing and split-brain for how the generation defeats a split-brain writer.

They cannot redirect a mount at an arbitrary host path. The ticket's target policy allow-lists the roots, and awcd enforces the prefix match. A path that shares a prefix string but is not beneath a root — /srv/awc/runsX under root /srv/awc/runs — is rejected.

They cannot poison a trusted build namespace by uploading content with a known digest label. Content addressing alone is not sufficient. Every object is verified on ingest or first trusted use, object keys are immutable, conditional creation prevents overwriting a digest, and the object kind is part of the digest domain. Trusted and untrusted producer classes MAY use separate CAS trust namespaces, and production build artifacts MUST NOT trust content solely because an untrusted agent uploaded the same digest label.

docs.title: Audit records what changed, never what was stored
docs.text:
The control plane records immutable audit events for privileged actions: snapshot publication and deletion, workspace creation, fork and deletion, lease acquisition, revocation and expiration, mount-ticket issuance, mount and unmount, checkpoint publication, export, retention-policy changes, host registration and revocation, recovery actions, and authorization failures.

The contract on contents is strict. An audit event records who acted, on what resource, from what state to what state, and whether it succeeded. It MUST NOT contain object contents, byte payloads, manifest bodies, file names from user data, credentials, tokens, or keys. Identifiers, certificate fingerprints, digests, and enum-valued verdicts are not secrets and are recorded for accountability. The action vocabulary uses a <resource>.<verb> shape — checkpoint.publish, host.revoke, signing_key.rotate, object_credential.issue — so the log sorts and greps by resource family.

docs.title: Limits and what is not wired yet
docs.text:
The security objectives are specified in full. Not all of them are exercised in the current build to the same degree.

  • The audit vocabulary is live for checkpoint publication, retention and TTL, garbage collection, host lifecycle, signing-key and object-credential rotation, and import and snapshot lifecycle. The categories for lease, mount session, export, recovery, and authorization failures are specified but their owning service layers have not been wired yet. Of these, only lease, mount_session, and export carry reserved resource_type constants; recovery and authorization-failure auditing are named in the spec but have no reserved constant yet.
  • mTLS enforcement is implemented for the control channel. Customer-managed keys per tenant and encrypted host volumes are deployment choices, not build facts, and are not verified here.
  • The sandbox-isolation guarantees are design requirements on awcd. This page does not re-verify them with an adversarial test suite; the tracked security tests are the home for that work.
  • AWC_DEV_MODE=1 disables the credential and TLS requirements described above. Never run with it set outside a local development machine.

docs.title: What is AWC
docs.text: Agent Workspace Cache (AWC) is an object-storage-backed, content-addressed workspace system for high-fan-out coding-agent fleets. You prepare one Linux environment and fork thousands of private workspaces from it. Each agent reads the shared bytes once and stores only its own changes.

docs.title: The problem AWC solves
docs.text:
A conventional coding-agent fleet gives each agent its own clone, volume, or sandbox snapshot. When hundreds of agents touch the same codebase, the fleet repeats the same work over and over:

  • copies identical repository bytes;
  • downloads identical packages;
  • reserves volumes for dormant branches;
  • retains full images for tiny changes.

The logical workload grows with the number of agent hypotheses. The physical data does not. Most agents share almost everything.

AWC makes the storage match the workload. Physical storage becomes unique immutable base content, plus unique branch deltas, plus cache overhead — not workspace count times full workspace size. For reads, the goal is that N agents requesting the same object on one cache domain cause one remote fetch and N local readers.

docs.title: The core promise
docs.text:
Prepare once, fork many, read common bytes once, and store only unique changes.

Four mechanisms carry this: immutable snapshots, constant-time logical forks, a shared host-local cache that coalesces concurrent reads, and explicit durable checkpoints.

docs.title: The five primitives
docs.text:
The whole user surface is five operations:

snapshot → fork → mount → checkpoint → diff/export

Each primitive exists to make one resource cheap:

  • snapshot encodes a prepared environment as a Merkle tree in a content-addressed store. You pay the byte cost once, at import.
  • fork creates only metadata. It references an existing snapshot plus an empty private delta. Fork cost must stay independent of snapshot size.
  • mount redeems a ticket into an ordinary Linux directory, with one exclusive writer lease. The agent sees normal paths and uses normal tools.
  • checkpoint quiesces the writer, converts the local delta into immutable objects, and advances the workspace head atomically. Writes before a checkpoint are local, not remotely durable.
  • diff and export compare snapshots by a Merkle-tree walk and ship changed bytes as a patch bundle, tar, or JSON.

Consider what changes if you alter a primitive. If fork copied bytes, fork would scale with workspace size, and you would be back to per-agent clones. If every write(2) were remotely durable, AWC would be a distributed filesystem. That brings distributed locking and coherence. The five-primitive surface is a deliberate cut. It covers the agent loop and nothing more.

docs.title: Who AWC is for
docs.text:
AWC serves fleets whose workload fits a narrow contract:

  • mostly immutable, reusable base state;
  • a private writable delta much smaller than the base;
  • at most one active writer per workspace;
  • explicit checkpoints as an acceptable durability boundary;
  • a minority of workspaces mounted at once;
  • heavy read overlap across agents on the same project;
  • Linux tools that expect normal filesystem paths.

If you need synchronous remote durability for every write, multi-host shared writes, or database-grade distributed locking, you sit outside the MVP contract.

docs.title: What AWC is not
docs.text:
AWC is an agent workspace cache, not a general filesystem or a platform layer. The MVP explicitly does not provide:

  • concurrent writers to one workspace;
  • shared mutable POSIX semantics across hosts;
  • distributed file locking;
  • remote durability after every ordinary write;
  • live migration of an active writer;
  • a build system, package registry, or remote execution engine;
  • an agent scheduler or model gateway;
  • Windows or macOS mounts;
  • a custom Linux kernel module.

The word cache is the point. The object store holds durable immutable truth. Host-local state is disposable acceleration. Losing it costs performance, never recoverability.

Adjacent features are deferred, not committed. Content-defined chunking, learned prefetch, package and build-cache views, live rebase, a shared mutable handoff directory, multi-region replication, and semantic diff and merge are future directions. Scope creep is a tracked risk. The team must keep the five-operation surface and demand economic evidence for adjacent work.

docs.title: The trade, stated honestly
docs.text:
AWC trades local simplicity for cross-host byte reuse. On one host, plain copy-on-write is hard to beat. The distinguishing value of AWC is the cross-host regime. Many hosts share one content-addressed base in the object store. The comparison is against a network copy that a local overlay cannot serve.

The MVP must cut remote workspace I/O per agent task, storage per workspace, or time to a prepared workspace by a clear margin. The decisive cross-host advantage is architecturally intended but not yet measured end to end. It needs a second host. Treat the cross-host economics as an open question, not a proven result.

For the how and the exact facts, read the tutorials, the how-to guides, and the reference. For the deeper why, continue to architecture, economics, and scope discipline.

docs.title: Back up and restore PostgreSQL
docs.text:
PostgreSQL holds the control-plane metadata: workspaces, leases, snapshots, mount tickets, and audit events (spec §8.7). The object store holds the immutable content-addressed bytes (spec §3.2). This runbook backs up the metadata database. Back up the object store separately for the content. See Handle object-store corruption.

Spec reference

This runbook follows spec §25.5 (PostgreSQL failover and restore runbook) and spec §17.6 (database failure). The schema is spec §8.7. Migrations MUST be backward-compatible during rolling deploys (spec §21.8).

AWC ships no backup tool

AWC does not include a backup or restore utility. You run PostgreSQL's own tooling: pg_dump, pg_basebackup, or a managed equivalent. The spec requires automated failover and point-in-time recovery (PITR) in production (spec §17.6).

docs.title: Detect
docs.text:
Run this runbook on any of these triggers:

  • Your scheduled backup cadence. The spec requires PITR in production, so the WAL archive runs continuously (spec §17.6). Take a new base backup on a fixed schedule so the WAL archive stays replayable in a reasonable time.
  • Before an upgrade or destructive maintenance on the database host. See Upgrade a deployment.
  • After a database failure. The restore path is part of Recover from a PostgreSQL failover.

docs.title: Back up the database
docs.text:
1. Take a consistent backup. Choose one of the two methods below.

    Logical (pg_dump)Physical (base backup + WAL)

    A logical dump is one transactional snapshot of the schema and data. It is consistent as of the moment pg_dump starts. It does not give PITR.

    # One consistent snapshot of the metadata database (spec §8.7).
pg_dump --format=custom --no-owner --no-privileges \
  "$DATABASE_URL" \
  -f "awc-$(date -u +%Y%m%dT%H%M%SZ).dump"

    Use this for a nightly copy, a restore drill, or a move between PostgreSQL major versions.

    A physical backup plus a WAL archive gives PITR. This is the method the spec requires for production (spec §17.6).

    # Base backup from the primary or a streaming replica.
pg_basebackup -D /var/backups/awc/base -Xs -P -c fast \
  -h "$PGHOST" -U repl

    Keep a continuous WAL archive. In postgresql.conf:

    archive_mode = on
archive_command = 'aws s3 cp --quiet %p s3://awc-wal-archive/%f'

  2. Copy the backup off the database host. Store it in a separate failure domain: another host, another rack, or object storage. Never leave the only copy on the database host. A backup that dies with the primary is not a backup.

docs.title: Restore to a target instance
docs.text:
1. Stop the AWC services that connect to the database. Stop awc-control and awc-worker so they do not reconnect mid-restore. awc-control reads DATABASE_URL at startup and refuses to run without it.

  2. Restore the backup to a fresh target instance. Use the method that matches your backup.

    Logical restore (pg_restore)Physical restore with PITR

    Restore into an empty database. Do not restore over a live database.

    createdb -T template0 awc_restored
pg_restore --dbname awc_restored --no-owner --no-privileges \
  awc-YYYYMMDDTHHMMSSZ.dump

    If you must reload an existing database, add --clean --if-exists so pg_restore drops each object before it recreates it.

    Replay WAL to a target time, then promote.

    # 1. Stop the target PostgreSQL. Clear its data directory.
# 2. Copy the base backup into the data directory.
# 3. Start PostgreSQL. It replays the WAL archive to the target, then
#    promotes.

    Set the recovery target in postgresql.auto.conf:

    restore_command = 'aws s3 cp --quiet s3://awc-wal-archive/%f %p'
recovery_target_time = '2026-08-12 14:30:00+00'
recovery_target_action = 'promote'

    Place an empty recovery.signal file in the data directory. Do not create standby.signal for a restore you intend to promote. Do not run AWC against a primary that is still replaying WAL (spec §25.5 step 2).

  3. Point AWC at the new primary. Set DATABASE_URL to the target connection string. Restart awc-control, then awc-worker.

  4. Confirm migrations applied. Both awc-control and awc-worker run every pending migration on startup through the embedded MIGRATOR. sqlx records each applied migration in the _sqlx_migrations table. The set is forward-only. Never revert a migration; a faulty migration is fixed by a forward corrective migration (spec §21.8).

  5. Reconcile metadata against the object store. After the restore, compare the five records the spec requires: published snapshot records, workspace versions, audit events, object-store snapshot manifests, and host-reported mount sessions (spec §17.6). See the Verify steps below.

docs.title: Verify
docs.text:
Confirm the restore when all of these hold:

  • _sqlx_migrations shows the full set applied, with no new failures, and it matches your other environments.

    SELECT version, success FROM _sqlx_migrations ORDER BY version;

  • Row counts match the source for the metadata tables.

    SELECT COUNT(*) AS workspaces     FROM workspaces;
SELECT COUNT(*) AS snapshots      FROM snapshots;
SELECT COUNT(*) AS leases         FROM workspace_leases;
SELECT COUNT(*) AS mount_sessions FROM mount_sessions;
SELECT COUNT(*) AS audit_events   FROM audit_events;
SELECT COUNT(*) AS idempotency    FROM idempotency_keys;

  • No workspace points at a missing snapshot. This count MUST be zero.

    SELECT COUNT(*) AS dangling_heads
FROM workspaces w
LEFT JOIN snapshots s ON s.id = w.head_snapshot_id
WHERE s.id IS NULL;

  • Every snapshots.manifest_digest resolves to an object in the object store. The object store is the source of truth for content (spec §3.2). A missing manifest is an object-store problem; see Handle object-store corruption.

  • An idempotency replay returns the committed result (spec §17.2). A replay with the same key that returns a different result signals divergence.
  • awc-control starts and logs both listeners: REST on AWC_CONTROL_LISTEN and gRPC on AWC_CONTROL_GRPC_LISTEN.
  • awc_lease_renewal_failures_total and awc_api_errors_total return to baseline.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text:
State the data risk plainly:

  • A logical backup is consistent as of the moment it started. Every metadata mutation after that is absent from the dump. PITR closes that gap.
  • A point-in-time restore loses every metadata mutation after the target time. That includes workspace head advances, leases, mount tickets, and audit events (spec §17.6). AWC cannot rebuild those rows.
  • The system never reconstructs a head from the object store. Orphan snapshot objects after a restore are immutable candidates, not inferred publications (spec §17.6). Leave them for garbage collection (GC).
  • This procedure does not back up content. The object store holds the immutable bytes (spec §3.2, §8.8). Back it up under its own policy. A restored database that points at missing objects is a degraded snapshot, not a recovered one.
  • Host writes are untouched by a database restore. Warm reads and local writes continue without the control plane (spec §17.5). See Recover from host loss if a host was also lost.

docs.title: Current scope
docs.text:
The build consumes PostgreSQL but does not manage it. Be aware of these gaps:

  • AWC ships no backup, restore, or failover tooling. Provision PITR and failover in your Postgres layer, for example with Patroni or a managed Postgres with a WAL archive. AWC consumes the primary through DATABASE_URL only (spec §17.6).
  • Migrations run automatically on startup. Both awc-control and awc-worker apply pending migrations through MIGRATOR. There is no separate migrate subcommand and no dry run. The set is forward-only and additive.
  • The connection pool is fixed at 16. awc-control and awc-worker each open at most 16 PostgreSQL connections. Size the new primary's connection budget for both, plus your job concurrency.
  • No database-specific metric exists. There is no awc_db or migration gauge in awc-telemetry. Confirm a restore from the verification queries above and from awc_lease_renewal_failures_total.

When the restore is part of a wider database failure, follow Recover from a PostgreSQL failover. When the object store itself is the failed dependency, follow Recover from an object-store outage.

docs.title: Build and package
docs.text: The packaging scripts build, sign, package, install, enroll, drain, and roll back AWC for a VM deployment. They work alongside the systemd units (see systemd units).

docs.title: Scripts
docs.text: Script What it does build-release.sh cargo build --release --locked for awcd, awc-worker, awc-control, awcctl with production FUSE and S3 features; stages stripped binaries under dist/staging/awc-<target>/bin/ sign.sh <staging-dir> Writes SHA256SUMS and a detached signature. Uses cosign sign-blob if available, otherwise gpg --detach-sign. Fails loudly if neither signer is present package.sh Runs the full pipeline: build, stage units, scripts, defaults, migrations, offline docs, golden vectors, and SBOM, sign, then dist/awc-<version>-<target>.tar.gz install.sh Idempotent, upgrade-safe install: versioned /opt/awc/versions/<v> with a current symlink, the awc system user, units, the health check, and default config (only if absent). Run as root enroll.sh Local host enrollment: writes /etc/awc/awcd.toml and awcd.env, creates state dirs, mints a host id and a placeholder control endpoint (provision mTLS identity separately) drain.sh [awcd\|worker\|control\|all] Graceful drain (SIGTERM; awcd reconciles live sessions), bounded by MAX_WAIT rollback.sh [version] Repoints /opt/awc/current to a prior version, reloads systemd, restarts active services awc-health-check.sh Minimal HTTP probe used by the units' ExecStartPost; installed to /usr/lib/awc/awc-health-check

docs.title: Build and package
docs.text:
packaging/package.sh
# -> dist/awc-<version>-<target>.tar.gz
#    dist/SHA256SUMS{,.bundle|.gpg}       (copied next to the tarball)
#    dist/staging/awc-<target>/{bin,lib/systemd/system,lib/awc,share/awc,install.sh,...,SHA256SUMS,.bundle|.gpg}

Override the target with TARGET=<triple>. The version is read from the workspace Cargo.toml. Signing uses cosign if it is on PATH, otherwise gpg.

docs.title: What the tarball carries besides binaries
docs.text:
Under share/awc/ in the tarball:

  • migrations/ — the control-plane PostgreSQL migrations (crates/awc-db/migrations/), so an offline host can inspect or replay the schema.
  • docs/ — kernel-compatibility.md, on-disk-format.md, golden-vectors.md, and upgrade.md, for offline reference.
  • golden-vectors/golden_vectors.json — the golden manifest vectors used by CI, for offline conformance checks.
  • sbom.spdx.json — an SPDX JSON SBOM of the repository, produced with syft.

docs.title: SBOM
docs.text:
package.sh scans with syft when it is on PATH. Without syft it writes share/awc/sbom.MISSING and continues. Set AWC_REQUIRE_SBOM=1 to make a missing SBOM fail the build instead. Release builds (the release workflow) always set it.

The SBOM lands inside the tarball before sign.sh runs, so SHA256SUMS covers it.

docs.title: Install and enroll (on the VM, as root)
docs.text:
tar xzf awc-<version>-<target>.tar.gz
cd awc-<target>
./install.sh
./enroll.sh --control-endpoint https://control.example.invalid
systemctl enable --now awcd

install.sh is safe to re-run for upgrades. It never overwrites /etc/awc/* and prunes to the last KEEP_VERSIONS (default 3), so rollback is always possible. See Upgrade a deployment.

docs.title: Verify a package
docs.text:
sha256sum -c SHA256SUMS
# cosign: cosign verify-blob --bundle SHA256SUMS.bundle SHA256SUMS
# gpg:    gpg --verify SHA256SUMS.gpg SHA256SUMS

docs.title: Layout on the host
docs.text:
/opt/awc/versions/<v>/{bin,lib/systemd/system,lib/awc,share/awc/{migrations,docs,golden-vectors}}
/opt/awc/current                        -> versions/<v>
/usr/bin/{awcd,awc-worker,awc-control,awcctl}
/usr/lib/awc/awc-health-check
/etc/systemd/system/{awcd,awc-worker,awc-control}.service
/etc/awc/{awcd.toml,awcd.env,worker.env,control.env}
/var/lib/awc/{basefs,cache,workspaces,binds}   (awc:awc, 0750)
/var/cache/awc  /var/log/awc                    (awc:awc)

See systemd units for capability boundaries, hardening, and the drain, restart, and rollback semantics.

docs.title: Cut a release
docs.text:
Pushing a v* tag triggers the release workflow. It re-runs the test gates, packages with AWC_REQUIRE_SBOM=1, signs the tarball keyless with cosign (OIDC; the certificate and rekor entry land in <tarball>.bundle), and creates a GitHub release with the tarball, SHA256SUMS, its bundle, the tarball bundle, the SBOM, and the cargo deny log. Release notes come from the matching section of CHANGELOG.md.

Steps:

  1. Update CHANGELOG.md (Keep a Changelog format) and wait for green CI on main.
  2. Push a rehearsal tag: git tag v0.1.0-rc1 && git push origin v0.1.0-rc1. An -rc* tag reuses the notes of the version it rehearses.
  3. Verify the release assets and the signature:
cosign verify-blob --bundle awc-<version>-<target>.tar.gz.bundle \
  awc-<version>-<target>.tar.gz \
  --certificate-identity-regexp '^https://github.com/nibzard/awc/' \
  --certificate-oidc-issuer https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com

The issuer is GitHub's OIDC token issuer; the identity is the workflow ref inside this repository. 4. Delete the rehearsal release and tag, then tag v0.1.0 on the same commit and push it.

The Postgres and minio service jobs from CI are not repeated in the release workflow: the tag points at a commit that already passed them on push.

docs.title: Checkpoint a workspace
docs.text:
Publish the writes of a mounted workspace as a new immutable snapshot. A checkpoint freezes writes, scans the OverlayFS upper delta, uploads new objects, and atomically advances the workspace head.

The new snapshot is durable only after the control plane publishes the new head in one transaction. Until then, local writes are not remotely durable.

Before you start: the workspace MUST be mounted read-write. You MUST hold the mount session id (the session field from awcctl workspace mount), not the workspace id. The checkpoint reaches the local host daemon over its Unix socket (--host-socket, default /run/awcd/awcd.sock). Set --control-endpoint (or AWC_CONTROL_ENDPOINT) for the status check in step 5.

  1. Capture the mount session id.

    awcctl workspace mount ws_01J... --target /workspace

    Read the session field from the output. awcctl workspace checkpoint takes this session id, not the workspace id.

  2. Choose a checkpoint mode. Pick one.

    Quiesced (default)Cooperative

    The only mode advertised as application-consistent. The daemon freezes the mount's execution cgroup, runs syncfs, scans a stable delta, publishes, then resumes the writer.

    The cgroup MUST be sealed into the mount ticket at mount time. A mount that has no cgroup is rejected (see the candid note below) with:

    quiesced checkpoint requires a ticket-sealed execution cgroup

    Use when the integration cannot be frozen. You assert that all writes have stopped before you run the command. The daemon skips the freeze but still runs syncfs. The result is consistent only if your assertion is true. The mode is recorded in provenance, and a cooperative checkpoint MUST NOT be labeled quiesced.

  3. Run the checkpoint. Pass the session id, the mode, and a message.

    awcctl workspace checkpoint sess_01J... \
  --mode cooperative \
  --message "retry-investigation-17 step 3" \
  --label agent_run=run_991 \
  --idempotency-key cp-run991-3

    The call goes to the local host daemon, which drives the full validate, quiesce, construct, upload, publish, and cleanup pipeline.

  4. Capture the new snapshot id and version. The result prints the snapshot, digest, and version fields.

    snapshot      snap_01J...
digest        sha256:...
version       4

    Add --output json to capture the id in a script. The snapshot is durable only once this result returns.

  5. Confirm the workspace head advanced. Run status against the workspace id.

    awcctl workspace status ws_01J...

    The head field now equals the new snapshot id and version incremented by one. If head did not change, the publish was rejected. The workspace head references only the complete prior or the complete new snapshot.

Idempotency key is required

The host daemon rejects a checkpoint that has an empty idempotency key. Pass --idempotency-key, or set AWC_IDEMPOTENCY_KEY. A retry with the same key returns the already-published snapshot instead of duplicating work.

Current build: CLI mounts have no cgroup

awcctl workspace mount issues a ticket with execution_cgroup unset. A quiesced checkpoint (the default) on a CLI-mounted workspace then fails with the string above. An integration that runs the writer under a managed cgroup seals that cgroup into the ticket at mount time. The local-development smoke therefore runs --mode cooperative (the local-dev smoke).

docs.title: Contribute to AWC
docs.text:
The implementation backlog in to-do.json is the canonical work queue. This guide builds the workspace, picks a task, writes code to the repo style, and runs the gate before you propose the change.

Spec reference

The reference technology choices, repo layout, and build are spec §22.1, §22.3, and §22.11.

  1. Build the workspace.

    make build

    make build runs cargo build --workspace --all-targets. The toolchain is Rust 1.94.0, pinned by rust-toolchain.toml with rustfmt and clippy. Install cargo-deny for the dependency audit:

    cargo install cargo-deny

  2. Read the backlog contract.

    AGENTS.md defines how project work runs. to-do.json is the single source of truth for implementation work, and to-do.schema.json validates it. The backlog is implementation-only. Read every document listed under source_files before you start.

  3. Pick the next task.

    Choose the lowest-numbered priority task with status todo, breaking ties by lexicographic id:

    jq '.tasks | map(select(.status == "todo")) | sort_by(.priority, .id) | .[0]' to-do.json

    Check the task depends_on list. Every dependency MUST be done before you start. Set the task to doing and update updated_at before you write code.

  4. Write code to the repo style.

    • Run make fmt to format in place. The config is edition = "2021" and max_width = 100.
    • Keep new crates #![forbid(unsafe_code)]. The manifest library MUST expose no unsafe deserialization path for untrusted objects (spec §22.4).
    • Clippy warnings are errors. Run make lint (clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings).
    • All components MUST consume the same versioned manifest library and test vectors (spec §22.2).

  5. Write docs in Simplified Technical English.

    Prose and doc pages follow docs/.style-guide.md. Keep sentences under 20 words. Spell out Latin abbreviations. The forbidden-words list applies to every page, including this one.

  6. Run the CI gate.

    make ci

    make ci is fmt-check plus lint plus test plus deny. GitHub Actions runs the same checks, then adds a production-feature compile and the service-backed suites (make ci-pg, make ci-s3). See run the test suite for those suites.

  7. Propose the change.

    Write commits in the conventional style the history already uses, for example fix(awc-fuse): permit root on the read-only basefs FUSE mount. When the task is complete, set it to done, update updated_at, and record paths in files or outcomes in details. Keep to-do.json at two-space indentation and valid against the schema. Open a pull request. The CI workflow MUST pass before merge.

Scope discipline

AWC is an agent workspace cache: snapshot → fork → mount → checkpoint → diff/export. Do not add a general filesystem, a sandbox, an agent scheduler, or a build cache (spec §3.2, §4.2, §26.12). Work that is deferred, not committed, is listed in spec §27.

docs.title: Deploy on Kubernetes
docs.text: The AWC Helm chart contains the Kubernetes deployment manifests for AWC. It provides control and worker Deployments, a privileged awcd DaemonSet, hostPath storage, RBAC, a NetworkPolicy, PodDisruptionBudgets, health probes, secret integration, and controlled node-drain behavior.

docs.title: Components
docs.text: Resource Purpose Default awcd DaemonSet privileged per-node mount/cache daemon; hostPath basefs/cache/upper volumes and /dev/fuse; health probes on /healthz, /readyz enabled awc-worker Deployment stateless background worker draining the PostgreSQL job queue; env from Secrets enabled, replicas=2 awc-control Deployment and Service REST API and mTLS internal gRPC API enabled Secrets database-url and object-store keys; placeholder unless *.existingSecret is set created ConfigMap awcd.toml and awcd.env created RBAC awcd ClusterRole (read-only Node and Pod) and binding created NetworkPolicy default-deny ingress per pod; DNS and dependency egress created PodDisruptionBudgets protect worker (and control when enabled) during voluntary disruption created

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
# Validate without a cluster:
helm lint deploy/helm/awc
helm template deploy/helm/awc

# Render with the control plane enabled:
helm template deploy/helm/awc --set control.enabled=true

# Install (provide real secrets out-of-band):
kubectl create secret generic awc-database \
  --from-literal=database-url='postgres://awc:REAL@postgres:5432/awc'
kubectl create secret generic awc-objectstore \
  --from-literal=endpoint=https://objects.example --from-literal=bucket=awc-cas \
  --from-literal=access-key-id=AKID --from-literal=secret-access-key=SECRET
helm install awc deploy/helm/awc \
  --set database.existingSecret=awc-database \
  --set objectStore.existingSecret=awc-objectstore

docs.title: Storage
docs.text: awcd mounts hostPath volumes under awcd.hostPathRoot (default /var/lib/awc): basefs, cache, workspaces, and binds, plus /run/awcd and /dev/fuse. The in-container paths match the mounted awcd config. Use a node-local disk sized for your workload. The chart does not provision that disk. Ensure the hostPath root is on a suitably sized local volume before you schedule agents.

docs.title: Probes and drain
docs.text:
• awcd exposes /healthz (liveness) and /readyz (readiness) on its loopback health port. The DaemonSet probes them. On SIGTERM, awcd reconciles sessions and preserves uppers. terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 60 bounds it.
  • Controlled node drain: cordon the node to stop new agent pods, then drain. The awcd pod receives SIGTERM and reconciles. Worker and control pods are protected by their PDBs, so a drain respects minAvailable. See Drain and restart a host.

docs.title: Secrets
docs.text: No real secret is templated. The chart creates placeholder Secrets only when no existingSecret is named. Replace those with provisioned Secrets in any real deployment. See Rotate credentials.

docs.title: Current scope
docs.text:
• Build images with packaging/build-release.sh. Release binaries include the S3 transports and awcd's real FUSE base filesystem. See Build and package.
  • Provision the internal TLS and credential Secrets documented in values.yaml before installation. The chart never generates production credentials.
  • PostgreSQL is external (managed or operator-provided). The chart consumes DATABASE_URL from a Secret. For a local cluster, reuse the PostgreSQL from Run locally.
  • AWC has no published OCI image yet. Set image.registry, image.repository, and image.tag to images you build with the packaging scripts.

docs.title: Deploy on Proxmox VE
docs.text:
This is the supported first-test topology for AWC: one Debian 12 or Ubuntu 24.04 KVM VM, with PostgreSQL in Docker, the AWC binaries running natively under systemd, and the object store either loopback MinIO (default) or a Backblaze B2 bucket. Everything local binds to loopback. Plain HTTP for the VM-internal services is deliberate for this local pilot; do not expose its ports outside the VM. The B2 path is HTTPS end to end.

The pilot exercises the real product path: S3-compatible CAS, shared read-only FUSE base filesystem, per-workspace OverlayFS, signed mount tickets, writer leases, cooperative checkpoints, and remount from the published head.

docs.title: Scope and security boundary
docs.text:
Included:

  • One KVM VM and one awcd host identity.
  • PostgreSQL 16 on 127.0.0.1 via Docker Compose, plus MinIO on 127.0.0.1 (default) or a Backblaze B2 bucket reached over HTTPS.
  • awc-control, awc-worker, and awcd as native systemd services.
  • Plain HTTP for REST, internal gRPC, and MinIO inside the VM.
  • Fixed development identity and signing key selected by AWC_DEV_MODE=1.
  • Cooperative checkpoints. They do not require an execution cgroup.

Deferred for a later deployment:

  • HTTPS/mTLS for the control plane, OIDC, S3 providers other than the supported B2 option, multi-host scheduling, HA, Kubernetes, sandbox namespace injection, and quiesced checkpoints.

AWC_DEV_MODE=1 is not a production security mode. Keep ports 5432, 8080, 8081, 9000, and 9001 on loopback and restrict SSH access to the VM.

docs.title: VM requirements
docs.text:
Use a KVM VM, not an unprivileged LXC container. Recommended minimums are 4 vCPUs, 8 GiB RAM, and an 80 GiB system disk. The guest needs:

  • Linux kernel 6.1 or newer with cgroup v2, FUSE, and OverlayFS.
  • ext4 or xfs for /var/lib/awc.
  • /dev/fuse, fuse3, findmnt, Docker Engine, and Docker Compose v2.
  • Internet access during installation for packages and container images.

For the first deployment, keep AWC on the system disk. A passed-through cache disk is supported only after you explicitly format it and mount it at /var/lib/awc before installation; the bootstrap never formats disks.

docs.title: 1. Build the package
docs.text:
On a Linux build host with Rust, libfuse3-dev, pkg-config, and signing tools:

packaging/package.sh

The result is dist/awc-<version>-<target>.tar.gz. Copy the tarball and guest-bootstrap.sh to the VM, for example with scp.

docs.title: 2. Create the VM
docs.text:
On the Proxmox node, download or reuse a Debian 12 cloud image and run:

VMID=9001 \
NAME=awc-pilot \
BRIDGE=vmbr0 \
SSHKEYS=/root/.ssh/authorized_keys \
SYSTEM_DISK=80G \
bash deploy/proxmox/provision-vm.sh

The script configures DHCP, the QEMU guest agent channel, a cloud-init drive, virtio networking, and an 80 GiB default disk. Discover the address with:

qm guest cmd 9001 network-get-interfaces

If the guest agent has not started yet, use qm terminal 9001 or inspect DHCP.

docs.title: 3. Prepare the guest
docs.text:
Inside the VM, install Docker Engine and the Compose v2 plugin using Docker's Debian/Ubuntu instructions. Verify the exact command AWC uses:

docker info
docker compose version
test -e /dev/fuse
findmnt -n -o FSTYPE /sys/fs/cgroup

The last command should report cgroup2.

docs.title: 4. Install and configure the local pilot
docs.text:
Run the bootstrap against the copied package:

sudo LOCAL_PILOT=1 \
  CONTROL_ENDPOINT=http://127.0.0.1:8081 \
  PACKAGE_FILE=/tmp/awc-0.1.0-x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu.tar.gz \
  bash /tmp/guest-bootstrap.sh

CONTROL_ENDPOINT is required by the common bootstrap interface; local-pilot mode writes the loopback endpoint shown above. The configurator:

  1. Runs awc-pilot-preflight for kernel, cgroup, filesystem, xattr, FUSE, OverlayFS, and free-space compatibility.
  2. Creates /opt/awc-pilot and random local database, MinIO, and token secrets.
  3. Starts PostgreSQL (and MinIO on loopback, creating awc-cas, unless AWC_OBJECT_STORE=b2 selects the remote bucket instead).
  4. Writes mutually consistent control, worker, daemon, bind-root, and CAS config.
  5. Starts awc-control, applies the schema, and seeds the fixed pilot identity.
  6. Starts awc-worker and awcd and waits for a real FUSE base mount.
  7. Writes root-readable CLI settings to /opt/awc-pilot/awcctl.env.

It is safe to rerun: Docker volumes and generated secrets are retained.

docs.title: Using Backblaze B2 instead of local MinIO
docs.text:
The pilot can store its CAS in a Backblaze B2 bucket so object data survives VM disposal and leaves the host disk. B2 speaks the S3 API over HTTPS only; AWC's transport signs with SigV4 and validates the webpki CA set, so no extra trust configuration is needed.

One-time operator setup in the B2 console:

  1. Create a private bucket (the pilot default is awc-test in eu-central-003).
  2. Set the bucket's file lifecycle to Keep only the last version. B2 does not implement conditional PutObject, so AWC's duplicate puts are idempotent overwrites; with "Keep all versions" those overwrites would stack versions and defeat GC reclamation.
  3. Create an application key restricted to that single bucket with only readFiles, writeFiles, deleteFiles, and listFiles capabilities (GC lists object versions, so listBuckets alone is not enough). If you also restrict the key to a file name prefix (awc/ is what the pilot expects), the configurator puts every CAS object under it via AWC_S3_KEY_PREFIX — B2_KEY_PREFIX in .b2.env defaults to awc; set it empty only for an unrestricted key, otherwise B2 rejects writes with AccessDenied: not entitled.

Then write the key to a root-owned file on the VM and bootstrap with AWC_OBJECT_STORE=b2:

mkdir -p /opt/awc-pilot
cat >/opt/awc-pilot/.b2.env <<'EOF'
B2_KEY_ID=<keyID>
B2_APPLICATION_KEY=<applicationKey>
EOF
chown root:root /opt/awc-pilot/.b2.env && chmod 0600 /opt/awc-pilot/.b2.env

sudo AWC_OBJECT_STORE=b2 LOCAL_PILOT=1 CONTROL_ENDPOINT=http://127.0.0.1:8081 \
  PACKAGE_FILE=/tmp/awc-0.1.0-x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu.tar.gz \
  bash /tmp/guest-bootstrap.sh

B2_ENDPOINT, B2_REGION, and B2_BUCKET may be set in .b2.env to target a different bucket; they default to https://s3.eu-central-003.backblazeb2.com, a region derived from the endpoint host (eu-central-003), and awc-test. The configurator probes the endpoint before starting anything so DNS/firewall failures surface immediately.

Rotate the application key once the pilot is verified, and treat the keyID and applicationKey like passwords: they never belong in the repository or on a command line that ends up in shell history. Switching an existing pilot from MinIO to B2 (or back) is a rerun of the configurator with the other AWC_OBJECT_STORE value; the CAS contents do not migrate.

docs.title: 5. Run the acceptance test
docs.text:
The bootstrap installs the acceptance command. Run:

sudo awc-pilot-acceptance

The test creates disposable AWC content and verifies all of the following:

  • all three systemd services are active and awcd is ready;
  • /var/lib/awc/basefs is a real FUSE mount;
  • an imported snapshot reaches READY through the worker;
  • a workspace target is a real writable OverlayFS mount;
  • lower content is readable and mutations/deletions are isolated in the upper;
  • a cooperative checkpoint publishes successfully;
  • unmount releases the writer lease; and
  • an immediate remount sees the checkpointed mutation and deletion; and
  • a full AWC/PostgreSQL/object-store service-stack restart retains the published head (MinIO restarts locally; a B2 bucket is remote and stays up, so only PostgreSQL restarts with the AWC services).

A passing run ends with AWC Proxmox pilot acceptance PASS.

After a VM reboot, rerun sudo awc-pilot-acceptance; this repeats the durable stack-restart check and creates a fresh end-to-end checkpoint cycle.

docs.title: Operations and troubleshooting
docs.text:
Useful checks:

systemctl status awc-control awc-worker awcd --no-pager
journalctl -u awc-control -u awc-worker -u awcd -n 100 --no-pager
curl -fsS http://127.0.0.1:9100/healthz
curl -fsS http://127.0.0.1:9100/readyz
findmnt /var/lib/awc/basefs
findmnt /var/lib/awc/binds/pilot-acceptance
cd /opt/awc-pilot && docker compose ps

Load the CLI environment with:

sudo -s
set -a
. /opt/awc-pilot/awcctl.env
set +a
awcctl status

Common failures:

  • Docker Compose v2 is required: install the docker compose plugin; legacy docker-compose is not used.
  • /dev/fuse missing: use a KVM VM and install/load FUSE in the guest.
  • basefs is not mounted with FUSE: inspect journalctl -u awcd; startup now fails rather than reporting healthy if the FUSE worker exits or times out.
  • mount target rejected: both sides must use /var/lib/awc/binds; the pilot writes AWC_MOUNT_TARGET_ROOTS and allowed_bind_roots consistently.
  • checkpoint asks for a cgroup: use --mode cooperative in this pilot.
  • disk-pressure rejection: keep at least 5 GB free on the filesystem containing /var/lib/awc.

To restart without destroying pilot data:

systemctl restart awc-control awc-worker awcd

To stop services while retaining data:

systemctl stop awcd awc-worker awc-control
cd /opt/awc-pilot && docker compose stop

Do not remove Docker volumes or /var/lib/awc unless you explicitly intend to destroy the pilot's database, CAS objects, caches, and local uppers. On a B2 pilot the CAS objects live in the bucket instead of the miniodata volume; emptying the bucket is equally destructive.

docs.title: Moving beyond the pilot
docs.text: Before exposing AWC or adding hosts, replace development authentication with TLS/mTLS and managed signing keys, move PostgreSQL and the CAS to backed-up services, use unique registered host identities, validate firewall policy, and exercise quiesced checkpoints with delegated execution cgroups. Those changes are intentionally outside this first local deployment.

docs.title: Deploy on a VM with systemd
Deploy on a VM with systemd
docs.text:
This guide stands up awcd and its dependencies as native systemd services on one Linux VM (spec §21.6). For a worked loopback pilot that runs PostgreSQL and MinIO in Docker, see Deploy on Proxmox VE.

Non-dev deploys need real TLS and signing keys

Development mode (AWC_DEV_MODE=1) is for loopback pilots only. For any host that is not loopback-only, provision mTLS identities and managed signing keys before you enable the services (spec §13.2). Agent processes SHOULD NOT receive object-store credentials or control-plane administrative tokens.

docs.title: 1. Provision a Linux VM that meets the host profile
docs.text:
The certified host profile requires (spec §15.1):

  • Linux kernel 6.1 or newer;
  • cgroup v2, FUSE, and OverlayFS enabled;
  • ext4 or XFS for the cache and workspace upper directories;
  • xattr support and /dev/fuse;
  • root or equivalent host capabilities for mount management;
  • a local SSD or NVMe for the cache volume;
  • outbound access to the control plane and the object store.

Use a full VM, not an unprivileged container. awcd needs the host mount namespace, /dev/fuse, and OverlayFS (spec §15.4). Put /var/lib/awc on a dedicated local volume. The cache and upper directories use that volume (spec §21.6).

docs.title: 2. Build and copy the package
docs.text:
On a Linux build host, build and sign the release tarball:

packaging/package.sh
# -> dist/awc-<version>-<target>.tar.gz

See Build and package for build options and signature verification. Copy the tarball to the VM.

docs.title: 3. Stand up PostgreSQL and an S3-compatible object store
docs.text:
Provision PostgreSQL and an S3-compatible object store. awc-control and awc-worker connect to PostgreSQL through a single DATABASE_URL. awcd and the worker read and write objects to the content-addressed store (CAS).

Keep the object-store credentials in /etc/awc/worker.env and /etc/awc/control.env. Do not pass them to agent processes (spec §13.2).

docs.title: 4. Install AWC, the awc user, and the unit files
docs.text:
On the VM, as root, unpack and install the package:

tar xzf awc-<version>-<target>.tar.gz
cd awc-<target>
./install.sh

install.sh creates the versioned layout under /opt/awc/, the unprivileged awc system user, the unit symlinks under /etc/systemd/system/, and default config under /etc/awc/. Default config is written only when absent. The script ends with systemctl daemon-reload. The install is idempotent and safe to re-run on upgrade.

The three unit files land at /etc/systemd/system/awcd.service, awc-worker.service, and awc-control.service. For the capability map, sandboxing, and the drain, restart, and rollback semantics, see systemd units. This guide does not repeat them.

docs.title: 5. Enroll the host and write the configuration
docs.text:
Enroll the host to write /etc/awc/awcd.toml and /etc/awc/awcd.env:

./enroll.sh --control-endpoint https://control.example.invalid

enroll.sh mints a host_id, writes the cache, workspace, and bind roots, and creates the state directories. Then fill in the deployment values:

  • /etc/awc/worker.env: DATABASE_URL, AWC_CAS_URL, and the S3 credentials.
  • /etc/awc/control.env: DATABASE_URL, the REST and gRPC listen addresses, the signing and service-token seeds, and the S3 credentials.

Install the PKI material that awcd.env and control.env reference:

/etc/awc/pki/ca.crt
/etc/awc/pki/awcd.crt        /etc/awc/pki/awcd.key
/etc/awc/pki/control.crt     /etc/awc/pki/control.key
/etc/awc/pki/mount-ticket.pub

awcd runs as the unprivileged awc user. It holds a bounded capability set, CAP_SYS_ADMIN included, so it can perform mount, FUSE, and cgroup operations without running as root (spec §15.3). The host identity uses an mTLS client certificate (spec §13.2). enroll.sh writes placeholder PKI paths only. It does not issue certificates.

docs.title: 6. Enable and start the units, then verify
docs.text:
Start the host daemon first, then the worker:

systemctl enable --now awcd
systemctl enable --now awc-worker

Enable awc-control only when your deployment has a control plane to serve. The ExecStartPost liveness gate marks awcd active only once /healthz answers (spec §19.6).

Verify the host:

awcctl status
curl -fsS http://127.0.0.1:9100/healthz
curl -fsS http://127.0.0.1:9100/readyz
journalctl -u awcd -f

awcd exposes liveness on /healthz and readiness for new mounts on /readyz (spec §19.6). Tail logs with journalctl -u <unit>. For drain, restart, and rollback, see Drain and restart a host and Upgrade a deployment.

docs.title: Current scope
docs.text:
• enroll.sh performs local enrollment: it mints a host_id and writes a placeholder control endpoint. For a real deployment, replace the placeholder with the control-plane endpoint and provision mTLS identity (spec §16.5). Host registration and the mTLS identity lifecycle are implemented.
  • awcd wires the control-plane client at startup: it attaches the lease lifecycle, the checkpoint publisher, and a background lease-renewal cache against the control endpoint. The endpoint is validated as a URL; a malformed endpoint disables the client but lets startup continue. Outside AWC_DEV_MODE=1, awcd and awc-control MUST present TLS credentials and fail to start without them (spec §13.2).
  • The awc-control, awcd, and awc-worker units are installed. Enable all three. See systemd units for the unit reference.
  • Quiesced checkpoints need a delegated execution cgroup. Cooperative checkpoints work without one.

docs.title: Diff and export workspaces
docs.text:
Compare two snapshots and write the change set between them to a file. A diff runs a Merkle-tree comparison of the two root trees, so unchanged directories are skipped without scanning their children (spec §5.6).

Both awcctl snapshot diff and awcctl snapshot export call the same endpoint, GET /v1/snapshots/{left}:diff?right={right} (spec §13.14). The first snapshot id is the old, left side. The second is the new, right side. An add-file entry means the path exists in the new side only. A delete-path entry means it exists in the old side only.

Before you start: point awcctl at the control plane with --control-endpoint (or AWC_CONTROL_ENDPOINT) and --token (or AWC_TOKEN). The call needs the export permission, and both snapshots MUST belong to your tenant.

  1. List your snapshots and copy the two ids.

    awcctl snapshot list

    Pick the older snapshot as the old, left side. Pick the newer snapshot as the new, right side.

  2. Print the change list to the terminal.

    awcctl snapshot diff snap_01J... snap_01K...

    Pass the old snapshot first and the new snapshot second. Each line shows the change kind and the path:

    modify-file   src/main.rs
add-file      docs/new.md
delete-path   tmp/old.log

    Add --output json to print the full structured DiffResponse.

  3. Export the change set to a file. Pass --format json.

    awcctl snapshot export snap_01J... \
  --against snap_01K... \
  --format json \
  --out changes.json

    export takes the same two sides as diff, in the same order. The first positional id is the old, left side. --against is the new, right side. --out writes the raw response bytes; - writes to standard output.

  4. Inspect the exported file.

    jq '.result.changes[] | {kind, path}' changes.json

    The file holds a DiffResponse. The inline form puts the list at result.changes[]. Each change carries kind, path, and the mode and content digest of the affected entry.

Only json is served today

The control plane serves --format json only. If you pass patch-bundle or tar, the API rejects the request with INVALID_ARGUMENT. The renderers for all three formats are implemented, but patch-bundle and tar are not wired to the HTTP endpoint. The default export format is patch-bundle, so you MUST pass --format json until the other formats ship.

Direction matches diff

export <left> --against <right> computes the same diff as diff <left> <right>. The change list goes from the old side to the new side. The flag name --against reads like a base, but in the wired code it is the new, right side. Pass the snapshots in the same order for both commands and the directions agree.

docs.text:
