  • Checkpoint a workspace
  • Content addressing

docs.title: Drain and restart a host
docs.text:
Take a host out of scheduling, let in-flight work settle, restart awcd, and return the host to service. This is the drain and restart half of the daemon upgrade runbook (spec §25.8). For the full upgrade, with binary and format compatibility checks and rollback, see Upgrade a deployment.

A clean drain and restart is not a crash. On a clean drain, awcd receives SIGTERM, finishes or cancels in-flight installs, persists mount-session metadata, and leaves mounted views in a defined state (spec §15.13). On restart it reconciles existing mounts rather than assuming they disappeared (spec §15.13, §17.3). A crash skips the drain. Restart recovery still runs, but writes that never reached the upper directory are gone. See Impact below.

docs.title: Detect
docs.text:
Run this procedure when any of these is true:

  • You planned a restart. You are patching the kernel, changing awcd configuration, swapping the binary, or doing host maintenance.
  • You are rolling a deployment. Follow Upgrade a deployment first; this page is the per-host drain and restart step inside it.
  • The unit restarted on its own and you want to confirm whether the host drained cleanly or crashed.

Read the current state before you drain:

awcctl status

The HostStatus response carries the fields you need:

Field Meaning Drain target state HostState: STARTING, HEALTHY, DEGRADED, STOPPING, STOPPED Starts at HEALTHY (or DEGRADED); ends at HEALTHY. base_mount_state Shared base filesystem state MOUNTED before and after. active_mount_count Live mount sessions on the host Falls to the post-drain count, then recovers.

Watch these metrics from GET /metrics on the health HTTP port while you drain:

  • awc_workspace_active_mounts falls as sessions unmount.
  • awc_active_writer_leases falls as writers release or finish.
  • awc_workspace_checkpoint_total rises if you flush uppers before drain.

Health HTTP is opt-in

awcd does not serve /healthz, /readyz, or /metrics unless you set health_http_listen (for example 127.0.0.1:9100). Without it, use awcctl status and journalctl -u awcd -f instead. Configure it before you need it (spec §19.6).

Distinguish a clean drain from a crash by the events that precede the restart:

  • Clean drain. The log shows the awcd shutdown sequence. HostState moves to STOPPING, then STOPPED. The unit goes inactive on its own.
  • Crash. The log stops mid-event with no shutdown sequence. systemd restarts the unit under Restart=on-failure (see systemd units). The next awcd started event follows no clean STOPPED.

docs.title: Procedure
docs.text:
1. Mark the host unschedulable for new mounts. Stop routing new mount tickets to the host at your scheduler or load balancer. The build has no in-daemon unschedulable toggle; you MUST stop admission at the scheduler. Confirm new mounts have stopped by watching awc_workspace_active_mounts hold steady.

  2. Wait for in-flight checkpoints to finish. A publication transaction that is open when you drain is recoverable (spec §17.9), but a clean finish is preferred. Check each writer:

    awcctl workspace status ws_01J...

    Let CHECKPOINTING workspaces return to MOUNTED. Do not cancel a checkpoint in progress unless you accept its recovery class.

  3. Preserve mount-session metadata. Do not delete the workspace upper or work directories, the local cache index, or the durable session store. On restart awcd recovers sessions from this durable state (spec §11.12, §17.3). The daemon MUST NOT delete an upper directory merely because the control plane is temporarily unreachable (spec §17.3).

  4. Drain awcd with a bounded stop. Send SIGTERM through systemd so the graceful shutdown path runs (spec §15.13):

    sudo systemctl stop awcd
# or, with a bounded wait and a status report:
packaging/drain.sh awcd

    On SIGTERM, awcd stops accepting new mounts and checkpoints, finishes or cancels in-flight object installs safely, persists local mount-session metadata, attempts to release leases, and avoids deleting uppers with uncheckpointed data (spec §15.13). The unit's TimeoutStopSec bounds the drain. If the unit is still active after the timeout, investigate before you force a kill. Do not SIGKILL a host that holds uncheckpointed uppers.

  5. Restart awcd:

    sudo systemctl start awcd
# or, if you only stopped it:
sudo systemctl restart awcd

  6. Confirm restart reconciliation ran. On startup awcd acquires the singleton host lock, scans the durable session store, classifies each session against the authoritative lease, and dispatches recovery (spec §17.3, §11.12). Read the reconcile summary in the health detail, or in the log:

    reconciled N session(s): renewed=A fenced=B deleted=C preserved=D

    For a clean drain against a reachable control plane, expect preserved=0. A non-zero preserved count means the control plane was unreachable for those sessions; their uppers are kept, not deleted (spec §17.3). See Recover from a control-plane outage if preserved is large.

  7. Renew valid leases and run read and write probes. The lease-renewal task refreshes on its interval (default leases.renew_interval_seconds: 30). Leases whose fencing generation is still current are renewed; stale generations are fenced (spec §17.3). Mount one workspace read-only and one writable, and confirm both serve:

    awcctl workspace mount ws_01J... --target /workspace --read-only
awcctl workspace mount ws_01J... --target /workspace

    Then unmount the probe sessions.

  8. Return the host to scheduling. Re-enable the host in your scheduler or load balancer. Confirm new mount tickets route to it and that awcctl status reports HEALTHY with base_mount_state MOUNTED.

docs.title: Verify
docs.text:
Confirm recovery when all of these hold:

  • awcctl status reports state HEALTHY and base_mount_state MOUNTED.
  • GET /healthz returns 200 and GET /readyz returns 200 (when health HTTP is enabled). /readyz reflects readiness to accept a new writable mount: base FUSE, cache, leases, kernel compat, no disk pressure, and control-plane and object-store connectivity (spec §19.6).
  • The reconcile summary reads renewed=... for the writer set you drained, with no unexpected fenced or preserved counts.
  • awc_active_writer_leases matches the writer count you expect on the host.
  • A read and a write probe both succeed on a freshly mounted workspace.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text:
State the data risk plainly:

  • A clean drain preserves uncheckpointed uppers. The shutdown path persists mount-session metadata and does not delete uppers with uncheckpointed data (spec §15.13, §17.3). On restart the daemon reconciles those sessions against the authoritative lease.
  • A checkpoint interrupted by drain is recoverable. Local checkpoint state records phases and idempotency keys (spec §17.9). Retry publication with the same idempotency key. Draining cleanly is still preferred over interrupting a checkpoint.
  • A crash loses writes that never reached the upper. Restart recovery reconstructs state from durable records (spec §11.12). It does not recover writes that the agent process or the kernel had not yet flushed to the upper directory.
  • Host loss destroys uncheckpointed uppers. If the host is lost instead of cleanly restarted, only the latest acknowledged checkpoint survives (spec §17.4). See Recover from host loss.
  • Fencing is deliberate. A session whose lease expired or whose generation is stale is fenced and cannot publish (spec §17.2, §17.3). This preserves the acknowledged workspace head.

docs.title: Current scope
docs.text:
The build implements graceful shutdown and restart reconciliation, but some operator surfaces lag the spec. Be aware of these gaps:

  • No in-daemon unschedulable toggle. Mark the host unschedulable at your scheduler or load balancer. /readyz reports readiness, but it does not stop a scheduler that ignores it. You MUST stop routing new mounts yourself.
  • Health HTTP defaults to off. Set health_http_listen to expose /metrics, /healthz, and /readyz. Without it, rely on awcctl status and journald.
  • Control-plane and object-store health components are not wired. Both report Unknown with the detail connectivity probe not wired. As a result /readyz can read 200 while the control plane is down. After a restart, do not trust /readyz alone to confirm the control plane is up. Check the lease counters and a probe publish instead. See Recover from a control-plane outage.
  • Lease provisioning from the mount path is partial. The renewal task and lease cache run, but a session whose record carries no lease id is never renewed. Reconciliation preserves it as ControlPlaneUnknown, which is safe but means step 7 may be a no-op for sessions created through awcctl until a lease is provisioned.
  • Restart reconciliation runs on the startup path. A live fence without a restart needs the lease-renewal task, which only renews sessions that carry a lease id.

docs.title: Fork a workspace
docs.text:
Create one or many private, metadata-only workspaces from a snapshot. A fork writes workspace metadata only. It MUST NOT copy content objects (spec §5.3), so the cost is independent of the snapshot size (spec §20.2, gate 1).

Before you start: the source snapshot MUST be in the READY state (spec §5.3, §6.4). Get its id from awcctl snapshot list or awcctl snapshot create. Set --tenant (or AWC_TENANT) and --project (or AWC_PROJECT).

  1. Confirm the source is ready.

    awcctl snapshot inspect snap_01J...

    A not-ready snapshot returns SNAPSHOT_NOT_READY. Fork the ready id only.

  2. Fork. Pick one mode.

    Single workspaceBatch (many workspaces)

    Fork one workspace from a snapshot. This calls POST /v1/workspaces (spec §13.6).

    awcctl workspace fork \
  --snapshot snap_01J... \
  --ttl 2h \
  --name retry-investigation-17 \
  --label agent_run=run_991

    --snapshot forks exactly one workspace. Pass --count only with --workspace.

    Fork many workspaces from an existing workspace's base, head, or a specific snapshot. This calls POST /v1/workspaces/{workspace_id}:fork (spec §13.7).

    awcctl workspace fork \
  --workspace ws_01J... \
  --from base \
  --count 10 \
  --name candidate \
  --ttl 2h

    --from accepts base, head (the default), or a snapshot id. The server caps a batch at 1000 workspaces (MAX_FORK_BATCH). For larger fan-out, repeat the call with a new --idempotency-key.

  3. Capture the workspace id. The new workspace starts in the IDLE state with version = 1 and base == head.

    • Single fork prints the workspace fields, including id, state, base, head, and expires.
    • Batch fork prints one line per workspace as id<TAB>state.

    Add --output json to capture ids in a script.

  4. (Optional) Inspect a workspace.

    awcctl workspace status ws_01J...

--ttl is required

--ttl sets the workspace lifetime. It accepts 2h, 30m, 3600s, a bare number of seconds, or 1d. The workspace expires after this duration.

Idempotent by default

Every fork honors --idempotency-key (spec §13.1). Repeat a fork with the same key and the server returns the original result instead of duplicating workspaces.

docs.title: Handle host disk pressure
docs.text:
Use this runbook when the host cache or the workspace filesystem runs low on free space or free inodes. The goal is to relieve pressure before it blocks new mounts or risks uncheckpointed writes.

awcd drives one host through six pressure states, in this order (spec §17.8):

NORMAL → CACHE_EVICTION → PREFETCH_DISABLED → NEW_MOUNTS_DISABLED
       → UPPER_WRITES_AT_RISK → EMERGENCY

The state is a single integer gauge, awc_host_disk_pressure_state (spec §19, §17.8):

Value State What the host does 0 NORMAL Nothing. 1 CACHE_EVICTION Evicts disposable cache objects. 2 PREFETCH_DISABLED Stops speculative prefetch. Demand reads continue. 3 NEW_MOUNTS_DISABLED Refuses new writable mounts. 4 UPPER_WRITES_AT_RISK Existing upper writes may fail with ENOSPC. 5 EMERGENCY Only warm reads continue.

Containment is strictly ordered. The cheap, safe lever fires first: the host MUST evict disposable cache before it touches workspace uppers (spec §17.8). The state machine computes and reports all six states; not every action is wired in the current build. See Current scope for what fires today.

docs.title: Detect
docs.text:
Watch for any of these signals:

  • The awc_host_disk_pressure_state gauge rises above 0. Scrape it from GET /metrics on the health HTTP port.
  • GET /readyz returns 503 while GET /healthz returns 200. This means the host is warm_read_ready: existing reads continue, but new writable mounts are not admitted.
  • The /healthz body shows the disk_pressure component as Degraded or Down. Its detail line reads state=<STATE>; uncheckpointed_upper_bytes=<N>.
  • A mount request fails with ResourceExhausted and the text disk pressure blocks new mounts.
  • An upper write returns ENOSPC (state UPPER_WRITES_AT_RISK or worse).
  • Free inodes drop to the inode threshold. The default is 1024 free inodes. At or below it, the host escalates to at least NEW_MOUNTS_DISABLED, even if free bytes are plentiful. The escalation shows in awc_host_disk_pressure_state; check the raw inode count with df -i on cache_root.
  • The event log (stderr) prints disk pressure elevated at UPPER_WRITES_AT_RISK or EMERGENCY.

Health HTTP is opt-in

awcd does not serve /healthz, /readyz, or /metrics unless you set health_http_listen (for example 127.0.0.1:9100). Without it, you have no HTTP signal for pressure. Configure it before you need it (spec §19.6).

The byte thresholds derive from one operator reserve, cache.min_free_bytes (spec §22.9). With the default 50 GiB reserve, the ladder is:

State Triggers when free bytes fall to CACHE_EVICTION 150 GiB (3 × reserve) PREFETCH_DISABLED 100 GiB (2 × reserve) NEW_MOUNTS_DISABLED 50 GiB (== reserve) UPPER_WRITES_AT_RISK ~33 GiB (2/3 × reserve) EMERGENCY ~16 GiB (1/3 × reserve)

Pressure stall information (PSI) can only escalate the state, never relax it. High I/O stall pushes the host up the ladder even when free bytes remain.

docs.title: Procedure
docs.text:
1. Read the current state. Fetch awc_host_disk_pressure_state from /metrics, or read the disk_pressure component in /healthz. Decide from the table above.
  2. Separate cache bytes from upper bytes. Cache objects live under cache_root (default /var/lib/awc/cache). Uncheckpointed uppers live in per-workspace overlay upper directories. The cache is disposable; the uppers are not.
  3. Do not rely on the cache reclaiming itself. The segmented-LRU policy is specified to evict on every admission to stay under cache.max_bytes and to preserve cache.min_free_bytes (spec §10.9), but in the current build eviction is not wired into the live cache path. The cache does not self-reclaim under pressure, and lowering cache.max_bytes will not free space until it is wired. Use the levers that work now: free upper bytes (step 5) or add capacity (step 7).
  4. Stop scheduling new writable mounts to the host. At NEW_MOUNTS_DISABLED the daemon already refuses them with a visible disk-full error. Drain your scheduler regardless, so it does not retry onto a host that cannot admit.
  5. Checkpoint or unmount healthy workspaces. Run awcctl workspace checkpoint to flush upper deltas to the object store. Then run awcctl workspace unmount with a disposition. This frees upper bytes on the host. See Checkpoint a workspace and Unmount a workspace.
  6. Do not delete active uppers. Never remove a workspace upper directory by hand to relieve pressure. The daemon MUST NOT silently delete uncheckpointed data (spec §17.8, §18.5). An upper may be removed only after a successful unmount disposition and the configured recovery grace.
  7. Add capacity or drain the host. Grow the filesystem that holds cache_root, or move workloads off the host. See Drain and restart a host.
  8. Verify the reserve and return to normal. Confirm the steps in Verify below.

Prefetch is specified to disable itself

You do not disable prefetch by hand. At PREFETCH_DISABLED the state machine flags prefetch off, and interactive demand reads keep priority over prefetch by design (spec §10.10). In the current build the prefetch path does not yet consult the pressure monitor, so prefetch is not actually stopped at this state. See Current scope below.

docs.title: Verify
docs.text:
Confirm recovery when all of these hold:

  • awc_host_disk_pressure_state returns to 0.
  • GET /readyz returns 200.
  • The /healthz body shows disk_pressure as Ok.
  • A new writable mount is admitted without a disk-full refusal.
  • Free bytes are above the cache.min_free_bytes reserve, and free inodes are above the inode threshold.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text:
State the data risk plainly:

  • Cache eviction is safe. Cached objects are disposable copies of immutable content-addressed objects (spec §8.5, §17.1). Eviction loses no committed data. A cold miss refetches the object from the object store.
  • Uncheckpointed uppers are ephemeral. Writes that have not been checkpointed are not durable (spec §6.8, §17.1). At UPPER_WRITES_AT_RISK or worse, existing upper writes may fail with ENOSPC.
  • Host loss destroys uncheckpointed uppers. If the host is lost while pressure is high, only durable artifacts survive: the latest acknowledged checkpoint and imported snapshots (spec §17.4). If pressure threatens the host, checkpoint first. See Recover from host loss.
  • The daemon never frees an upper to relieve pressure. It reports the disk-full state and refuses new mounts instead (spec §17.8).

docs.title: Current scope
docs.text:
The build computes and reports the full pressure state machine and wires the new-mount admission gate, but two containment actions and several operator surfaces lag the spec. Be aware of these gaps:

  • Health HTTP defaults to off. Set health_http_listen to expose /metrics, /healthz, and /readyz. Without it, only the disk pressure blocks new mounts mount error and the stderr event surface the condition.
  • The pressure gauges are populated every 5 s. With health_http_listen set, /metrics reports awc_host_disk_pressure_state, awc_host_free_bytes, awc_host_free_inodes, and awc_host_upper_usage_bytes. awc_host_cache_bytes follows every 30 s and needs the fuse feature. Without the listener, fall back to df and df -i on cache_root.
  • Per-workspace upper usage is not yet wired. The monitor can account per-workspace upper bytes (spec §17.8), but the mount path does not feed it yet. The uncheckpointed_upper_bytes detail reads 0 until it is connected.
  • Cache eviction is not wired into the live path. The segmented-LRU EvictionPolicy is specified (spec §10.9) and unit-tested, but its enforce step has no production caller; the cache store defers admission and eviction to task T024. The CACHE_EVICTION state is reported, but no cache objects are reclaimed automatically. There is also no pressure-triggered eviction loop and no awcctl command to force cache eviction. To reclaim space now, free upper bytes by checkpointing and unmounting workspaces, or add capacity. Durable object-store garbage collection is a separate job; see Run garbage collection.
  • Prefetch is not gated by pressure. The PREFETCH_DISABLED state is reported, but the prefetch path does not yet consult the pressure monitor, so speculative prefetch continues at this state. Spec §10.10 is the target.
  • Some health components report unknown. Control-plane and object-store connectivity probes are not yet wired, so they cannot confirm or deny an outage alongside pressure.

docs.title: Handle object-store corruption
docs.text:
Use this runbook when a durable object is missing or when its bytes no longer match its content digest. The goal is to restore integrity without serving wrong bytes.

Every AWC object is content-addressed. An object is accepted only when its computed digest equals its claimed digest. Content addressing makes corruption detectable, but objects are immutable. You restore them from a trusted copy. You do not repair them in place.

Two failures are distinct and actionable:

  • Missing — no object exists under the digest. It may be recoverable from a trusted replica.
  • Corrupt — an object exists, but its bytes do not re-hash to the digest. The key is immutable, so wrong bytes under a correct address cannot be repaired by re-writing.

docs.title: Detect
docs.text:
Watch for any of these signals:

  • A read or mount returns an integrity error. The API returns ObjectCorrupt or ObjectMissing as HTTP 422. awcctl exits with code 8 (INTEGRITY) for ObjectCorrupt, and code 7 (REMOTE_IO) for ObjectMissing.
  • The local cache rejects a digest mismatch. On download the cache recomputes the digest. A mismatch raises DigestMismatch and the cache row moves to the CORRUPT state.
  • The durable store returns a distinct integrity error. A verified read returns DigestMismatch for wrong bytes, or ObjectNotFound for a missing object. The fault classifier maps a mismatch to Corruption.
  • A background scrub marks the snapshot DEGRADED. The scrub job re-verifies every object in a snapshot's closure.
  • awcctl snapshot list --state DEGRADED returns snapshots the scrub has flagged.

Missing is not always corruption

A transient object-store outage can also surface ObjectNotFound. Confirm the outage is over before you treat a missing object as durable loss. See Recover from an object-store outage.

docs.title: Procedure
docs.text:
1. Distinguish local-cache corruption from durable-object corruption. A local mismatch quarantines a disposable cache copy. A durable mismatch affects the immutable object under its content address.
  2. Clear a local-cache mismatch first. The cache row is already CORRUPT. Evict it and refetch from the object store. The fetch path re-verifies the digest on download. If the refetched bytes verify, the corruption was local only. If they mismatch again, the durable object is corrupt. Continue.
  3. Identify the affected object and the snapshots that reference it. Read the snapshot.scrub audit event for the snapshot. Its detail lists each incident: digest, kind, severity (structural or leaf), problem (missing or corrupt), recovery, and actual_digest for corruption.

  4. List every degraded snapshot. Run the command below to find all snapshots the scrub has flagged.

    awcctl snapshot list --state DEGRADED

  5. Pin the closure against garbage collection (GC). The scrub writes the closure digests into the gc_integrity_holds table. Do not run a GC sweep that deletes held objects. See Run garbage collection.

  6. Restore the object from a trusted copy. Pick a source.

    Trusted replica or versionRe-import the source

    Restore verified bytes from a configured replica or an object-store version. The scrub writes the object only if the key is absent, then re-verifies it. A missing object may clear this way. A corrupt object will not, because the key already holds bytes.

    Re-import the original source to produce a fresh, verified object graph. See Import from Git and Import from a directory.

  7. Restore only with verified bytes. A corrupt object is immutable under its address. The store has no overwrite. You cannot repair wrong bytes in place. You must restore the correct bytes from a trusted source, or into a clean store.

  8. Keep the snapshot unmounted while degraded. A DEGRADED snapshot is readable where objects survive, but it is not mountable as a writable workspace. Do not fork or mount it until it returns to READY.
  9. Record the incident and rotate credentials if you must. The scrub emits a snapshot.scrub audit event. If you suspect overwrite or unauthorized access, rotate the object-store credentials. See Rotate credentials.

docs.title: Verify
docs.text:
Confirm recovery when all of these hold:

  • The snapshot state returns to READY. Confirm with awcctl snapshot inspect <id>.
  • A re-run of the scrub returns status: clean with zero incidents.
  • The affected snapshot mounts. awcctl workspace mount succeeds. Only a READY snapshot is mountable.
  • The gc_integrity_holds rows for the closure are released.
  • The restored object's digest matches its content address.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text:
State the data risk plainly:

  • Objects are immutable. Content addressing makes corruption detectable, but you restore objects rather than repair them.
  • Corruption is unrecoverable without a trusted copy. The store has no overwrite, so wrong bytes under a correct address cannot be fixed in place. You must restore from a replica, a version, or a re-import.
  • A missing object may be recoverable. A trusted replica can restore a missing object. Without one, the object is lost.
  • Structural loss is worse than leaf loss. A missing or corrupt structural object (snapshot manifest, tree, or file manifest) makes the closure untraversable. A leaf blob loss degrades file content, but the snapshot is still walkable.
  • A degraded snapshot is not mountable. It stays readable where objects survive. It cannot be mounted or forked until it returns to READY.
  • Workspace writes are not affected. Uncheckpointed writes live in the host upper directory and are independent of the durable store. See Checkpoint a workspace.

docs.title: Current scope
docs.text:
The build implements the integrity primitives and the scrub engine, but some operator surfaces lag the spec. Be aware of these gaps:

  • No scrub is scheduled yet. The scrub handler is registered in the worker, but no scheduler enqueues scrub jobs. There is no awcctl snapshot scrub command. To run a scrub, enqueue a scrub job directly. The control plane enqueues only a closure presence check at publication. That check does not re-verify the bytes of published objects over time.
  • No recovery replica is configured. The worker wires the trusted recovery store as None. The automated recovery path therefore returns NoSource for a missing object and Unrecoverable for a corrupt one. Restoring from a replica or re-importing the source is an operator action until the recovery store is wired.
  • GC holds are empty until a scrub runs. The gc_integrity_holds table exists and the GC sweep honors it, but nothing populates it until a scrub job runs.
  • The cache-corruption metric is not emitted. awc_host_cache_corruption_total is defined but is not recorded at runtime. Until it is wired, detect local-cache corruption from the CORRUPT cache row state and the DigestMismatch error.

docs.title: Handle a stale writer
docs.text:
Fence a workspace whose writer lease expired or was superseded by a higher generation. The goal is one outcome: only the authoritative generation can publish, and the old writer cannot advance the workspace head (spec §14.4, §25.2).

A stale writer is a mount session whose lease no longer authorizes publication. Its local bytes may still exist on the host. Those bytes are not remotely durable and cannot become the canonical head through normal publication (spec §14.4, §6.8).

docs.title: Detect
docs.text:
Watch for one or more of these signals:

  • The control plane reports the lease as EXPIRED or REVOKED. Only an ACTIVE or RELEASING lease may publish (spec §12.4).
  • A higher generation was issued elsewhere for the same workspace. Every writer lease carries a monotonically increasing fencing generation (spec §9.10).
  • A checkpoint publish is rejected. Publication succeeds only when lease.generation == supplied_generation, the lease is active, the mount session matches, and the expected workspace version and head match (spec §14.3). A mismatch fails without changing the head.
  • The metric awc_lease_renewal_failures_total rises on the awcd /metrics endpoint (needs health_http_listen). awc_active_writer_leases is declared but not emitted in this build.
  • The awcd health detail reads reconciled N session(s): renewed=... fenced=... deleted=... preserved=.... A non-zero fenced count means the daemon has classified a session as StaleGeneration.

docs.title: Procedure
docs.text:
1. Confirm the workspace and its head. Run status against the workspace id.

    awcctl workspace status ws_01J...

    Record the head, the version, and the mount session id of the suspect writer.

  2. Identify the authoritative generation. The authoritative writer is the live lease with the highest generation for the workspace. A host with an older generation MUST NOT publish a checkpoint (spec §9.10, §14.4).

  3. Confirm publication is already blocked for the old generation. The awcd reconciler classifies a live mount whose lease does not authorize as StaleGeneration, sets may_publish to false, and emits a Fence action (spec §11.12). This is the fence. The old writer cannot advance the head even if its process resumes.

  4. Run the fence pass. In the current build, the reconciler executes on the daemon restart path. Restart the daemon to reconcile all sessions against the authoritative leases.

    sudo systemctl restart awcd

    The fence executor force-closes the stale session record (MountSessionState::Closed). It never publishes.

  5. Pause the fenced writer if its process is still running. Stop the agent, or freeze the execution cgroup that the mount ticket sealed (spec §13.8). The daemon does not remount the kernel overlay read-only itself; you MUST stop new writes from the stale writer by hand.

  6. Preserve the stale upper for the recovery grace period. Do not delete the session directory. The daemon refuses to delete a session whose upper still holds uncommitted data (spec §17.3). The PreservedDelta class promotes to SafeToDelete only after the configured grace window (spec §11.11, §11.12).

  7. Choose a disposition with the workspace owner. Pick one.

    Discard the stale changesExport the stale changes

    The uncheckpointed upper is not the workspace head. Once the owner confirms, let the grace window elapse and let GC reclaim the session.

    Recover the upper as an offline patch bundle (spec §17.11). This path MUST NOT advance the original head automatically. It records that the bytes came from unacknowledged local state and needs explicit authorization. Do not execute any workspace content from the bundle.

  8. Never merge the stale delta into the authoritative head automatically. A stale host MAY keep local bytes, but they can become canonical only through an explicit recovery path (spec §14.4, §17.11).

  9. Release host resources after disposition. Once the owner discards or exports the delta, the session moves to SafeToDelete and the daemon reclaims its upper directory.

docs.title: Verify
docs.text:
Confirm the workspace now has exactly one active writer:

  • awcctl workspace status ws_01J... shows the head and version that the authoritative generation published.
  • Exactly one active writer lease exists, at the authoritative generation. awc_active_writer_leases is not emitted in this build, so confirm with the awcctl workspace status output.
  • The awcd health detail shows fenced=N for this pass and no new stale-publication rejections.
  • A retry of the stale writer's checkpoint fails with the §14.3 publication predicate. It does not change the head.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text:
Uncheckpointed writes are not durable

The fenced writer's local upper is not remotely durable (spec §6.8). It will not become the workspace head through publication. It survives only in the host-local upper directory for the grace window. If the owner discards it, or the grace window elapses, those writes are lost. The authoritative head is whatever the higher-generation writer published.

Current build: leases are not yet issued for CLI mounts

The control-plane lease path is still being wired. Sessions created by awcctl workspace mount do not yet carry a lease_id, so the renewal task does not renew them and the reconciler preserves them rather than fencing. A live fence against a confirmed stale generation requires a session that the mount path issued a lease for. Until then, treat any CLI-mounted writer as preserved-delta, not fenced.

docs.title: Import a snapshot from a directory
docs.text:
Turn a local directory tree into a READY, immutable, content-addressed snapshot (spec §5.2). Directory import is the launch-critical path and the one fully implemented import route.

Before you start

You need a running control plane. Set a tenant and project with --tenant and --project (or AWC_TENANT and AWC_PROJECT). Select an object store with --object-store-endpoint or AWC_CAS_URL (memory:// for local, s3:// for S3). The create command fails without these.

  1. Choose the source directory and a normalization policy.

The policy is recorded in snapshot provenance and MUST be declared (spec §9.8).

  • source-normalized (the default) keeps only the file type and the executable bit. It zeroes mtime and collapses mode bits, so the same tree imports to the same digest every time. Build tools that key on mtime rebuild from the normalized timestamps.

  • environment-preserving keeps the captured mode bits and mtime; setuid and setgid are cleared by default. Use it for prepared build or dependency environments where tools read mtime. The digest is then sensitive to the captured timestamps.

  • Create the snapshot.

awcctl --output json snapshot create \
    --from-dir /path/to/prepared-dir \
    --name backend-main-8e3a2f \
    --label revision=8e3a2f

--from-dir is required. --source-type defaults to directory; you MAY omit it. Pass --normalization environment-preserving to override the default. Repeat --label KEY=VALUE to tag the snapshot.

  1. Capture the snapshot id from the JSON.

The command returns the id and a VALIDATING state (spec §13.5).

{
  "snapshot_id": "snap_01J...",
  "state": "VALIDATING",
  "snapshot_manifest_digest": "sha256:...",
  "root_tree": "sha256:...",
  "logical_bytes": 2147483648,
  "file_count": 8123,
  "unique_objects": 9001,
  "unique_bytes": 1999348096
}
  1. Poll until the state is READY.
awcctl snapshot inspect snap_01J...

The worker validates the object closure before publication (spec §13.5, §12.1). A snapshot becomes mountable only at READY. On a validation failure it moves to FAILED.

  1. Confirm the totals.

Read files and bytes (the logical size) from the inspect output, with the manifest and root-tree digests. Compare them against your source tree to confirm the import captured what you expect.

  1. Use the snapshot as a workspace base.

Only a READY snapshot can back a new workspace (spec §12.1). See fork a workspace.

docs.title: Provenance variants
docs.text:
--source-type git and --source-type tar record a different source kind in provenance, but the create command always imports the directory at --from-dir. It does not clone a repository or extract an archive. For those flows, see import from Git and import from a tar archive.

Resumable uploads

Object writes are idempotent. If the create command is interrupted, re-run it. Objects already present in the store are reused and are not re-written.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• Import from Git

  • Fork a workspace
  • Normalization

docs.title: Import a snapshot from Git
docs.text:
Record a Git tree as an AWC snapshot. The manifest stores the source kind as git and records the imported directory path as the locator.

AWC does not clone for you

--source-type git only sets the source kind in the manifest. AWC does not clone, fetch, or parse a Git URL today. The import code path is the same as a directory import. You MUST materialize the tree yourself.

The CLI does not populate source.immutable_revision. It is always null. Record the revision in a label instead.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
• Set AWC_TENANT and AWC_PROJECT, or pass --tenant and --project. Snapshot create requires both (spec §13.3).
  • Configure an object store. Export AWC_CAS_URL, or pass --object-store-endpoint. The value must start with memory:// or s3://.

docs.title: Procedure
docs.text:
1. Materialize the Git tree to a local directory.
git clone https://example.com/acme/backend.git backend
git -C backend checkout 8e3a2f1

Note the checked-out revision. You pass it as a label in the next step.

  1. Import the directory and record Git provenance.
awcctl snapshot create \
  --from-dir backend \
  --source-type git \
  --name backend-8e3a2f \
  --label repository=acme/backend \
  --label revision=8e3a2f1

--source-type git sets the manifest source kind to git. The default normalization is source-normalized (spec §9.8). It zeroes owner, group, and mtime, and keeps file type plus the executable bit. Pass --normalization environment-preserving to keep captured modes and mtimes. The command prints the snapshot id and a state of VALIDATING.

  1. Poll the snapshot until it reaches READY.
awcctl snapshot inspect snap_01J...

A worker validates object closure, then advances the state VALIDATING -> READY (spec §13.5, §12.1). The snapshot is mountable only at READY.

  1. Confirm the Git source kind.
awcctl snapshot inspect snap_01J...

Read the source line. It shows git. The inspect record exposes the source kind only. The locator and immutable_revision are held in the manifest, which awcctl does not print.

docs.text:

docs.title: Import a snapshot from a tar archive
docs.text:
Record a tar archive as an AWC snapshot. The manifest stores the source kind as tar and records the imported directory path as the locator.

AWC does not ingest a tar stream

--source-type tar only sets the source kind in the manifest. AWC does not read, extract, or stream a tar archive today. The import code path is the same as a directory import. You MUST extract the archive yourself first.

The source.locator points at the extracted directory, not at the archive. source.immutable_revision is always null. Record the archive name or digest in a label instead.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
• Set AWC_TENANT and AWC_PROJECT, or pass --tenant and --project. Snapshot create requires both (spec §13.3).
  • Configure an object store. Export AWC_CAS_URL, or pass --object-store-endpoint. The value must start with memory:// or s3://.

docs.title: Procedure
docs.text:
1. Extract the archive to a local directory.
mkdir extracted
tar -xf backend-build-42.tar -C extracted

The directory is what AWC imports. The archive itself is not recorded as a path in the manifest.

  1. Import the directory and record Tar provenance.
awcctl snapshot create \
  --from-dir extracted \
  --source-type tar \
  --name backend-build-42 \
  --label archive=backend-build-42.tar

--source-type tar sets the manifest source kind to tar. The default normalization is source-normalized (spec §9.8). It zeroes owner, group, and mtime, and keeps file type plus the executable bit. Pass --normalization environment-preserving to keep captured modes and mtimes. The command prints the snapshot id and a state of VALIDATING.

  1. Poll the snapshot until it reaches READY.
awcctl snapshot inspect snap_01J...

A worker validates object closure, then advances the state VALIDATING -> READY (spec §13.5, §12.1). The snapshot is mountable only at READY.

  1. Confirm the manifest records the Tar source kind.
awcctl snapshot inspect snap_01J...

Read the source line. It shows kind: tar and locator set to the extracted directory path. immutable_revision is null today.

docs.title: Install AWC
docs.text: Build the AWC binaries from source and put awcctl on PATH. AWC runs on Linux only.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• A Linux host, kernel 6.1 or newer, with cgroup v2, FUSE, and OverlayFS enabled.
  • Rust 1.94.0. rust-toolchain.toml pins the channel plus rustfmt and clippy. Rustup selects it automatically inside the repo.
  • cargo-deny, for the dependency audit. Install it with cargo install cargo-deny.

docs.title: 1. Confirm the host and the toolchain
docs.text:
uname -r             # expect 6.1 or newer
rustc --version      # expect rustc 1.94.0

If rustup is installed, it reads rust-toolchain.toml and installs the pinned toolchain on the first build.

docs.title: 2. Build all crates and binaries
docs.text:
make build

make build runs cargo build --workspace --all-targets. The README lists the other make targets, and .cargo/config.toml mirrors them as cargo aliases.

Default features are the lifecycle core

make build turns the fuse and s3 cargo features off. The binaries use a no-op base mount and the memory:// object store. That is enough to exercise the CLI and the host socket. For a real read-only FUSE base mount and the S3 transport, enable those features or use the release package in step 6. See Run locally.

docs.title: 3. Locate the binaries
docs.text:
make build writes debug binaries under target/debug/:

target/debug/awcd         host daemon
target/debug/awc-worker   background worker
target/debug/awc-control  control plane
target/debug/awcctl       CLI

docs.title: 4. Put awcctl on PATH
docs.text:
cp target/debug/awcctl ~/.local/bin/
awcctl --version

For development, add the build directory to PATH instead of copying:

export PATH="$PWD/target/debug:$PATH"

docs.title: 5. Verify the CLI
docs.text:
awcctl --help

awcctl status probes a running awcd over its Unix socket. It resolves the socket from --host-socket or AWC_HOST_SOCKET (default /run/awcd/awcd.sock), so it needs a live daemon. To stand one up, follow Run locally.

docs.title: 6. Build a release package (optional)
docs.text:
For stripped, signed binaries with the production FUSE and S3 features, run the packaging pipeline:

packaging/package.sh
# -> dist/awc-<version>-<target>.tar.gz

package.sh builds, signs, and tars the stripped binaries. The tarball also ships the database migrations, offline reference docs, golden manifest vectors, and an SPDX SBOM. For the install, enroll, and rollback steps on a VM, see Build and package.

docs.title: Next
docs.text:
• Run locally — stand up the services and run the smoke.
  • Your first workspace — the end-to-end workflow.
  • Configuration — daemon and worker options.

docs.title: Mount a workspace
docs.text:
Mount a workspace as a writable directory on a host. The mount runs behind a signed, replay-protected ticket that the control plane issues and the host daemon awcd redeems (spec §13.8, §13.9).

Before you start: get a workspace id from fork a workspace. Confirm the target path is under the host allow-list, which is the configured workspace_root plus allowed_bind_roots. awcd MUST be running with its socket present at /run/awcd/awcd.sock. Set --control-endpoint (or AWC_CONTROL_ENDPOINT) and a bearer --token (or AWC_TOKEN) for the control plane.

  1. Confirm the workspace and target.

    awcctl workspace status ws_01J...

    The target MUST be an absolute path under an allow-listed root. awcd rejects relative paths, .. or . segments, sibling prefixes, and any path outside the roots (spec §13.9). It MUST NOT accept an arbitrary host path from an untrusted caller.

  2. Mount the workspace read-write.

    awcctl workspace mount ws_01J... --target /var/lib/awc/workspaces/run-991

    The CLI learns the host id, issues a signed ticket over the control plane, then redeems it at awcd. For a read-write mount the control plane acquires an exclusive writer lease first (spec §5.4, §13.8). At most one unexpired writer lease may exist per workspace (spec §6.6).

  3. Capture the mount session id.

    session    ms_01J...
target     /var/lib/awc/workspaces/run-991
merged     /var/lib/awc/workspaces/ws_01J.../3/merged
root       sha256:...
lease gen  3

    Save the session value. You pass it to checkpoint and unmount.

  4. Confirm the kernel mounted OverlayFS.

    findmnt -n -o FSTYPE --target /var/lib/awc/workspaces/run-991

    The command prints overlay. awcd builds a merged OverlayFS view and bind-mounts it into your target, so the target carries the overlay type (spec §5.4).

  5. For a read-only mount, add --read-only.

    awcctl workspace mount ws_01J... \
  --target /var/lib/awc/workspaces/review \
  --read-only

    A read-only mount MAY be created without an exclusive writer lease (spec §5.4, §13.8). --target is required either way.

  6. To release the mount later, see unmount a workspace.

Namespace bind targets are not wired

The spec lets awcd bind the merged view into an authorized sandbox mount namespace or a configured host target (spec §15.4). The current build supports the host-target path only. A request that carries a namespace target returns UNIMPLEMENTED.

See also: fork a workspace, checkpoint a workspace, unmount a workspace, overlay, cache, and singleflight.

docs.title: Recover from a control-plane outage
docs.text:
Use this runbook when hosts cannot reach the control plane. The control plane is the awc-control API plus its PostgreSQL database. The goal is to keep hosts serving mounted workspaces while you restore the plane, then renew leases and confirm no workspace was fenced by mistake.

The control plane and the data plane are separate. Existing warm reads and local writes on a host do not require the control plane (spec §17.5). What fails is coordination: lease renewal, checkpoint publication, new mount tickets, and workspace fork or delete. See Architecture for the split.

docs.title: Detect
docs.text:
Watch for any of these signals:

  • The awc_lease_renewal_failures_total counter rises and keeps climbing. Scrape it from GET /metrics on each host's health HTTP port.
  • awc_api_errors_total rises across many workspaces at once.
  • Lifecycle RPCs fail. awcctl workspace fork, awcctl workspace mount, and awcctl workspace checkpoint return errors, and a workspace cannot be forked or deleted (spec §17.5). A sustained run of retryable statuses (408, 425, 429, and 5xx other than 501 and 505) against many workspaces signals a plane-wide outage, not one bad call.
  • A new mount ticket does not issue. The mount path cannot authorize without the control plane (spec §17.5).
  • awc-control or PostgreSQL is down on the control-plane host. Confirm both, because the API cannot serve without the database (spec §17.6).

Health HTTP does not detect this outage today

The control_plane health component reports Unknown with the detail connectivity probe not wired. It does not flip to Down, so /healthz stays 200 and /readyz does not change. Do not rely on readiness probes to detect a control-plane outage. Use the lease-renewal counter and the lifecycle RPC failures instead.

A host often looks healthy while the plane is down. awcctl status (the host-local GetHostStatus RPC) reports the host's own mount state, not the control plane. A healthy host status plus failing lifecycle RPCs is the signature of this outage.

docs.title: Procedure
docs.text:
1. Confirm the control plane is the failed dependency. Check awc-control and PostgreSQL together. Correlate the failure across more than one host, so you do not chase a single host's network.
  2. Stop scheduling new lifecycle operations. New forks, mounts, deletes, and checkpoint publications MUST fail or queue with explicit errors, not retry onto a dead plane (spec §25.4). Pause your scheduler so it does not pile up retries.
  3. Let hosts keep serving mounted workspaces. Existing warm reads and local writes continue without the control plane (spec §17.5). Do not restart or drain hosts only because the plane is down.
  4. Watch the lease grace windows. awcd MAY keep a writable mount through the disconnected grace, default leases.disconnected_grace_seconds: 60. After grace it MUST deny checkpoint publication and SHOULD remount the workspace read-only or pause the sandbox per policy (spec §17.5, §22.9).
  5. Hold checkpoint publication. Do not force a publish while the plane is down. A checkpoint cannot be published without the authoritative lease (spec §17.5). Uncheckpointed writes stay local and ephemeral.
  6. Restore or fail over the control plane. Bring back PostgreSQL first, then the API. If PostgreSQL failed, follow Recover from a PostgreSQL failover before you trust the API.
  7. Confirm hosts re-register and renew leases. The lease-renewal task refreshes on its interval (default leases.renew_interval_seconds: 30) and moves each session out of the ControlPlaneUnknown class (spec §11.12, §22.9).
  8. Drain the idempotent retry backlog. Lifecycle and publication retries with a stable idempotency key return the committed result (spec §17.2). Let them run; do not reissue with a new key.
  9. Confirm no workspace was fenced by mistake. Compare the acknowledged workspace head in PostgreSQL against each host session. A session fenced for an expired or stale lease is correct fencing, not a false fence (spec §17.5).

docs.title: Verify
docs.text:
Confirm recovery when all of these hold:

  • awc_lease_renewal_failures_total stops climbing. Its rate returns to zero over a few renewal intervals.
  • awc_active_writer_leases reflects the expected writer count.
  • A new mount ticket issues, and a new fork succeeds.
  • A checkpoint publishes without a lease or publication error.
  • The reconcile report holds no ControlPlaneUnknown sessions. Each session is either ActiveLeaseValid (renewed) or correctly fenced as StaleGeneration.
  • The acknowledged workspace head version in PostgreSQL matches the host sessions. No head diverged.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text:
State the data risk plainly:

  • Reads and local writes on mounted workspaces are safe during the outage. They do not touch the control plane (spec §17.5). The outage itself loses no data.
  • Uncheckpointed writes are ephemeral. Writes that have not been published are not durable (spec §17.1, §6.8). An outage blocks publication. If a host is then lost, those writes are lost. See Recover from host loss.
  • Publication is blocked, not lost. A checkpoint held by the outage can be retried with the same idempotency key once the plane returns (spec §17.9). Do not reissue it with a new key.
  • Fencing is deliberate. A host whose lease expired or whose generation is stale is fenced and cannot publish (spec §17.2, §17.5). This prevents stale hosts from diverging the head; it is the safe behavior.
  • The system never guesses a head from the object store. PostgreSQL alone determines the acknowledged workspace head (spec §17.6). Unreferenced objects are left for garbage collection.

docs.title: Current scope
docs.text:
The build implements the reconcile and lease-renewal paths, but some operator surfaces lag the spec. Be aware of these gaps:

  • The control_plane health component is not wired. It reports Unknown with the detail connectivity probe not wired, so /healthz and /readyz cannot confirm or deny an outage. Detect the outage from awc_lease_renewal_failures_total and lifecycle RPC failures instead. The object_store component is Unknown for the same reason.
  • Lease provisioning from the mount path is partial. The renewal task and lease cache run, but a session whose record carries no lease id is never renewed. Reconciliation preserves it as ControlPlaneUnknown until a lease is provisioned, which is safe but means the renewal step may be a no-op for those sessions.
  • Health HTTP defaults to off. Set health_http_listen to expose /metrics, /healthz, and /readyz. Without it, the lease counter is not reachable over HTTP.
  • Per-host head comparison is manual. There is no single command that diffs the acknowledged head against every host session. Run the comparison from the database and from awcctl status on each host.

docs.title: Recover from host loss
docs.text:
Use this runbook when a host disappears while it holds active writers. The goal is to fence the lost host, recover each workspace from its last acknowledged checkpoint, and return capacity to the pool.

Host loss is permanent loss of that host's local state. The local cache, the active mount state, the uncheckpointed upper deltas, and any preserved local recovery deltas on that host are gone. What survives is the immutable truth: imported snapshots, acknowledged checkpoints, workspace metadata, audit events, and retained patch exports. See The durability model.

Leases and fencing prevent split-brain. Every writer lease carries a monotonic generation. A lost host keeps an old generation. Even if its process resumes, it cannot publish. See Fencing and split-brain.

docs.title: Detect
docs.text:
Watch for one or more of these signals:

  • The host does not answer awcctl status. The GetHostStatus host RPC fails, times out, or refuses the connection. The host's SSH session and health probe also fail.
  • Renewals for the host's writer leases stop. The control plane still shows live leases with host_id equal to the lost host, but their expires_at passes with no renewal.
  • awc_active_writer_leases keeps counting the lost host's leases as live. They stay live until a new acquire fences them (see Current scope).
  • Lifecycle RPCs that target the host fail. A new awcctl workspace mount on that host returns an error, because the host cannot serve it.

A short partition is not host loss

Confirm the host is gone, not briefly unreachable. A host that recovers on its own needs Handle a stale writer, not this runbook. Wait long enough to rule out a transient network failure.

docs.title: Procedure
docs.text:
1. Mark the lost host unschedulable. Stop your scheduler from sending new mounts to it. This prevents new work from targeting a host that cannot serve it.

  2. Confirm the host is lost. Probe awcctl status, the health endpoint, and SSH. Correlate the failure with the lost host's stalled leases. If the host might return, follow Handle a stale writer instead.

  3. List the affected workspaces. Query the control-plane database for live leases whose host_id equals the lost host. Record each workspace_id, the acknowledged head, and the lease generation.

  4. Wait out the lease TTL (time to live). Renewals from the lost host have stopped. After expiry_seconds (default 90), each lease is past-due and a new acquire can fence it. Do not delete lease rows by hand.

  5. Confirm the acknowledged checkpoint survived. The workspace head in PostgreSQL points at a published snapshot. Verify that snapshot's objects are readable in the object store. Only an acknowledged checkpoint is guaranteed to survive host loss.

  6. Reassign each workspace to a healthy host. Mount the same workspace there, or fork a new workspace from the acknowledged head.

    awcctl workspace mount ws_01J... --target /workspace
awcctl workspace fork --workspace ws_01J... --from head

    The new lease acquire fences the lost host's past-due lease to EXPIRED and issues the next generation. This is the fence.

  7. Treat uncheckpointed writes on the lost host as lost. They were never remotely durable. Do not try to make them the head. If the host's disk returns later, you MAY export its upper as an offline patch bundle that never advances the head automatically.

  8. Retire the lost host's identity. Once you are sure it will not return, retire it so its mTLS (mutual TLS) identity is no longer honored. A resurrected host then cannot reauthenticate as a trusted writer.

docs.title: Verify
docs.text:
Confirm recovery when all of these hold:

  • Each affected workspace has one active writer lease on a healthy host. That lease holds a generation higher than the lost host's.
  • awc_active_writer_leases shows the expected writer count. No live lease remains on the lost host.
  • The workspace head and version in PostgreSQL match the last acknowledged checkpoint. They are unchanged unless a new checkpoint was published on the replacement host.
  • A publish attempt with the lost host's old generation fails with StaleGeneration. No double-write was possible, because only one generation can publish.
  • The lost host is UNSCHEDULABLE or RETIRED in the host table.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text:
Uncheckpointed writes on the lost host are lost

Writes that were not checkpointed before the host disappeared are gone. They lived only in the host-local upper directory. They were never remotely durable, and they cannot become the workspace head. The authoritative head is the last acknowledged checkpoint.

Acknowledged checkpoints and metadata survive

Imported snapshots, acknowledged checkpoints, workspace metadata, audit events, and retained patch exports live in the object store and PostgreSQL. Host loss does not touch them. The workspace recovers from its last published head.

No split-brain

The generation fence means the lost host could never have published alongside the new writer. Even if the old process resumes, its stale generation is rejected at publication. There is no window in which two writers advance the same head.

docs.title: Current scope
docs.text:
The build implements the lease-acquire fence and the publication predicate, but some operator surfaces lag. Be aware of these gaps:

  • Leases are fenced lazily, not by a background sweeper. A lease moves to EXPIRED only when the next writer lease for that workspace is acquired. Waiting out the TTL makes the lease past-due. Step 6 of the procedure performs the fence. There is no timer that auto-expires a lease on its own.
  • There is no awcctl host drain command. Marking a host UNSCHEDULABLE or RETIRED is a control-plane database or API operation.
  • Finding workspaces by host is manual. There is no single command that lists the active leases for a host. Query the workspace_leases table for rows with the lost host_id and a live state.
  • Lease provisioning from the CLI mount path is partial. A session created by awcctl workspace mount may not yet carry a lease_id. The fence path applies only to sessions the mount path issued a lease for. See Handle a stale writer.
  • The control_plane health component is not wired. It reports Unknown, so readiness probes cannot confirm or deny host loss. Detect the loss from the unreachable host and its stalled leases instead. See Recover from a control-plane outage.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• Handle a stale writer
  • The durability model
  • Fencing and split-brain
  • Recover from a control-plane outage

docs.title: Recover from an interrupted checkpoint
docs.text:
Resume a checkpoint that crashed during publish. The goal is one outcome: the workspace head advances exactly once, or not at all.

Publication is one atomic database transaction. A crashed publish either committed the new head or left the prior head unchanged. You never repair a partial head by hand. Recovery is idempotent retry: re-run the checkpoint with the same idempotency key, and the control plane returns the committed result for that key instead of duplicating work.

docs.title: Detect
docs.text:
Watch for one or more of these signals:

  • A checkpoint call returned an error, was cancelled, or its event stream dropped before the Result event.
  • awcctl workspace status ws_01J... shows the head and version unchanged from before the attempt. The head references the complete prior snapshot or the complete new snapshot, never both.
  • The daemon restart reconciliation line reads reconciled N session(s): renewed=... fenced=... deleted=... preserved=.... An interrupted checkpoint counts toward N but not toward renewed, fenced, deleted, or preserved. The session is class CheckpointInterrupted or CleanupIncomplete.
  • The metric awc_workspace_checkpoint_total shows no outcome="published" sample for the attempt (the interrupted stream, if any, counted outcome="failed"). Requires health_http_listen on the awcd host.
  • The file checkpoint.json exists in the session state directory with a phase other than COMPLETE.

docs.title: Procedure
docs.text:
1. Capture the workspace id, the mount session id, and the current head and version.

    awcctl workspace status ws_01J...

    Record head, version, and the session id of the attempt.

  2. Read the persisted recovery record. The record is checkpoint.json in the session state directory, <workspace_root>/<workspace-id>/<generation>/ (default workspace_root is /var/lib/awc/workspaces).

    sudo cat /var/lib/awc/workspaces/ws_01J.../3/checkpoint.json

    Read phase and idempotency_key. The phase tells you how far the attempt reached. Each phase maps to one recovery case:

    phase Reached Recovery action STARTED Identity recorded only Re-run construction, upload, then publish BUILT Candidate manifest persisted Re-run the closure upload, then publish UPLOADED Closure durable Re-issue publication only PUBLISHED Head already advanced Run post-publish cleanup only COMPLETE Fully done Nothing to recover

  3. Confirm the writer lease still authorizes publication. Only an ACTIVE lease at the current generation may publish. If the lease is EXPIRED, REVOKED, or fenced by a higher generation, stop here. Follow Handle a stale writer. A stale fencing token MUST NOT publish.

  4. Restart the daemon to run restart reconciliation. The pass finishes post-publish cleanup for a PUBLISHED attempt and preserves the session for every earlier phase.

    sudo systemctl restart awcd

    The daemon never deletes an upper directory while the checkpoint state is uncertain.

  5. Re-run the checkpoint with the same idempotency key. Pass the same session id and mode as the original attempt.

    awcctl workspace checkpoint sess_01J... \
  --mode cooperative \
  --idempotency-key cp-run991-3

    The re-run is safe for every phase. Immutable uploads are no-ops on objects already present, and the build is deterministic, so the re-run reproduces the same candidate.

  6. Capture the result snapshot id and version.

    snapshot      snap_01J...
digest        sha256:...
version       4

    If the original publish committed and only its response was lost, this re-run returns that same committed snapshot. The version does not advance a second time.

docs.title: Verify
docs.text:
Confirm the head advanced exactly once:

  • awcctl workspace status ws_01J... shows head equal to the result snapshot and version exactly one higher than before the attempt.
  • The checkpoint.json record now reads phase: COMPLETE. The attempt retired.
  • awc_workspace_checkpoint_total incremented once with outcome="published", not twice. Requires health_http_listen on the awcd host; otherwise confirm via the head, version, and phase checks above.
  • Mount the workspace and read back the checkpointed state. The merged view equals original lower + accumulated upper.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text:
Uncheckpointed writes are not durable

If the crash happened before publication and you do not re-run the checkpoint, the upper delta stays local to the host. It is not remotely durable. A later host loss destroys it. The acknowledged head is whatever the last successful publish committed.

Current build: the daemon does not auto-resume a crashed publish

Restart reconciliation classifies an interrupted checkpoint (CheckpointInterrupted, CleanupIncomplete) and finishes post-publish cleanup. It does not re-issue publication. You MUST re-run awcctl workspace checkpoint by hand. The library functions that decide and drive the resume are implemented and unit-tested, but the live daemon executor does not yet dispatch them.

Current build: CLI mounts have no writer lease

A checkpoint requires a writer lease. The call fails with session has no writer lease when the session has no lease_id. Sessions created by awcctl workspace mount do not yet carry one, so the recovery re-run needs a session that the mount path issued a lease for.

The checkpoint counter needs the health listener

awc_workspace_checkpoint_total counts every terminal checkpoint event with an outcome label (published, failed, cancelled). It renders only when awcd runs with health_http_listen set. Without the listener, detect and verify the recovery with the head and version values and the checkpoint.json phase instead.

Publication is atomic

You cannot advance the head twice. The control plane completes every mutable update in one PostgreSQL transaction and deduplicates a repeated publish on the idempotency key. A retry either commits the new snapshot now or returns the one already committed.

docs.title: Recover from an object-store outage
docs.text:
Use this runbook when hosts cannot reach the object store. The goal is to keep mounted workspaces on the host cache while the store is down, then restore the store and confirm that fetches resume and nothing was marked corrupt by mistake.

The object store holds the immutable objects behind every snapshot. The read hierarchy does not pass through the control plane. It is:

Linux page cache
  → awcd in-memory manifest cache
  → host-local NVMe CAS cache
  → regional/network object storage

Only the last tier is affected by this outage. Objects already resident on the host keep serving. Objects not yet cached do not. See Architecture for the read path.

During the outage, awcd MUST keep cached reads serving, and cold misses MUST return a clear transient I/O error after bounded retries. It MUST NOT fabricate empty or stale content. Checkpoint publication MUST fail without advancing the workspace head.

docs.title: Detect
docs.text:
Watch for any of these signals:

  • A cold read fails with a transient I/O error. The FUSE layer maps a fetch failure to EIO. The agent sees the read fail; the mount does not return wrong bytes.
  • awc_singleflight_leader_fetches_total climbs and keeps climbing on the host health HTTP port (GET /metrics). Every cache miss that becomes a remote fetch is a leader fetch. A sustained rise with failing reads means the store is down, not one bad object.
  • A checkpoint fails at the upload phase. The pipeline uploads every immutable object before it advances the head. An upload that cannot complete cancels the checkpoint and leaves the head unchanged.
  • The object-store provider endpoint fails its own health check, or the provider reports an availability, throttling, or authentication fault.

awcd classifies every object-store fault into one of six categories:

Class Retryable Meaning Availability Yes General failure. Connection reset, DNS, or 5xx. Throttling Yes Provider rate-limited the request. Timeout Yes The operation timed out. Authentication No Bad or denied credentials. MissingObject No No object exists under the digest. Corruption No Bytes do not re-hash to the digest.

Availability, Throttling, and Timeout drive the retry path. Authentication, MissingObject, and Corruption do not.

Health HTTP will not detect this outage today

The object_store health component reports Unknown with the detail connectivity probe not wired. It does not flip to Down, so /healthz stays 200 and /readyz does not change. Do not rely on readiness probes. Use the leader-fetch counter and the cold-read EIO failures instead.

Missing is not corruption during an outage

A down store surfaces ObjectNotFound, which classifies as MissingObject, not Corruption. Confirm the outage is over before you treat a missing object as durable loss. See Handle object-store corruption.

docs.title: Procedure
docs.text:
1. Confirm the object store is the failed dependency. Correlate the EIO reads and the rising leader-fetch counter across more than one workspace, and check the provider endpoint. Do not chase one bad object or one host's network.
  2. Disable prefetch and nonessential imports. Prefetch issues remote fetches for metadata and high-value files on mount. Stop it, and pause any import or fork that must pull from the store. Demand reads take priority over prefetch.
  3. Keep warm reads serving. Cached objects and resident manifest metadata MUST continue to resolve. Do not restart or drain hosts only because the store is down. A host that holds the working set stays useful.
  4. Let cold misses fail clearly. A cold miss retries with bounded exponential backoff, then returns a transient EIO. The terminal failure is negatively cached for a short bounded interval so repeated misses do not hammer the store. Do not script an unbounded retry loop around the FUSE request.
  5. Hold checkpoint publication. Do not force a publish while the store is down. The pipeline uploads objects before it advances the head, so a failed upload cancels the checkpoint and leaves the head unchanged. Uncheckpointed writes stay local and ephemeral.
  6. Watch local upper growth. Local upper writes MAY continue during the outage. They land on the host upper directory and do not touch the store. A long outage lets the upper grow, which costs delta efficiency and disk space. Track awc_host_upper_usage_bytes. If the upper fills the disk, follow Handle host disk pressure.
  7. Restore the object store. Fix the provider: credentials, network, capacity, or the backend itself. For an authentication fault, rotate the object-store credentials before you declare recovery (see Rotate credentials).
  8. Let the caches clear and refill. The negative cache expires on its short TTL, and the retry path fetches on demand. If a provider circuit breaker has tripped, reset it gradually by letting half-open probes through rather than flooding the store. Watch awc_singleflight_leader_fetches_total fall back to its idle rate.
  9. Retry idempotent uploads and publications. Re-issue a held checkpoint with the same idempotency key. It returns the committed result, or it publishes now that the store is back. Do not reissue with a new key.

docs.title: Verify
docs.text:
Confirm recovery when all of these hold:

  • A fresh cold read succeeds. Pick a path the host has not cached, mount its snapshot, and read it. The read returns bytes, not EIO.
  • awc_singleflight_leader_fetches_total settles. Its rate returns to the idle pattern over a few sample intervals, and the negative cache stops serving remembered errors.
  • A checkpoint publishes without a cancellation. The upload phase completes and the workspace head advances exactly once.
  • The acknowledged workspace head in PostgreSQL matches the host sessions. No head advanced during the outage.

  • No snapshot was marked corrupt by mistake. The outage surfaces MissingObject, not Corruption. Run the command below and confirm it returns no new entries.

    awcctl snapshot list --state DEGRADED

  • A sampled object re-verifies. Read a few objects from a recovered snapshot and confirm their digests match their content addresses. If any object still mismatches, that is real corruption, not an outage artifact. See Handle object-store corruption.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text:
State the data risk plainly:

  • Cached reads and local writes survive. Objects resident on the host, the manifest cache, and the upper directory are independent of the store. The outage itself loses no data on a host that holds the working set.
  • Cold reads fail. A read for an object that is not cached returns EIO after bounded retries. The agent sees a transient I/O error.
  • Checkpoint publication is blocked, not lost. A checkpoint held by the outage can be retried with the same idempotency key once the store returns. The head does not advance until publication succeeds.
  • Uncheckpointed writes are ephemeral. Writes that have not been published are not durable. If the host is lost during the outage, those writes are lost. See Recover from host loss.
  • The system never fabricates content. A cold read fails rather than return empty or stale bytes.
  • Prefetch warming pauses. Metadata and content prefetch on mount stall until the store returns. Mounts of cold snapshots are slower to warm.

docs.title: Current scope
docs.text:
The build implements the fetch, retry, and negative-cache path, but some operator surfaces lag the spec. Be aware of these gaps:

  • The provider circuit breaker is not wired into the running daemon. The fetch coordinator is constructed without the remote controls, so no per-provider breaker or concurrency bound is attached. In a live outage the active mechanisms are singleflight, bounded retry, and the negative cache. "Reset the breaker gradually" (step 8) is, in the current build, letting the negative-cache TTL expire and letting on-demand retries through.
  • Retry and negative-cache numbers are fixed at build time. The coordinator defaults to 3 attempts, a backoff of 10 ms to 1000 ms, and a negative-cache TTL of 5000 ms. There is no runtime knob to widen them for a long outage.
  • The object_store health component is not wired. It reports Unknown, so /healthz and /readyz cannot confirm or deny the outage. Detect it from awc_singleflight_leader_fetches_total and cold-read EIO failures instead.
  • Per-tenant and global remote-fetch bounds are not enforced yet. The concurrency limiter ships with the coordinator but is not attached. A storm of cold misses during the outage is bounded only by singleflight and the negative cache, not by an admission limit.
