docs.title: Recover from a PostgreSQL failover
docs.text:
Use this runbook when the control-plane database has failed and you must fail over or restore it. The control-plane database is PostgreSQL. It holds every mutable record: workspaces, leases, mount tickets, snapshots, audit events, and idempotency keys. The goal is to bring a new primary online, point awc-control at it, and confirm that no acknowledged snapshot is lost.

PostgreSQL alone determines the acknowledged workspace head. The system MUST never reconstruct a head by guessing from object-store contents. Object-store snapshots are immutable candidates. PostgreSQL picks which one is current.

AWC does not ship a failover manager or a backup tool. PostgreSQL MUST be deployed with automated failover and point-in-time recovery (PITR). You provision that layer. AWC only consumes the primary through DATABASE_URL.

docs.title: Detect
docs.text:
Watch for any of these signals:

  • awc-control fails to start, or exits after it logs a PostgreSQL connection error. It reads DATABASE_URL at startup and refuses to run without it.
  • Lease renewals fail. awcd renews each leased mount session against the control plane in the background. A dead primary makes those renewals fail. Each renewal pass adds its failed sessions to awc_lease_renewal_failures_total on the awcd /metrics endpoint (needs health_http_listen). Failures also surface as RPC errors on the next lease-protected operation, and as fenced sessions on the next reconcile.
  • awc_api_errors_total rises on the worker. The worker emits this counter (label component=worker), so a broad rise means background jobs are failing against the dead primary.
  • Lifecycle RPCs fail across the board. awcctl workspace fork, awcctl workspace mount, and awcctl workspace checkpoint return errors. A sustained run of the awcctl retryable set (408, 425, 429, and 5xx other than 501 and 505) against many workspaces is a plane-wide signal.
  • No new publication, lease acquisition, or authoritative lifecycle mutation succeeds. This is the database row of the failure matrix.
  • PostgreSQL itself reports the primary as down or read-only, a replica is being promoted, or you are replaying a write-ahead log (WAL) archive.

Health HTTP will not detect this outage

The control_plane and object_store health components report Unknown with the detail connectivity probe not wired. They do not flip to Down, so /healthz stays 200 and /readyz does not change. Detect this outage from the awc-control startup error and the awc_api_errors_total rise on the worker, not from readiness probes.

Warm reads and local writes on a mounted workspace do not touch the control plane. The outage is invisible to a running workspace until a lease needs renewal or a checkpoint must publish.

docs.title: Procedure
docs.text:
1. Confirm PostgreSQL is the failed dependency. Correlate the signals across more than one host so you do not chase a single host's network. Check the Postgres primary directly: it is down, read-only, or unreachable. Decide between replica promotion and backup restore.
  2. Promote the healthy replica, or restore from a point-in-time backup. Run this in your Postgres layer, with streaming replication plus a WAL archive or a managed equivalent. Do not run AWC against a primary that is still promoting or still replaying.
  3. Keep mutations disabled until the new primary is authoritative. Stop your scheduler so it does not pile new forks, mounts, and checkpoints onto a primary that is not yet consistent.
  4. Point awc-control at the new primary. Set DATABASE_URL to the new primary's connection string, then restart awc-control. It connects through a fixed 16-connection pool and refuses to start when DATABASE_URL is unset.
  5. Confirm migrations applied. On startup awc-control runs every pending migration before it accepts traffic. awc-worker runs the same migrations on its own startup, so restarting either binary against the new primary applies pending migrations. The migrations are forward-only and additive, so an older binary reading a newer schema still works during a rolling deploy. Check the sqlx migrations ledger for failures. Never revert a migration; a faulty migration is a forward corrective migration.
  6. Verify snapshots and workspaces are intact. Confirm every workspaces.head_snapshot_id resolves to a snapshots row. Confirm that workspace version and lease constraints held through the failover. A checkpoint publishes only through a locked compare-and-set on the workspace row, so a half-applied publication cannot advance the head.
  7. Run metadata and object reconciliation. Restart each awcd host so its restart reconcile classifies sessions against the restored control plane. Then compare the five records the model requires: published snapshot records, workspace versions, audit events, object-store snapshot manifests, and host-reported mount sessions.
  8. Compare audit sequence and idempotency records, and fence stale sessions. Confirm audit_events are contiguous and idempotency_keys match the publications you expect. A replay with the same key MUST return the committed result; a different result signals divergence. Fence any session created after the restore point unless you can prove it published. awcd preserves a session whose lease is missing as ControlPlaneUnknown rather than deleting it.
  9. Resume mutations in controlled stages. Re-enable the scheduler one tenant or host at a time. Do not infer missing publications from orphan snapshot objects. PostgreSQL alone sets the acknowledged head, and unreferenced immutable objects are left for garbage collection (GC).

Idempotent retries need no new key

Lifecycle and publication retries that carry a stable idempotency key return the committed result. Let them run after the failover. Do not reissue them with a new key, or you may create a duplicate.

docs.title: Verify
docs.text:
Confirm recovery when all of these hold:

  • awc-control logs show both listeners up: REST on AWC_CONTROL_LISTEN and gRPC on AWC_CONTROL_GRPC_LISTEN. The startup migration reported no error.
  • The sqlx migrations ledger shows the full set applied, with no new failures, and it matches your other environments.
  • Lease-protected RPCs succeed. A fork, a mount, and a checkpoint publish all return without error, which means renewals reach the primary again.
  • awc_api_errors_total returns to baseline.
  • A new mount ticket issues. A fork and a checkpoint publish both succeed.
  • Each host reconcile report shows sessions renewed as ActiveLeaseValid or correctly fenced as StaleGeneration. The preserved count (ControlPlaneUnknown plus PreservedDelta) is what you expect.
  • Database and object-store inventories agree. Every snapshots.manifest_digest is present in the object store. No head_snapshot_id is dangling. An idempotency replay returns the committed result.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text:
State the data risk plainly:

  • A clean replica failover loses no committed data. Streaming replication carried every committed mutation to the replica before promotion.
  • A point-in-time restore loses every database mutation after the restore point. That includes workspace head advances, leases, mount tickets, and audit events. Those rows are gone. AWC cannot rebuild them.
  • The system never reconstructs a head from the object store. Orphan snapshot objects after a restore are immutable candidates, not inferred publications. GC handles them.
  • Host writes are untouched by a database failover. Warm reads and local writes continue without the control plane. If a host is also lost, only durable artifacts survive: the latest acknowledged checkpoint and imported snapshots. See Recover from host loss.
  • Stale sessions are fenced on purpose. A session that predates the restore point and lost its lease is fenced and cannot publish. awcd preserves its uncheckpointed upper as ControlPlaneUnknown for offline export, then GC collects it. This is the safe behavior.

docs.title: Current scope
docs.text:
The build consumes PostgreSQL but does not manage it. Some operator surfaces lag the spec. Be aware of these gaps:

  • AWC ships no failover manager or PITR tooling. Provision automated failover and point-in-time recovery in your Postgres deployment, for example with Patroni or a managed Postgres with a WAL archive. AWC consumes the primary through DATABASE_URL only. For the backup procedure, see Back up and restore PostgreSQL.
  • No database-specific metric exists. There is no database, migration, or reconcile gauge, and the lease-renewal failure counter is defined but not yet emitted. Detect a database failure indirectly: awc-control fails to start, or awc_api_errors_total climbs on the worker. The control_plane and object_store health components report Unknown (connectivity probe not wired), so /healthz and /readyz do not reflect a database outage.
  • Migrations run automatically on startup. Both awc-control and awc-worker run pending migrations on startup. There is no separate migrate subcommand and no dry run. The set is forward-only and additive, enforced in CI. For the upgrade and rollback contract, see Upgrade a deployment.
  • Cross-check reconciliation is manual. awcd reconciles host sessions against the control plane on restart, but no single command diffs the database against the object store. Run the audit, idempotency, and manifest comparisons from SQL and an object-store listing.
  • The connection pool is fixed at 16. awc-control opens at most 16 PostgreSQL connections. Confirm the new primary's connection budget can absorb awc-control, awc-worker, and your job concurrency together.

When the database outage is part of a wider control-plane failure, also follow Recover from a control-plane outage. When the failover exposes a corrupt or missing object, follow Handle object-store corruption. When the object store itself is the failed dependency, follow Recover from an object-store outage.

docs.title: Rotate credentials
docs.text:
Use this runbook to rotate AWC credentials with no outage. Rotation covers four credential types (spec §13.2, §16.5):

Credential Used by Lifetime Service-account token The external API caller (awcctl, platforms) Revocable, scoped Host mTLS certificate Internal gRPC from awcd to the control plane Short-lived where supported Mount-ticket signing key The control plane signs; the host verifies Rotated with overlap Tenant-scoped object credential A host accesses the CAS for one tenant Short-lived, max 1 h

The rule that protects you during every rotation is overlap (spec §16.5). The old and the new credential MUST both be trusted until every in-flight use has expired. For signing keys, the overlap window MUST exceed the maximum mount-ticket lifetime.

docs.title: Detect
docs.text:
Rotate on any of these signals:

  • A credential nears its not_after. mTLS certificates and signing keys carry explicit validity windows. Track expiry on a calendar.
  • The object-corruption runbook tells you to. Spec §25.3, step 9, says rotate or revoke when overwrite or unauthorized access is suspected.
  • A host fails to renew its lease over internal gRPC. The control plane returns Unauthenticated. This points at an expired or revoked mTLS certificate.
  • A new mount fails with ControlPlaneUnavailable and the text no active mount-ticket signing key when the control plane has no active signing key. An empty host verifying set, after a botched cut-over, instead fails ticket verification on the host. This ControlPlaneUnavailable error comes from the rotation-aware credential service, which is not wired yet (see Current scope). Today the single-key env path cannot emit it at run time; a missing or invalid AWC_MOUNT_TICKET_SEED stops the control plane from starting instead.
  • The audit log shows signing_key.revoke (see spec §16.11).

docs.title: Procedure
docs.text:
Steps 2 through 9 assume the rotation API. That API is not wired yet; see Current scope for the env-var-and-restart path you use today.

  1. Inventory the credentials in use. List all four types from the table above. Confirm that no long-lived object-store credentials sit inside an agent sandbox. They MUST NOT (spec §16.5).
  2. Read the active signing key and its window. Check the audit trail for signing_key.rotate and signing_key.retire events. Note the retiring key id and its not_after.
  3. Stage the new credential alongside the old. For a signing key, add the new key whose validity opens now, and leave the retiring key trusted until its own not_after. Size the overlap to exceed the maximum mount-ticket lifetime. For an mTLS certificate, renew with a fresh fingerprint. The old certificate stays honored until its own not_after.
  4. Distribute the new verifying material to hosts. Publish the public verifying key set so hosts accept tickets signed during the overlap. Register the new mTLS identity. Hosts trust both old and new during the overlap window.
  5. Reload the control plane and each host. They must pick up the new trusted set. Do this inside the overlap window. See Deploy on Proxmox VE and Deploy a VM under systemd for the service and env files.
  6. Cut traffic over to the new credential. New tickets are signed with the new active key. New host connections present the new mTLS certificate.
  7. Retire the old credential. Set the old signing key not_after past the last in-flight ticket expiry. Revoke the old mTLS fingerprint. Revoke at once, do not retire, if you suspect compromise (spec §25.3).
  8. Confirm the audit trail. The log records signing_key.rotate, signing_key.retire, signing_key.revoke, and object_credential.issue against the signing_key and object_credential resource types. The detail holds only key ids and validity windows. No secret material is logged (spec §16.5).
  9. Keep rotating inside the overlap until every host confirms the new set. Do not let the overlap close before the last host reloads.

docs.title: Verify
docs.text:
Confirm recovery when all of these hold:

  • A new mount ticket verifies on a host. A fresh awcctl workspace mount succeeds.
  • Existing mounts keep serving. Reads and writes continue. Leases renew over mTLS without Unauthenticated errors.
  • A checkpoint publishes successfully. See Checkpoint a workspace.
  • The old credential no longer verifies after its not_after. If you revoked it, it no longer verifies at once.
  • The audit log shows the rotate, retire, or revoke events.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text:
State the risk plainly:

  • Overlap is the only thing that prevents an outage. If you cut over without overlap, or you outlive the window, new mount tickets cannot be issued or verified. New mounts and new lease renewals fail. Existing mounted reads and writes continue during a bounded lease grace period (spec §17.5), then the host fences publication and remounts the workspace read-only.
  • Rotation does not touch tenant content. No committed object, snapshot, or checkpoint is at risk. Data-loss risk is the same as a control-plane outage: uncheckpointed uppers are ephemeral (spec §17.1, §17.4). See Recover from a control-plane outage.
  • Secrets never reach logs or telemetry. Rotation audit events carry key ids and validity windows only (spec §16.5).

docs.title: Current scope
docs.text:
The overlap rotation mechanism is implemented and unit-tested, but the operator-facing surface lags the spec. Be aware of these gaps:

  • No rotation API or CLI yet. The credential service in awc-control implements add, retire, revoke, issue, and the public verifying-set publication. The host credential registry implements renew and revoke with overlap. None of these are exposed over an HTTP route or an awcctl command. There is no /v1/signing-keys endpoint and no awcctl credentials subcommand.
  • Today you rotate through env vars and a restart. The control plane reads AWC_MOUNT_TICKET_SEED and AWC_SERVICE_TOKEN_KEY. Each host reads AWC_MOUNT_TICKET_PUBLIC_KEY or AWC_MOUNT_TICKET_PUBLIC_KEY_FILE. mTLS material is AWC_CONTROL_TLS_CERT, AWC_CONTROL_TLS_KEY, AWC_CONTROL_TLS_CLIENT_CA, and AWC_CONTROL_TLS_CA on the host. This path loads a single key, so it does NOT give overlap. Plan a maintenance window. Drain the host, restart, and re-verify. New mount-ticket issuance fails during the restart gap. See the configuration reference and environment variables.
  • Dev mode is not a production security mode. AWC_DEV_MODE=1 selects a fixed development signing seed and skips TLS (spec §9.11). It binds to loopback only. To rotate, leave dev mode and provision real mTLS and managed seeds. See Deploy on Proxmox VE.
  • Host credentials persist in awc-db. The host credential registry is an in-memory, tested core. A production deployment persists short-lived host credentials in the hosts table.

docs.title: Run garbage collection
docs.text:
Use this runbook to reclaim durable content-addressed objects that no retained snapshot, workspace, or checkpoint can reach. The reclaim target is the object store, not the host cache.

Garbage collection (GC) runs as a mark-and-sweep epoch over one tenant (spec §18.3, §18.4). It deletes only objects that are both unreachable and older than the safety grace. Reachable content survives. Shared content survives deletion of one fork, because objects are deduplicated inside a tenant (spec §18.2, §16.12). See content addressing for the object model.

GC is separate from host cache eviction (spec §18.5). Cache loss affects speed only (spec §6.7). To reclaim space on a full host, run Handle host disk pressure instead.

docs.title: Detect
docs.text:
No gauge reports unreachable bytes yet (see Current scope). Detect the condition from what has changed and measure it with a dry run:

  • A tenant deleted workspaces or snapshot aliases. Logical deletion removes the reference; it does not free durable bytes at once (spec §16.12, §18.2).
  • Tenant-unique durable bytes, or the storage bill, do not fall after those deletions. Tenant-unique bytes are the basis GC reclaims (spec §18.7).
  • You want to confirm that no orphaned objects remain from a failed import or an interrupted checkpoint. Such objects are safe orphans until GC runs (spec §11.6, §17.6).

The authoritative measurement is a dry-run GC epoch. It plans candidates and records their bytes without deleting anything (spec §18.3 step 7). Run it first, then read the counts back from the database.

docs.title: Procedure
docs.text:
GC is implemented in the awc-gc crate and runs as an awc-worker job of kind gc_sweep (spec §8.2). The worker claims the job, drives one epoch, and records the result. A worker process must be running to claim the job.

The worker reads four knobs from the environment:

Variable Default Meaning AWC_GC_GRACE_SECS 86400 Safety grace. Objects newer than now - grace are never swept (spec §18.4). AWC_GC_BATCH_SIZE 1000 Max candidates one epoch deletes. Bounds each run as a canary. AWC_GC_CANARY_SIZE 10 Size of the leading batch inside an epoch. AWC_GC_DRY_RUN false Plan only. Delete nothing (spec §18.3 step 7).

The worker reads these variables once at startup. Restart the worker when you change one, or a run you expect to be a dry run can delete for real.

  1. Start a dry run to measure. Set AWC_GC_DRY_RUN=1 on the worker, then enqueue a gc_sweep job for the tenant. The epoch snapshots the retained roots and the grace cutoff, completes the mark phase, ingests the inventory, and writes the plan (spec §25.7 steps 1 to 4). Enqueue against the job queue:
INSERT INTO jobs
  (kind, tenant_id, state, payload, max_attempts,
   scheduled_at, available_at, created_at, updated_at)
VALUES
  ('gc_sweep', 'tnt_demo', 'PENDING',
   '{"tenant_id":"tnt_demo"}'::jsonb, 3,
   now(), now(), now(), now());

The handler reads the tenant from payload.tenant_id. A missing or blank tenant fails the job permanently; any epoch error is retried (spec §26.11).

  1. Wait for the epoch to reach COMPLETED, then compare the marked set against the inventory. The gc_runs row records every count (spec §25.7 step 3):
SELECT epoch, state, dry_run, cutoff, roots_count, marked_count,
       inventory_count, candidate_count, deleted_count, reclaimed_bytes
FROM gc_runs
WHERE tenant_id = 'tnt_demo'
ORDER BY epoch DESC
LIMIT 5;

marked_count is the set reached from retained roots. inventory_count is what the object store holds for the tenant. The gap is the unreachable set.

  1. Inspect the deletion candidates and their bytes (spec §25.7 step 4). Each candidate is one row in gc_deletion_plans:
SELECT kind, state, count(*) AS n, sum(size_bytes) AS bytes
FROM gc_deletion_plans
WHERE epoch = <EPOCH>
GROUP BY kind, state;

In a dry run every candidate stays in state CANDIDATE and deleted_count is 0. Confirm the bytes are worth reclaiming before you delete.

  1. Enforce the safety grace and the holds (spec §25.7 step 5). Confirm cutoff equals now - AWC_GC_GRACE_SECS. An object uploaded after the roots were snapshotted is protected by timestamp, even if it is not yet reachable (spec §18.4). Integrity holds fence off any digest pinned by a degraded snapshot's recovery, so recovery content is never swept (spec §17.10 step 6, §25.3). Objects of unknown age are never candidates.

  2. Disable dry run and run one bounded epoch. Set AWC_GC_DRY_RUN=0 and enqueue a second gc_sweep job. The sweep deletes a leading canary batch of AWC_GC_CANARY_SIZE objects, then continues in batches up to AWC_GC_BATCH_SIZE total (spec §25.7 step 6). Treat the first real epoch as the canary. Keep AWC_GC_BATCH_SIZE modest until you trust the run.

  3. Verify retained snapshots still mount (spec §25.7 step 7). Fork and mount a known snapshot, then read files from it:

awcctl workspace fork --snapshot <SNAPSHOT_ID> --ttl 1h
awcctl workspace mount <WORKSPACE_ID> --target /workspace
ls /workspace

A missing-object error here means GC deleted reachable content. Stop and open an incident (spec §17.10).

  1. Expand the batches by running further epochs (spec §25.7 step 8). Each epoch deletes at most AWC_GC_BATCH_SIZE candidates and leaves the rest pending for the next epoch. Repeat until a dry run reports candidate_count = 0.

  2. Record reclaimed bytes and keep the manifests (spec §25.7 steps 9 and 10). Each COMPLETED epoch records reclaimed_bytes on its gc_runs row, and a gc.sweep audit event is appended (spec §16.12). The gc_deletion_plans rows persist as the auditable deletion manifest; the physically removed rows move to state DELETED.

A failed epoch deletes nothing

If the mark phase hits a missing object or a kind mismatch, the epoch is recorded FAILED and nothing is deleted (spec §26.11). Do not treat a FAILED row as a partial reclaim. Read the error column and resolve the corruption first. See Handle object corruption.

docs.title: Verify
docs.text:
Confirm a safe reclaim when all of these hold:

  • The epoch row is COMPLETED, not FAILED.
  • deleted_count and reclaimed_bytes match what you expected, or are 0 if nothing was unreachable.
  • A known retained snapshot still forks, mounts, and reads.
  • A follow-up dry run reports candidate_count = 0, or only objects younger than the grace remain.
  • The gc.sweep audit event is present for the epoch.

docs.title: Impact
docs.text:
State the data risk plainly:

  • GC deletes only unreachable, grace-expired durable objects (spec §18.3, §18.4). It does not touch the host cache, workspace uppers, or any live root.
  • Shared content survives. Deleting one snapshot alias does not delete an object that another snapshot or workspace still reaches (spec §18.2, §16.12). GC reclaims tenant-unique durable bytes, not summed logical snapshot bytes (spec §18.7).
  • A reachability bug could delete shared reachable content (spec §26.11). The mitigations are immutable roots, the epoch cutoff, the safety grace, the dry run, the canary batch, integrity holds, and the audit trail. The mark phase aborts on the first inconsistency, so a buggy run fails closed.
  • A FAILED epoch is safe. It records the reason and deletes nothing.
  • Cache eviction is separate and safe. Losing every host-local cache affects performance only (spec §6.7, §18.5). It does not affect recoverability.

docs.title: Current scope
docs.text:
The engine is complete and tested, but the operator surfaces lag the spec:

  • No awcctl gc command. The CLI exposes only status, snapshot, and workspace. Run GC by enqueuing a gc_sweep job into the PostgreSQL job queue, with an awc-worker process running to claim it.
  • No GC auto-scheduler. The control plane enqueues snapshot_validate on import, but it never enqueues gc_sweep. You must trigger each epoch by hand.
  • The storage gauges are not yet emitted. awc_tenant_unreachable_grace_bytes, awc_tenant_unique_durable_bytes, and awc_snapshot_logical_bytes are specified (spec §19.2) but are not wired in awc-telemetry. Until they ship, measure unreachable bytes with a dry-run epoch, not with a gauge.
  • GC knobs are environment-wide, not per tenant. The worker reads the AWC_GC_* variables once at startup. A per-project retention policy (spec §18.6) is prospective and does not yet drive the sweep.
  • The mark phase roots at READY snapshots and integrity holds. The epoch marks reachability from the manifest digests of every READY snapshot, plus the digests pinned by gc_integrity_holds for degraded-snapshot recovery (spec §18.1, §17.10). It does not mark from an in-flight import session directly. Objects an import has uploaded but not yet sealed into a READY snapshot are protected by the safety grace timestamp, not by reachability. An import that runs longer than AWC_GC_GRACE_SECS (default 24 hours) without producing a READY snapshot can have its not-yet-reachable objects become candidates. Finish long imports first, or raise the grace for the run.

docs.title: Run locally
docs.text:
The local-dev harness is a reproducible, single-machine environment for running and exercising AWC end to end on a developer laptop. It stands up the external dependencies the AWC services rely on (PostgreSQL and an S3-compatible object store) in containers, runs the AWC binaries themselves on the host (so the code under development is what executes), generates the credentials and configuration they need, and runs a smoke script that proves the real cross-process paths work, including a byte-for-byte read of an imported snapshot through a real /dev/fuse base mount.

It targets the single-machine variant of the reference topology.

docs.title: Topology
docs.text:
host
 ├── docker compose ──────────────────────────────────────
 │    postgres:16   control-plane metadata store (awc-db)
 │    minio         S3-compatible object store (tenant CAS target)
 │    minio-init    one-shot: creates the awc-cas bucket
 │ ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
 ├── awc-control   control plane: REST + gRPC, migrates schema, dev-token
 ├── awc-worker    background worker: drains the job queue over the s3:// CAS
 ├── awcd          host daemon: Unix-socket gRPC + health HTTP + real FUSE base mount
 └── awcctl        CLI — drives the control plane + host daemon

All container ports bind to 127.0.0.1, so nothing is exposed off the host. The four AWC binaries are built once with their object-store and FUSE cargo features and then invoked directly. Cargo's default feature set would rebuild the wrong variants.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Docker Engine and the docker compose plugin, with a reachable daemon.
  • The Rust toolchain pinned by rust-toolchain.toml (for the build step).
  • python3, curl, and common coreutils on the host.
  • Linux with a usable FUSE stack: /dev/fuse present, and fusermount (or fusermount3) on PATH. awcd mounts a real read-only FUSE base filesystem.
  • For non-root use: user_allow_other enabled in /etc/fuse.conf. The FUSE base mount uses AutoUnmount, which adds the allow_other FUSE option. FUSE only honours allow_other for non-root mounters when user_allow_other is set. As root this is not required.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
cd deploy/local-dev
bin/generate-credentials.sh     # writes .env, config/{awcd.toml,worker.env,control.env}
sudo ./smoke.sh                  # writable OverlayFS needs mount privilege; verifies end to end

A green smoke prints == SMOKE PASS == and leaves PostgreSQL, MinIO, and the three host services running for further use. Tear everything down with:

./clean.sh          # stop containers, keep volumes + config
./clean.sh -v       # also remove the postgres + minio volumes
./clean.sh --purge  # full reset: volumes, generated config, and runtime data

First time? Read the tutorial

For a guided, step-by-step walk that explains each step, see Your first workspace. This page is the reference procedure for repeating the local-dev smoke.

docs.title: What the smoke verifies
docs.text:
Each step fails loudly if the real path does not work. There are no mocked successes.

  1. cargo build of awc-control, awc-worker, awcd, awcctl with their s3 and fuse features (CARGO_INCREMENTAL=0 keeps the build off the disk cliff).
  2. PostgreSQL and MinIO become healthy. The awc-cas bucket is created.
  3. awc-control connects to PostgreSQL, applies the awc-db schema migrations, serves REST and gRPC, and the dev bootstrap mints a service token (captured from the log).
  4. The seed identity rows (seed/seed.sql) load with the Admin role on the dev project.
  5. awc-worker connects to PostgreSQL over the durable s3:// MinIO CAS and starts its run loop.
  6. awcd starts from the generated config/awcd.toml, mounts a real read-only FUSE base filesystem over MinIO, and serves its host API. The kernel is polled until it reports a fuse* filesystem at the basefs mountpoint. /healthz corroborates that the base-fuse component is up.
  7. awcctl snapshot create runs the full import protocol (session over the control plane, objects uploaded straight to the MinIO CAS, completion over the control plane) and reports the snapshot id, manifest digest, and file count.
  8. awcctl snapshot inspect and list round-trip against the control plane.
  9. The just-imported snapshot is read through the FUSE base mount. Bytes are fetched from MinIO on demand, content-verified, served, and compared byte-for-byte with the source fixture.
  10. The worker validates the snapshot object closure by reading it back from the CAS, and advances it VALIDATING -> READY. The smoke polls until READY.
  11. awcctl workspace fork from the READY snapshot, then mount (the ticket is issued over the control plane and redeemed at the host daemon; the session is registered), then unmount.

Inspect intermediate output under run/ (build.log, control.log, worker.log, awcd.log, bucket.log, seed.log, awcctl.log).

docs.title: Generated credentials and configuration
docs.text:
bin/generate-credentials.sh produces:

File Contents .env Random POSTGRES_PASSWORD, MINIO_ROOT_PASSWORD, and AWC_SERVICE_TOKEN_KEY, plus reproducible identifiers and ports config/awcd.toml awcd config: host_id, roots under data/, loopback health port, cache/checkpoint/lease limits, and the control_plane_endpoint at the control gRPC port config/worker.env DATABASE_URL, AWC_CAS_URL=s3://…, worker tuning, and the S3 staging variables config/control.env awc-control env: DATABASE_URL, REST and gRPC listen addresses, the shared MinIO CAS and S3 variables, the service-token key, and the dev-bootstrap identity

Secrets are random. Identifiers (for example host_01arz3ndektsv4rrffq69g5fav) are fixed and reproducible so the seeded host row matches awcd's configured host_id. Re-running the generator reuses an existing .env so its password keeps matching an initialized PostgreSQL volume. Pass --force to regenerate secrets, then run ./clean.sh -v, since a new password does not match the old volume. Generated files are gitignored and never committed.

awcctl is driven through environment variables in local-dev. The smoke sources config/worker.env (for the MinIO CAS upload) and sets the control-plane and host endpoints and the dev token:

set -a; . config/worker.env; set +a
export AWC_CONTROL_ENDPOINT="http://127.0.0.1:8080"
export AWC_HOST_SOCKET="$PWD/run/awcd.sock"
export AWC_TENANT  AWC_PROJECT        # the seeded dev tenant/project
export AWC_TOKEN="<dev service token>"  # minted by awc-control on startup
awcctl snapshot create --from-dir seed/source --name demo
awcctl status                          # host health via awcd

See configuration and environment variables for the full key and variable reference.

docs.title: Manual bring-up
docs.text:
The smoke automates all of this. The individual steps for a manual run:

bin/generate-credentials.sh
docker compose up -d postgres minio
docker compose run --rm minio-init            # create the CAS bucket

# awc-control migrates the schema on startup and mints the dev token.
set -a; . config/control.env; set +a
awc-control &  CONTROL_PID=$!
DEV_TOKEN=$(grep -m1 'awc-control dev token:' run/control.log | sed 's/.*awc-control dev token: //')

docker compose exec -T postgres psql -U awc -d awc < seed/seed.sql

set -a; . config/worker.env; set +a
awc-worker &

awcd config/awcd.toml run/awcd.sock &

export AWC_CONTROL_ENDPOINT="http://127.0.0.1:8080" AWC_HOST_SOCKET="$PWD/run/awcd.sock"
export AWC_TENANT AWC_PROJECT AWC_TOKEN="$DEV_TOKEN"
awcctl snapshot create --from-dir seed/source --name demo

docs.title: Current scope (honest)
docs.text:
This environment wires every component that is implemented today and is explicit about what is not, rather than faking a working service.

Verified working end to end by the smoke:

  • awc-control is a live service (REST and gRPC). It migrates the schema, serves /v1/*, verifies bearer service tokens, and writes imports into the durable MinIO CAS. Completing an import enqueues a snapshot_validate job, so the worker advances snapshots VALIDATING -> READY.
  • The worker reads from MinIO (AWC_CAS_URL=s3://awc-cas), not an in-process store. It drains the queue and validates snapshot object closure against the real CAS.
  • awcd mounts a real read-only FUSE base filesystem, not a no-op. Objects are fetched from MinIO on demand, content-verified, and served. The smoke reads an imported snapshot through $BASEFS/tenants/<tenant>/snapshots/<manifest>/… and compares bytes with the source.

The privileged smoke also verifies the writable path. It checks that the target is OverlayFS, mutates and deletes files, publishes a cooperative checkpoint, unmounts, immediately reacquires the writer lease, and verifies the changes from the new immutable head after remount.

Not exercised by this smoke:

  • Production mTLS. The smoke sets AWC_DEV_MODE=1 and uses loopback plaintext. Outside that mode, awcd and awc-control require mutually authenticated TLS and fail startup on missing credentials. See the security model.

docs.title: Files
docs.text:
local-dev/
├── docker-compose.yml        postgres + minio + minio-init
├── .env.example              tunables (committed); .env is generated
├── bin/
│   └── generate-credentials.sh
├── config/
│   ├── awcd.toml.example     generated shape (committed); awcd.toml is generated
│   ├── worker.env.example    generated shape (committed); worker.env is generated
│   └── control.env.example   generated shape (committed); control.env is generated
├── seed/
│   ├── seed.sql              deterministic identity rows (tenant/project/principal/host)
│   └── source/               fixture dir the snapshot-import flow uploads
├── smoke.sh                  end-to-end verification
├── clean.sh                  teardown
└── README.md                 in-tree pointer to this page

docs.title: Run the test suite
docs.text:
Run the AWC test suites and the full continuous-integration (CI) gate on your machine. The test program spans several corpora: unit, property and fuzz, manifest golden, differential filesystem, integration, kernel compatibility, fault injection, security, scale, performance, and soak.

The toolchain is pinned by rust-toolchain.toml. Dependencies are locked by Cargo.lock and audited by cargo-deny (deny.toml). Every test corpus is a workspace member, so one --workspace run picks it up.

docs.title: 1. Run the workspace suite
docs.text:
make test

make test runs cargo test --workspace --all-targets. It builds every crate and test target, then runs the unit and integration tests. The manifest golden tests and the checkpoint fault-injection tests run here.

docs.title: 2. Verify formatting
docs.text:
make fmt-check

make fmt-check runs cargo fmt --all -- --check. It fails if any source is not formatted. Run make fmt to fix the formatting in place.

docs.title: 3. Lint the workspace
docs.text:
make lint

make lint runs cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings. Every warning is an error.

docs.title: 4. Audit dependencies
docs.text:
make deny

make deny runs cargo deny check. It audits licenses, advisories, bans, and sources across the workspace, as configured in deny.toml.

docs.title: 5. Run the full CI gate
docs.text:
make ci

make ci runs make check plus make deny. make check is the fast local gate: fmt-check, lint, and test. The Makefile marks make check as network-free. make ci adds the dependency audit, which may fetch the advisory database on the first run. This is the same gate CI enforces on every change.

Corpora that degrade, not fail

Some corpora report reduced coverage instead of failing when the host lacks privileges or tools. They still run under make test.

  • The overlay kernel matrix corpus: the static probes run privilege-free on any Linux host. The functional, mount-requiring probe reports NotAssessed without CAP_SYS_ADMIN. Run it privileged to exercise the functional categories.
  • The tool compatibility corpus: it materializes a snapshot to a plain directory and runs one documented operation of each certified tool. A tool absent from your PATH is skipped with a note, not failed. No privileges or /dev/fuse are required.
  • The fuse differential and security corpora drive the pure read-path core and the policy gates. They need no /dev/fuse and no privileges.

docs.title: 6. Run the tests with the production features
docs.text:
make test-prod

make test-prod runs the test suites of awcd, awc-control, awc-worker, and awcctl with the exact feature set the release binaries carry: the fuse and s3 features enabled together. The default make test target runs default features only; CI compiles the production union and executes it through make test-prod on every change. Tests that need a real /dev/fuse device stay #[ignore]'d and do not run here either.

docs.title: 7. Run the backing-service suites
docs.text:
make test skips the #[ignore]'d suites that need a live database or object store. Run them separately.

Postgres integration tests:

make ci-pg DATABASE_URL=postgres://localhost/awc_ci

make ci-pg sets AWC_PG_TESTS=1, targets the awc-db, awc-control, awc-worker, awc-gc-safety-tests, and awc-end-to-end-tests packages, and runs --ignored --test-threads=1. Point DATABASE_URL at a fresh database.

minio or S3 transport test (feature s3):

make ci-s3 AWC_S3_ENDPOINT=http://127.0.0.1:9000 AWC_S3_BUCKET=awc-cas \
    AWC_S3_ACCESS_KEY_ID=minio AWC_S3_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=minio123 \
    AWC_S3_ALLOW_HTTP=1

An http:// endpoint additionally needs AWC_S3_ALLOW_HTTP=1 (plaintext is an explicit opt-in; https is the default), and a real provider needs its SigV4 region via AWC_S3_REGION. Both targets fail loudly if a required variable is unset, so a misconfiguration cannot pass silently.

docs.title: 8. Run a single crate or corpus
docs.text:
Target one workspace package by name:

cargo test -p awc-manifest --all-targets
cargo test -p awc-overlay-kernel-matrix-tests

Run one test by name:

cargo test -p awc-manifest golden

The .cargo/config.toml aliases mirror the Makefile targets, so cargo lint, cargo fmt-check, and cargo deny-check run the same checks.

docs.title: Measure coverage
docs.text:
make coverage writes an lcov report for the whole workspace. It needs cargo-llvm-cov and the llvm-tools component:

rustup component add llvm-tools
cargo install cargo-llvm-cov --locked
make coverage
# -> lcov.info

The report has no threshold gate. In CI, the coverage workflow runs the same command weekly (Monday 05:23 UTC) and on dispatch, appends the summary to the job summary, and uploads lcov.info as a 14-day artifact.

docs.title: Measure performance
docs.text:
make test runs the deterministic regression gates as ordinary tests. The wall-clock benchmarks are separate. They run on a reference host, not in CI:

cargo run -p awc-performance --bin awc-perf --release

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Package a build with the build and package guide.
  • Read the contribution guide before you push.
  • Browse the fuzz targets and the kernel compatibility reference.

docs.title: Unmount a workspace
docs.text:
Release the writer lease and tear down a mounted workspace. The disposition controls what happens to your local, uncheckpointed writes (spec §11.11, §13.13).

Before you start: hold the mount session id. This is the session field that mount a workspace prints, not the workspace id. The host daemon awcd MUST be running.

  1. Capture the mount session id.

    awcctl workspace mount ws_01J... --target /workspace

    Read the session field from the output. AWC does not list live session ids from the command-line interface (CLI). If you lost the id, you cannot unmount that session.

  2. Choose a disposition for your local writes. Pick one.

    discard-local (default)checkpointpreserve-local

    Drop uncheckpointed writes and delete the private upper directory. The spec says destructive discard MUST be explicit when uncheckpointed changes exist (spec §11.11). This is the CLI default.

    Cut a checkpoint from the upper, then unmount. A checkpoint disposition returns both the checkpoint result and the unmount result (spec §13.13).

    Unmount but keep the upper on the host for a bounded recovery window (spec §11.11). Use it when you are not ready to checkpoint or discard.

  3. Unmount the session. Pass the session id and the disposition.

    awcctl workspace unmount sess_01J... --disposition preserve-local

    Omit --disposition to use the default, discard-local. The command prints unmounted sess_01J.... Pass --idempotency-key (or set AWC_IDEMPOTENCY_KEY) so a retry does not double-submit (spec §13.1).

  4. Confirm the lease released and the mount is gone.

    awcctl status

    The mounts field drops by one. Run the unmount a second time on the same session. It returns NOT_FOUND, which proves the session record is gone.

discard-local is destructive

discard-local drops writes you have not checkpointed. The spec requires that destructive discard be explicit when uncheckpointed changes exist (spec §11.11). To keep your writes, use checkpoint or preserve-local. Or run checkpoint a workspace first.

Current build: --disposition is accepted but not honored

The CLI parses --disposition and sends it on the wire, but awcd does not yet act on it. The daemon unmounts the merged view and removes the session record. It releases the writer lease when a control-plane client is configured. It does not:

  • cut a checkpoint for --disposition checkpoint;
  • enforce the explicit-discard gate for --disposition discard-local;
  • delete or retain the upper for --disposition preserve-local.

The full disposition policy is implemented and tested, but it is not wired into the daemon. To save writes today, run checkpoint a workspace before you unmount.

Releasing the lease frees the workspace for another writer

A forced unmount MUST release the writer lease and MUST prevent later publication from that lease generation (spec §11.11, §9.10). The fencing generation keeps a paused or partitioned old host from publishing after a new writer takes over (spec §14.4).

docs.title: Upgrade a deployment
docs.text:
This page is the operational upgrade and compatibility runbook for AWC. It states the compatibility guarantees the implementation must preserve across a rolling upgrade, the daemon upgrade procedure operators follow, the artifacts every release ships, and how each guarantee is verified in CI. It is written for an operator who is not on the core implementation team.

The testable guarantees below are turned into machine-checked assertions run in CI.

docs.title: Scope
docs.text:
An "upgrade" is any change to the awcd, awc-worker, awc-control, or awcctl binaries deployed to a running fleet without erasing state — a rolling deploy where, for a time, mixed binary versions and mixed on-disk/object formats coexist. This document covers four compatibility axes:

  1. Manifest formats — immutable, versioned on-disk and object content formats.
  2. Control-plane database schema — PostgreSQL migrations.
  3. API and RPC protocols — external /v1 HTTP and internal gRPC, including host and control registration.
  4. Mount tickets — short-lived signed capabilities carried between control plane and host.

docs.title: Compatibility guarantees
docs.text:
These guarantees are normative. Each is verified in CI (see "Verification" column); a release that breaks one must not ship.

# Guarantee What it means operationally Verification G1 Manifest formats are versioned and immutable. Every serialized manifest carries a format version; a given (version, payload) always decodes to the same logical object. A format, once published, is never silently reinterpreted. Decoded against golden manifest vectors in CI. G2 New daemons MUST read every non-retired prior format. After an upgrade, awcd, awc-worker, and the import and checkpoint paths still decode snapshots and trees written by every older, non-retired version. No on-disk rewrite is required to read them. Decodes vectors for every supported read version in CI. G3 Writers create only the configured current format. The version written by import and checkpoint is a single configurable current write version (default = the newest supported version), never an arbitrary or stale one. Rolling forward is therefore monotone and intentional. Asserts a single configured current write version in CI. G4 Control-plane schema migrations MUST be backward-compatible during rolling deploys. During the window where old and new binaries share one database, both must function. Migrations are additive only (no destructive DDL), so an old binary reading a newer schema continues to work. Scans the embedded migration set for destructive DDL and pins monotonic versions in CI. G5 Mount tickets include protocol version and expiry. A ticket names the protocol version it was minted under and an absolute expiry, so a host can reject a ticket minted for an incompatible version or one that is stale after a long partition. Ticket versioning and expiry exercised in CI. G6 A daemon upgrade MUST not require rewriting existing snapshots. Upgrading awcd never rewrites or re-hashes existing snapshots or CAS objects. Snapshots are immutable; the upgrade only changes code and (additively) schema. Asserts no snapshot is rewritten on upgrade in CI.

docs.title: API and RPC protocol compatibility
docs.text:
• External API is versioned by path (/v1). Additive fields are allowed within a version; removing a field or changing its semantics requires a new API version. Clients MUST tolerate unknown additive fields.
  • Internal gRPC (host ↔ control plane over mTLS) reserves removed protobuf field numbers so an old reader ignores fields a newer writer adds.
  • Protocol-range negotiation: during host registration, the host and the control plane exchange the ranges of protocol versions each supports and select the newest mutually-supported version. A pair with empty overlap fails registration with an explicit error rather than proceeding with mismatched assumptions.

The negotiation is pure logic: a set intersection over [min, max] ranges. The helper is unit-tested in isolation so the contract is fixed before the live registration RPC is wired.

docs.title: Daemon upgrade runbook
docs.text:
To upgrade awcd on a host without losing in-flight work:

  1. Mark the host unschedulable for new mounts — stop admitting new privileged mount operations. Existing mounts keep serving reads.
  2. Wait for in-flight checkpoints to finish. Do not proceed while a publication transaction is open; an interrupted checkpoint is recoverable, but draining it cleanly is preferred.
  3. Preserve mount-session metadata. Do not delete upper or work directories or the local cache index on upgrade. They are reconciled on restart. Never delete an upper merely because the control plane is unreachable.
  4. Verify binary and format compatibility. Confirm the new binary supports every non-retired manifest version present in the cache and object store.
  5. Restart awcd (for example, systemctl restart awcd).
  6. Reconcile shared FUSE and overlay mounts. On restart awcd re-walks mount-session metadata and re-establishes overlays that were live before the restart, recovering all host-local crash classes.
  7. Renew valid leases. Leases whose fencing generation is still current are renewed; stale generations are fenced off and routed to offline export so the acknowledged head is preserved.
  8. Run read and write probes (health and readiness, plus a sample mount).
  9. Return the host to scheduling.
  10. Roll back if compatibility or latency checks fail.

docs.title: Rollback
docs.text:
Rollback is the reverse procedure against the previous binary and the previous configuration, not a schema rollback: because every migration is additive (G4), the newer schema remains readable by the older binary, so rolling back the code is safe without touching the database. Operators:

  1. Mark the host unschedulable (step 1 above).
  2. Reinstall the previous binary (the versioned layout under /opt/awc keeps prior versions; rollback.sh repoints /opt/awc/current).
  3. Restart awcd and re-run the probes (steps 5–8).
  4. Return the host to scheduling.

Never roll back by reverting a database migration. If a migration is genuinely faulty, that is a forward fix (a corrective additive migration), not a revert.

docs.title: Release artifacts
docs.text:
Every release MUST produce the artifacts below. package.sh puts the ones marked tarball inside share/awc/ of the release tarball, so SHA256SUMS covers them (see Build and package):

  • signed binaries or images (sign.sh, package.sh);
  • software bill of materials (tarball, sbom.spdx.json via syft);
  • database migration bundle (the additive, forward-only migration set) (tarball, migrations/);
  • manifest-format compatibility report (G1–G3, verified against golden vectors in CI, not a standalone file);
  • supported kernel matrix (tarball, docs/kernel-compatibility.md);
  • upgrade and rollback notes (this document; tarball copy at docs/upgrade.md);
  • security scan results;
  • performance regression report;
  • golden manifest vectors (tarball, golden-vectors/golden_vectors.json).

docs.title: Current status (honest)
docs.text: Axis Status Manifest format versioning (G1–G3) Implemented: every manifest carries a version. The decoder accepts every supported read version (minus retired versions) and rejects all others. Writers stamp the current write version (1 today). Verified in CI. Database migrations (G4) Implemented: embedded migrations are additive and enforced forward-only in CI. Mount-ticket versioning (G5) Implemented: mount tickets carry a protocol version and an absolute expiry, and are Ed25519-signed. The daemon rejects an incompatible protocol version. Verified in CI. Snapshot immutability on upgrade (G6) Guaranteed by construction: snapshots and CAS objects are immutable and are never rewritten by an upgrade. Verified in CI. Protocol-range negotiation Implemented: host registration exchanges and negotiates supported protocol-version ranges, rejecting disjoint ranges. Verified in CI. Live host drain / reconcile (runbook) awcd reconciles host-local state and renews leases on restart. The operator-facing drain toggle and rollback tooling ship as systemd units and packaging scripts. awc-control Live REST and mutually authenticated internal gRPC service. Worker CAS transport Production releases include the S3 transport; an in-memory transport remains available for tests and explicit development. awcd base mount Production release builds use the real FUSE base mount; featureless CI builds retain a no-op lifecycle test double.

docs.title: Configuration reference
docs.text: This page lists every awcd configuration knob. It covers the file keys, the matching environment variables, the defaults, and the validation rules. The normative source is spec §22.9.

docs.title: Sources and precedence
docs.text:
awcd resolves its configuration from layered sources. Later sources override earlier ones, field by field. A field that is left unset falls back to the next source, and then to its default.

file  <  environment  <  flags
Source How it is supplied Notes File First positional argument to awcd. Parsed as TOML. See awcd daemon reference. Environment Variables with the AWC_ prefix. Nested keys use a __ separator. Flags A pre-built layer passed to the awc-config library. The awcd binary does not apply a flags layer. It uses the file and environment sources only.

Merge rules:

  • A set value in a later layer replaces the value from an earlier layer.
  • Nested tables merge field by field. A file [cache] max_bytes and an environment AWC_CACHE__MAX_REMOTE_FETCHES both survive.
  • Numeric limits fall back to their spec defaults when no layer sets them.
  • Mandatory deployment fields have no default. At least one layer must set them.

docs.title: File format
docs.text: The daemon parses the file as TOML. The config library also supports JSON, but awcd uses TOML only. Spec §22.9 shows the keys in a YAML block. The keys match; the surface syntax differs. Use TOML on disk.

docs.title: Daemon invocation
docs.text:
awcd <config.toml|-> [socket-path]
  • <config.toml>: path to a TOML file. Use - to skip the file and configure from the environment only.
  • [socket-path]: host API Unix socket. Falls back to AWCD_SOCKET, then to /run/awcd/awcd.sock.

The daemon exits with FAILURE when the config path is missing, when a required field is unset, or when validation fails. See awcd daemon reference for the full lifecycle.

docs.title: Configuration keys
docs.text: Every key below can be set in the file or in the environment. The Env var column gives the exact environment name. Top-level keys use a flat name. Keys under [cache], [checkpoint], and [leases] use an AWC_<SECTION>__<KEY> name.

docs.title: Top-level keys
docs.text: Key Type Default Env var Validation and effect host_id string (host_<ulid>) required AWC_HOST_ID Identifier of the local host. Must parse as host_ followed by a ULID (spec §9.1). control_plane_endpoint URL required AWC_CONTROL_PLANE_ENDPOINT Control plane endpoint. Must use the http or https scheme. Used for lease lookup and checkpoint publish. basefs_mount absolute path required AWC_BASEFS_MOUNT Mount point for the read-only base filesystem. Must be absolute and distinct from the other roots. cache_root absolute path required AWC_CACHE_ROOT Root directory of the local content cache. Must be absolute and distinct from the other roots. workspace_root absolute path required AWC_WORKSPACE_ROOT Root directory for per-workspace merged mounts. Must be absolute and distinct from the other roots. allowed_bind_roots array of absolute paths [] (empty) AWC_ALLOWED_BIND_ROOTS Host paths that may be used as bind targets. Environment value is a comma-separated list. Every entry must be absolute. health_http_listen string (host:port) unset (disabled) AWC_HEALTH_HTTP_LISTEN Loopback address for the liveness, readiness, and metrics HTTP endpoints (spec §19.6). When unset, the HTTP server is disabled and the host API stays on the Unix socket. Should be a loopback address.

docs.title: [cache]
docs.text: Key Type Default Env var Validation and effect max_bytes u64 1000000000000 AWC_CACHE__MAX_BYTES Total byte limit of the local cache. Must be greater than zero. min_free_bytes u64 50000000000 AWC_CACHE__MIN_FREE_BYTES Free space to preserve on the host filesystem. Drives the disk-pressure governor ladder (spec §17.8). max_remote_fetches u32 128 AWC_CACHE__MAX_REMOTE_FETCHES Bound on object-store read concurrency. max_remote_fetches_per_tenant u32 32 AWC_CACHE__MAX_REMOTE_FETCHES_PER_TENANT Per-tenant bound on object-store read concurrency. Must not exceed max_remote_fetches. max_prefetch_fetches u32 8 AWC_CACHE__MAX_PREFETCH_FETCHES Prefetch concurrency. Must not exceed max_remote_fetches.

docs.title: [checkpoint]
docs.text: Key Type Default Env var Validation and effect max_concurrent u32 4 AWC_CHECKPOINT__MAX_CONCURRENT Maximum concurrent checkpoint uploads. Must be greater than zero. freeze_timeout_seconds u64 10 AWC_CHECKPOINT__FREEZE_TIMEOUT_SECONDS Freeze or quiesce timeout for cutting a checkpoint. Must be greater than zero. preserve_local_grace_seconds u64 3600 AWC_CHECKPOINT__PRESERVE_LOCAL_GRACE_SECONDS Grace period for preserving local changes after a checkpoint. Must be greater than zero.

docs.title: [leases]
docs.text: Key Type Default Env var Validation and effect renew_interval_seconds u64 30 AWC_LEASES__RENEW_INTERVAL_SECONDS How often the holder renews the lease. Must be strictly less than expiry_seconds. expiry_seconds u64 90 AWC_LEASES__EXPIRY_SECONDS Lease lifetime before automatic expiry. disconnected_grace_seconds u64 60 AWC_LEASES__DISCONNECTED_GRACE_SECONDS Grace period for a disconnected holder before revocation. Must be greater than zero.

docs.title: Object-store endpoint
docs.text:
The object-store endpoint is environment only. It is not part of awcd.toml. The daemon reads AWC_CAS_URL to select the transport, then reads the transport-specific variables.

Env var Required Default Validation and effect AWC_CAS_URL no memory:// Selects the verified-cache transport. Accepted values are memory:// for the in-memory store and s3:// for the S3-compatible transport. The s3:// value requires that awcd was built with the s3 feature. Any other value fails startup. AWC_S3_ENDPOINT yes, when AWC_CAS_URL=s3:// none Service endpoint, as scheme plus host and optional port. Must be an absolute URL. AWC_S3_BUCKET yes, when AWC_CAS_URL=s3:// none Bucket name. May not be empty. AWC_S3_REGION no us-east-1 SigV4 signing region. AWC_S3_KEY_PREFIX no empty Key prefix applied before the canonical CAS key. A single bucket can host several deployments under disjoint prefixes. AWC_S3_ACCESS_KEY_ID no none Access key id. Credentials activate only when this and AWC_S3_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY are both set. AWC_S3_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY no none Secret access key. Credentials activate only when this and AWC_S3_ACCESS_KEY_ID are both set. AWC_S3_SESSION_TOKEN no none Optional session token. Ignored when empty.

The object-store request path is scoped to a tenant prefix (spec §9.2). Agents do not receive object-store credentials (spec §13.2).

docs.title: Validation invariants
docs.text:
Startup rejects contradictory or unsafe settings (spec §22.9). The resolver checks the following before the daemon starts:

  • basefs_mount, cache_root, and workspace_root are three distinct paths.
  • cache.max_remote_fetches_per_tenant is less than or equal to cache.max_remote_fetches.
  • cache.max_prefetch_fetches is less than or equal to cache.max_remote_fetches.
  • cache.max_bytes is greater than zero.
  • checkpoint.max_concurrent is greater than zero.
  • checkpoint.freeze_timeout_seconds is greater than zero.
  • checkpoint.preserve_local_grace_seconds is greater than zero.
  • leases.renew_interval_seconds is strictly less than leases.expiry_seconds.
  • leases.disconnected_grace_seconds is greater than zero.
  • control_plane_endpoint uses the http or https scheme.
  • Every entry in allowed_bind_roots is an absolute path.
  • host_id parses as host_<ulid>.
  • health_http_listen parses as a host:port socket address when set.

docs.title: Worked example
docs.text:
host_id = "host_01arz3ndektsv4rrffq69g5fav"
control_plane_endpoint = "https://control.example"
basefs_mount = "/var/lib/awc/basefs"
cache_root = "/var/lib/awc/cache"
workspace_root = "/var/lib/awc/workspaces"
allowed_bind_roots = ["/var/lib/agent-sandboxes"]
health_http_listen = "127.0.0.1:9100"

[cache]
max_bytes = 1000000000000
min_free_bytes = 50000000000

[checkpoint]
max_concurrent = 4

[leases]
renew_interval_seconds = 30
expiry_seconds = 90
disconnected_grace_seconds = 60

With the file above, an operator can narrow the cache limit from the environment without editing the file:

export AWC_CACHE__MAX_BYTES=200000000000
awcd /etc/awc/awcd.toml

docs.title: Current scope
docs.text:
• The flags layer is a capability of the config library. The awcd binary does not feed command-line flags into the config layer. Its only positional arguments are the config path and the socket path.
  • The library can parse a JSON config file. The daemon hardcodes TOML and ignores JSON on disk.
  • The object-store endpoint, the mount-ticket verifier key, and the checkpoint cgroup roots are environment only. The socket path is a positional argument with an AWCD_SOCKET fallback. None of them has a key in awcd.toml. These runtime variables are covered on the environment variables page.
  • Every knob listed in spec §22.9 is implemented and validated in the current build.

docs.title: Data model reference
docs.text:
This page lists the identifiers, object kinds, manifest fields, and mutable control-plane records that make up AWC. Immutable object fields come from the object manifests. Mutable record columns come from the control-plane database rows and the API types.

For the byte-level canonical CBOR encoding, see On-disk format. For the SQL schema, see Database schema.

docs.title: Identifiers
docs.text:
Human-facing resources use opaque, sortable identifiers of the form <prefix>_<ulid>. The ULID is 26 characters, case-insensitive, and monotonic. The prefix is fixed per resource kind.

Resource Prefix Identifier type Tenant ten_ TenantId Project prj_ ProjectId Snapshot snap_ SnapshotId Workspace ws_ WorkspaceId Writer lease lease_ LeaseId Host host_ HostId Import session import_ ImportSessionId Mount session mount_ MountSessionId

A second _ in the ULID portion is rejected. Each kind is a distinct type, so a TenantId never aliases a ProjectId. The mount-session prefix (mount_) is not in the standard prefix list; it is defined separately.

Content objects do not use these identifiers. They are named by digests.

docs.title: Object digests
docs.text:
An immutable object is named by an algorithm-qualified digest.

sha256:<64 lowercase hexadecimal characters>
Property Value Canonical algorithm sha256 Raw length 32 bytes Wire form <algorithm>:<hex>, lowercase hex only Supported algorithms Sha256 only

The algorithm enum exists so keys and digests can migrate later without a format break. The MVP writes and reads sha256 only. Uppercase hex is rejected on parse.

docs.title: Digest domain
docs.text:
A digest is computed over a kind-specific domain:

SHA256("awc:v1:" || object_kind || 0x00 || canonical_payload)
  • object_kind is the ASCII label BLOB, FILE, TREE, or SNAPSHOT.
  • 0x00 is one separator byte.
  • For BLOB, canonical_payload is the raw blob bytes.
  • For FILE, TREE, and SNAPSHOT, canonical_payload is the deterministic canonical CBOR encoding.

Object kind is part of the hashed domain. The same byte payload cannot be interpreted as two kinds.

docs.title: Tenant-scoped content addressing
docs.text:
Content deduplication is scoped to a tenant. Identical bytes share one object within a tenant, never across tenants.

The canonical remote object key is:

cas/v1/tenants/<tenant-id>/<algorithm>/<first-2>/<next-2>/<digest>

For example:

cas/v1/tenants/ten_01.../sha256/ab/cd/abcd1234...

<first-2> and <next-2> are the first two and next two hex characters of the digest. A digest collision across tenants does not create a shared object or a shared cache key.

The host-local cache uses the same tenant scoping:

Layer Key Singleflight (tenant_id, digest) Cache index primary key (tenant_id, digest) On-disk path objects/<tenant-id>/sha256/<first-2>/<next-2>/<hex>

The cache index also records object_kind and validates it, although the digest domain already includes the kind.

docs.title: Object kinds
docs.text:
The CAS stores four immutable object kinds.

Kind Label Holds BLOB BLOB Raw file or chunk bytes FILE FILE File metadata and references to one or more blobs TREE TREE Sorted directory entries SNAPSHOT SNAPSHOT Immutable root metadata and provenance

A BLOB payload is unstructured bytes. Compression at rest is allowed only when the object-store key still names the digest of the uncompressed bytes and the stored envelope records the codec. The MVP default is no application compression for source-code-sized blobs.

docs.title: FILE manifest
docs.text:
A file is stored whole when it is smaller than the inline threshold, and split into fixed chunks otherwise.

Field Type Notes version uint Always FORMAT_VERSION (1) size uint Logical file size in bytes mode uint POSIX mode bits mtime_ns int \| null Nanoseconds since the epoch, or null chunks array One or more chunk entries content_digest text Plain SHA-256 of the complete logical bytes

Chunk fields:

Field Type Notes offset uint Byte offset within the logical file length uint32 Chunk length in bytes digest text Domain-separated blob digest of the chunk bytes

Layout rules:

Constant Value Behavior INLINE_THRESHOLD_BYTES 8 MiB Files with size < threshold use one blob reference CHUNK_SIZE_BYTES 4 MiB Files at or above the threshold split into fixed chunks
  • Chunks are contiguous, non-overlapping, start at offset zero, and sum to size.
  • The final chunk may be smaller.
  • An empty file is one zero-length chunk that references an empty blob.
  • Each chunks[].digest is a domain-separated blob digest.
  • content_digest is the plain SHA-256 of the logical bytes. It is independent of chunking.
  • Content-defined chunking is deferred. The format permits it later.

docs.title: TREE manifest
docs.text:
A tree is a sorted list of directory entries.

Field Type Notes version uint Always FORMAT_VERSION (1) entries array Sorted, de-duplicated entries

Tree entry fields:

Field Type Notes name bytes Raw filename bytes; no UTF-8 assumption type text FILE, TREE, or SYMLINK digest text Digest of the referenced object mode uint POSIX mode bits symlink_target bytes | null Raw target bytes; only for SYMLINK

Rules:

  • Entries are sorted lexicographically by raw name bytes.
  • A name must be non-empty. A name must not contain / (0x2f) or NUL (0x00).
  • Duplicate names are invalid.
  • A SYMLINK entry must carry a non-empty symlink_target. The target is stored verbatim and is never followed during import.
  • Directory identity depends on entry names, types, metadata, and child digests.

A SYMLINK entry references a BLOB object that carries the link target.

docs.title: SNAPSHOT manifest
docs.text:
A snapshot pins a root tree and records provenance and aggregate counters.

Field Type Notes version uint Always FORMAT_VERSION (1) root_tree text Digest of the root TREE manifest parent_snapshot text | null Parent snapshot digest, or null logical_bytes uint Total logical bytes reachable from the root tree file_count uint Files reachable from the root tree tree_count uint Trees reachable from the root tree normalization_policy text source-normalized or environment-preserving source map Provenance; see below created_by text Opaque principal reference created_at int Unix nanoseconds since the epoch labels map Free-form text to text; sorted by key

source sub-fields:

Field Type Notes type text directory, git, tar, or checkpoint locator text | null Source path or URL immutable_revision text | null Immutable revision, for example a Git commit

The snapshot content digest excludes mutable control-plane aliases and retention state. Human-readable names point to a snapshot record. They are not part of content identity.

docs.title: Snapshot closure
docs.text: A snapshot may enter READY only when every object reachable from its root manifest is present and valid in the tenant CAS. The graph validator walks the snapshot, checks object kinds, and confirms that logical_bytes, file_count, and tree_count match the traversed graph.

docs.title: Format versioning
docs.text:
Every serialized manifest includes a version field.

Constant Value Meaning FORMAT_VERSION 1 Alias for the current write version CURRENT_WRITE_VERSION 1 Version every new manifest is written at SUPPORTED_READ_VERSIONS [1] Versions a new daemon must read RETIRED_VERSIONS [] Versions no longer read

A decoder accepts only a supported, non-retired version. Unknown optional fields are ignored so newer formats stay decodable. The digest domain prefix awc:v1: carries its own version tag, so the hash algorithm or structure can migrate without ambiguity with existing objects.

docs.title: Normalization policies
docs.text:
Snapshot creation must declare one normalization policy. The wire form is kebab-case.

Policy Wire value Purpose SourceNormalized source-normalized Deterministic reuse for source repositories. Normalizes UID and GID to zero, normalizes mtime to zero, clears setuid and setgid bits, removes unsupported xattrs. EnvironmentPreserving environment-preserving Prepared dependency and build environments. Preserves mtime. Normalizes UID and GID to zero unless configured. Clears setuid and setgid bits by default.

The selected policy is recorded in snapshot provenance.

docs.title: Snapshot record (control plane)
docs.text:
The database row for a snapshot:

Column Type Notes id String snap_<ulid> tenant_id String ten_<ulid> project_id String prj_<ulid> manifest_digest String Digest of the SNAPSHOT object root_tree_digest String Digest of the root TREE object state String Snapshot state wire value; see below logical_bytes i64 Denormalized from the manifest file_count i64 Denormalized from the manifest parent_snapshot_id String? Parent snapshot record id source_type String directory, git, tar, or checkpoint normalization_policy String source-normalized or environment-preserving created_by String Principal reference created_at DateTime labels jsonb

Snapshot state values:

Value Meaning UPLOADING Object upload is in progress VALIDATING Objects uploaded; integrity checks are running READY Immutable and usable as a workspace base FAILED Validation or publication failed DELETING A delete is in progress DELETED The snapshot and its objects are removed DEGRADED Readable, but some backing objects are unavailable

Only READY snapshots may be used as new workspace bases.

docs.title: Workspace record
docs.text:
The database row for a workspace:

Column Type Notes id String ws_<ulid> tenant_id String project_id String base_snapshot_id String head_snapshot_id String version i64 Optimistic concurrency state String Workspace state wire value writer_lease_generation i64 Current fencing generation ttl_expires_at DateTime TTL expiry time name String? Control-plane alias; not part of content identity created_by String created_at DateTime updated_at DateTime labels jsonb

A fork creates a workspace whose base_snapshot_id and head_snapshot_id initially reference the same snapshot. The name column is a control-plane alias and is not part of content identity.

Workspace state values:

Value Meaning CREATING Being created from its base snapshot FAILED Creation failed IDLE Created and not mounted MOUNTED Mounted on at least one host CHECKPOINTING A checkpoint is being published EXPIRING TTL is expiring DELETED Removed from the control plane

docs.title: Writer lease record
docs.text:
The database row for a writer lease:

Column Type Notes id String lease_<ulid> workspace_id String generation i64 Monotonic fencing token host_id String mount_session_id String? state String Lease state wire value granted_at DateTime Time the lease was granted expires_at DateTime released_at DateTime? Time the lease was released, if it was

The generation is a monotonically increasing fencing token. A host with an older generation may keep local bytes but must not publish a checkpoint.

Lease state values:

Value Live Can publish Meaning ISSUED yes no Issued, not yet claimed by a mount ACTIVE yes yes Held by a mounted writer RELEASING yes yes Holder is releasing and publishing final state RELEASED no no Released cleanly EXPIRED no no Reached lifetime without release REVOKED no no Forcibly revoked by the control plane

Only an ACTIVE or RELEASING lease may advance the workspace head.

docs.title: Mount session record
docs.text:
The database row for a mount session:

Column Type Notes id String mount_<ulid> workspace_id String host_id String mode String READ_ONLY or READ_WRITE state String Mount session state wire value lease_id String? Set for a writable mount root_snapshot_digest String Digest of the sealed root target_path String Configured mount target path started_at DateTime ended_at DateTime?

Mount session state values:

Value Meaning REQUESTED Received, not yet authorized AUTHORIZED Authorized, preparation not started PREPARING FUSE and overlays are being prepared MOUNTED Live and serving I/O UNMOUNTING Unmount in progress CLOSED Closed cleanly (terminal) FAILED Mount failed or was lost (terminal)

docs.title: Mount ticket
docs.text:
A mount ticket is a short-lived, signed capability. The typed API struct is MountTicket. The signed payload is MountTicketClaims.

MountTicket fields:

Field Type Notes ticket_id String Opaque ticket id tenant_id TenantId workspace_id WorkspaceId snapshot_id SnapshotId Snapshot the mount is sealed against root_digest Digest Content digest of the sealed root tree host_id HostId The single audience host mode MountMode READ_ONLY or READ_WRITE lease_generation u64? Fencing generation for READ_WRITE; null for read-only target_policy TargetPolicy Allowed bind roots issued_at Timestamp expires_at Timestamp nonce String Single-use replay defeat protocol_version u32 Internal protocol version signed_ticket String Opaque, server-signed token for MountWorkspace

The signed claims (MountTicketClaims) carry the same identity fields and add sealing for checkpoint safety:

Claim Type Notes snapshot_manifest_digest Digest? Digest of the sealed SNAPSHOT manifest lease_id String? Control-plane lease identity mount_session_id String? workspace_version u64? Optimistic version sealed into the capability execution_cgroup String? Cgroup path for quiesce

Tickets should use Ed25519 signatures and must be verifiable by awcd without a synchronous control-plane call. The persisted ticket row stores signed_ticket and does not store root_digest. The root digest lives on the typed struct, the signed claims, and the mount session row.

docs.title: Patch bundle
docs.text:
A patch bundle describes a delta against a declared base snapshot.

Field Type Notes version u32 PATCH_BUNDLE_VERSION (1) base_snapshot_digest Digest? Base the delta is computed against result_snapshot_digest Digest? Result snapshot changes array Ordered PatchChange entries embedded_blobs array Complete binary payloads provenance ExportProvenance Free-form export provenance

PatchChange variants:

Variant Carries AddFile path, mode, digest, content ModifyFile path, old_mode, new_mode, old_digest, new_digest, content ChangeMode path, old_mode, new_mode DeleteFile path, mode AddDir path, mode DeleteDir path AddSymlink path, target ModifySymlink path, old_target, new_target DeleteSymlink path

FileContent representation:

Variant Carries Text unified_diff Binary blob_digest (reference into embedded_blobs)

EmbeddedBlob fields:

Field Type Notes digest Digest FILE manifest digest the payload belongs to size u64 Logical size in bytes data bytes Raw payload

ChangeMode, ModifySymlink, and DeleteSymlink are separate operations rather than implicit.

docs.title: Object-graph limits
docs.text:
The graph validator enforces structural ceilings on an untrusted graph.

Limit Value Meaning MAX_OBJECT_BYTES 64 MiB Hard cap on a single object payload MAX_TREE_ENTRIES 100,000 Maximum entries in one tree MAX_TREE_DEPTH 64 Maximum tree nesting depth (root tree at depth 0)

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• On-disk format — canonical CBOR encoding and digest domains.
  • Database schema — SQL tables and columns.
  • Limits — operational and per-object limits.
  • Content addressing — why tenant scope is the deduplication boundary.

docs.title: Current scope
docs.text:
This page reflects the current build. The following items are specified but not yet implemented:

  • No second hash algorithm. Only sha256 is implemented. No other algorithm is wired in.
  • No content-defined chunking. Files split only at fixed 4 MiB boundaries. Content-defined chunking is deferred.
  • No application-level blob compression envelope. The codec field is not implemented; blobs are stored raw.
  • Hard links. The MVP may store hard links as independent file entries. It does not preserve hard-link identity.
  • root_digest on the ticket. root_digest is present on the ticket struct and the signed claims. The persisted ticket row stores signed_ticket instead and carries the root digest on the mount session row.

docs.title: Database schema
docs.text: tags: - reference - database

docs.title: Control-plane data model
docs.text:
The AWC control plane stores its state in PostgreSQL. Schema changes apply as forward-only migrations. A version, once applied, cannot be rolled back by the migrator. To revert, restore a database snapshot.

Both the control service and the worker service run migrations on startup before they accept traffic. Applied versions are recorded in the migrations table. Either service advances the schema to the latest version.

docs.title: Conventions
docs.text:
• Resource IDs are opaque, prefix-qualified ULIDs stored as text. Common prefixes are ten_, prj_, snap_, ws_, lease_, host_, import_, and mount_.
  • Content digests use the canonical form sha256:<64 hex>.
  • Lifecycle states are stored as text and match the API value.
  • Timestamps are stored as UTC.
  • Labels and structured payloads are stored as JSON.
  • A row is mutable unless its table is append-only.

docs.title: Identity and tenancy
docs.text:
A tenant is the top-level isolation boundary. Every other row belongs to a tenant.

A project groups snapshots and workspaces inside a tenant. A project carries a name and a lifecycle state.

A principal is a human user or a machine service account. A kind field tells the two apart. Credential material lives outside this row. A project membership binds a principal to a project with a role, such as viewer, developer, operator, admin, or billing viewer.

A host is a registered worker host. The row holds both the registration data and the time of the last heartbeat. A host moves through the states REGISTERED, ACTIVE, DRAINING, and RETIRED.

A token revocation records a bearer token that is denied before its natural expiry. The row is keyed by the JWT ID. Rows past expiry can be purged.

docs.title: Snapshots and imports
docs.text:
A snapshot is an immutable, content-addressed version of a tree of files. Each snapshot belongs to a tenant and a project. A snapshot can name a parent snapshot to form a history. A snapshot moves through states such as UPLOADING, VALIDATING, READY, DEGRADED, and DELETED. A READY snapshot can be mounted or used as a workspace base.

An import session is a resumable snapshot upload. It reuses the snapshot state names and expires after a set time.

docs.title: Workspaces and leases
docs.text:
