Must differ from the other roots. cache_root AWC_CACHE_ROOT required Absolute path. Must differ from the other roots. workspace_root AWC_WORKSPACE_ROOT required Absolute path. Must differ from the other roots. allowed_bind_roots AWC_ALLOWED_BIND_ROOTS [] Comma-separated absolute paths. health_http_listen AWC_HEALTH_HTTP_LISTEN unset (off) Loopback host:port, for example 127.0.0.1:9100. cache.max_bytes AWC_CACHE__MAX_BYTES 1000000000000 (1 TiB) Total byte limit of the local cache. cache.min_free_bytes AWC_CACHE__MIN_FREE_BYTES 50000000000 (50 GiB) Free-space reserve. Drives the pressure ladder. cache.max_remote_fetches AWC_CACHE__MAX_REMOTE_FETCHES 128 Global object-store read concurrency. cache.max_remote_fetches_per_tenant AWC_CACHE__MAX_REMOTE_FETCHES_PER_TENANT 32 Cannot exceed max_remote_fetches. cache.max_prefetch_fetches AWC_CACHE__MAX_PREFETCH_FETCHES 8 Cannot exceed max_remote_fetches. checkpoint.max_concurrent AWC_CHECKPOINT__MAX_CONCURRENT 4 Concurrent checkpoint uploads. checkpoint.freeze_timeout_seconds AWC_CHECKPOINT__FREEZE_TIMEOUT_SECONDS 10 Quiesce timeout for cutting a checkpoint. checkpoint.preserve_local_grace_seconds AWC_CHECKPOINT__PRESERVE_LOCAL_GRACE_SECONDS 3600 Grace period for preserved local changes. leases.renew_interval_seconds AWC_LEASES__RENEW_INTERVAL_SECONDS 30 Must be strictly less than expiry_seconds. leases.expiry_seconds AWC_LEASES__EXPIRY_SECONDS 90 Lease lifetime. leases.disconnected_grace_seconds AWC_LEASES__DISCONNECTED_GRACE_SECONDS 60 Grace period before revocation.

Defaults come from spec §22.9. Startup rejects contradictory or unsafe settings. The three roots must be distinct paths.

docs.title: Other environment variables
docs.text:
These are read by awcd directly, not through the config layer.

Variable Default Purpose AWC_CAS_URL memory:// Object store for the verified cache. Accepts memory:// or s3://. The s3:// transport needs the s3 feature. AWC_MOUNT_TICKET_PUBLIC_KEY unset Mount-ticket verifier public key, 64 hex characters. Required outside dev mode. AWC_MOUNT_TICKET_PUBLIC_KEY_FILE unset Path to a file that holds the public key. AWC_DEV_MODE unset Set to 1 to enable a built-in dev ticket key and to allow http:// control-plane endpoints. AWC_CGROUP_ROOTS unset Colon-separated cgroup roots for the checkpoint runner. fuse feature only. AWCD_SOCKET unset Fallback for the optional socket-path argument.

docs.title: What awcd does
docs.text:
Responsibility Status Maintain the shared read-only base filesystem Wired with the fuse feature. A NoopBaseMount runs without it. Maintain the host-local content cache Wired. The cache lives under cache_root. Resolve snapshot manifests Wired. Fetch and verify content-addressed objects Wired. Coalesce concurrent fetches Wired through the singleflight FetchCoordinator. fuse feature only. Manage private upper directories Wired. Build and tear down OverlayFS mounts Wired. fuse feature only. Bind mounts into authorized namespaces Wired. Acquire and renew writer leases Wired through the control-plane client. Track mount and fencing state Wired. Pause and resume an execution cgroup for checkpointing Wired through the checkpoint runner. fuse feature only. Scan the writable delta and build a new snapshot Wired through the checkpoint runner. fuse feature only. Upload new objects to the tenant CAS Wired. fuse feature only. Publish checkpoints through the control plane Wired through the control-plane client. fuse feature only. Expose a local Unix-domain gRPC API Wired. Report metrics and mount status Partial. See "Emitted metrics" and "Current scope".

awcd fails closed for new privileged mount operations when ticket verification or host authorization fails (spec §8.3).

docs.title: Control-plane client
docs.text:
At startup, awcd builds a tonic client against control_plane_endpoint:

Client gRPC service Purpose LeaseClient LeaseService Renew each leased session and cache the verdict. CheckpointClient CheckpointService Publish checkpoints. fuse feature only.

A malformed endpoint is handled differently per client. The mount-lifecycle LeaseClient and the CheckpointClient abort startup: awcd exits with status 1. The lease-renewal LeaseClient is the exception. A malformed endpoint disables that client only, startup continues, and the lease cache stays cold, so restart reconciliation preserves sessions (spec §17.3).

docs.title: Capabilities
docs.text:
awcd runs as the unprivileged awc user. It holds a minimal capability set so it can perform privileged mount operations and access /dev/fuse. The packaged systemd unit grants these capabilities:

Capability Reason CAP_SYS_ADMIN Mount, cgroup, and setns operations. CAP_DAC_READ_SEARCH Checkpoint upper-directory bookkeeping. CAP_DAC_OVERRIDE Overlay-over-FUSE lowerdir resolution. CAP_CHOWN Checkpoint upper-directory bookkeeping. CAP_FOWNER Checkpoint upper-directory bookkeeping.

The unit allows /dev/fuse as a device. It does not set the systemd directives that create a private mount namespace, because awcd must publish its mounts into the host namespace (spec §15.4).

docs.title: Health HTTP listener
docs.text:
The health and metrics surface is off by default. Set health_http_listen to a loopback host:port to enable it. The host API stays on the Unix socket.

When enabled, awcd serves three paths. All accept GET only.

Path Success Failure Body /healthz 200 503 Liveness report as JSON. /readyz 200 503 Readiness report as JSON. /metrics 200 none Prometheus-style text exposition.

/healthz returns 200 when the process is up and the base filesystem is mounted. /readyz returns 200 only when the base filesystem, kernel compatibility, leases, free space, and control-plane and object-store connectivity are all verified. A host can stay ready for warm reads while /readyz returns 503 (spec §19.6).

Other HTTP methods return 405. Unknown paths return 404.

docs.title: Disk pressure
docs.text:
awcd probes the filesystem that holds cache_root through statfs, and the I/O pressure stall through /proc/pressure/io. It classifies the host into one of six monotone states (spec §17.8). A background sampler refreshes the state every 5 seconds.

Rank State Wire label Containment 0 Normal NORMAL None. 1 CacheEviction CACHE_EVICTION Evict disposable cache. 2 PrefetchDisabled PREFETCH_DISABLED Stop speculative prefetch. 3 NewMountsDisabled NEW_MOUNTS_DISABLED Reject new writable mounts. 4 UpperWritesAtRisk UPPER_WRITES_AT_RISK Existing upper writes may fail with ENOSPC. Warn the agent and the platform. 5 Emergency EMERGENCY Only warm reads continue.

Containment is strictly ordered. The cheap, safe lever fires first. Inode scarcity and PSI stalls can only escalate the state, never relax it.

The byte thresholds derive from cache.min_free_bytes (the reserve R):

Threshold Multiple of R eviction_free_bytes 3 * R prefetch_disabled_free_bytes 2 * R new_mounts_disabled_free_bytes R upper_risk_free_bytes 2/3 * R emergency_free_bytes 1/3 * R checkpoint_reserve_bytes R

Default PSI thresholds: some stall 50 percent (5000 basis points), full stall 80 percent (8000 basis points). Default inode scarcity line: 1024 free inodes.

New writable mounts are refused while pressure blocks admission. The refusal is a visible disk-full error. awcd never deletes uncheckpointed upper data to relieve pressure (spec §17.8).

docs.title: Emitted metrics
docs.text:
These metrics have a live emit site in awcd. The full metric catalog is in the metrics reference.

Metric Type Source Notes awc_host_disk_pressure_state gauge pressure sampler Severity rank 0 through 5. Sampled every 5 seconds. awc_singleflight_leader_fetches_total counter singleflight sampler fuse feature only. Sampled every 5 seconds. awc_singleflight_follower_requests_total counter singleflight sampler fuse feature only. Sampled every 5 seconds. awc_workspace_active_mounts gauge mount and unmount paths awc_workspace_mounts_total counter mount path awc_workspace_unmounts_total counter unmount path

The registry caps distinct label sets per instrument at 128. Recordings beyond the cap roll into a synthetic cardinality_overflow label (spec §19.2).

docs.title: Signals and exit codes
docs.text:
Signal Effect SIGINT Start a graceful drain. SIGTERM Start a graceful drain.

On a graceful drain, awcd stops the lease renewal task and the HTTP server, lets the gRPC server drain, reconciles live sessions against the authoritative lease, preserves uppers while the control plane is unreachable, and tears down mounts (spec §17.3).

Exit code Cause 0 Clean shutdown after a drain signal. 1 Config, ticket-verifier, or control-plane client configuration error; health HTTP bind failure; base-mount build failure; daemon start failure; or a server exit with an error.

A missing config argument also prints usage and exits 1.

docs.title: Current scope
docs.text:
This section tracks what is specified but not yet implemented or emitted in the current build. The build lags the spec in these areas.

Item Status Detail Cache eviction Specified-only The pressure state machine computes the CacheEviction state and the evict_cache action, but no worker reclaims disposable cache objects. The module is pure. Prefetch gate Specified-only The prefetch_allowed flag is computed from the state. No speculative prefetch path exists in awcd to read it. awc_host_free_inodes gauge Emitted The pressure sampler sets it every 5 s from the newest probe sample. awc_host_upper_usage_bytes Emitted, total only The pressure sampler sets the host total every 5 s. Per-workspace breakdown (spec §17.8) has no emit site. Cache corruption probe Not wired The CACHE health component reports ok with the detail "operational; corruption probe not wired". Control-plane connectivity probe Not wired The CONTROL_PLANE health component reports unknown. Object-store connectivity probe Not wired The OBJECT_STORE health component reports unknown. Remote-read admission limiter Not attached Spec §10.10. The FetchCoordinator coalesces fetches but applies no concurrency bound. Provider circuit breakers Not attached Spec §10.11. AWCD_HEALTH_PORT Indirect The systemd unit sets AWCD_HEALTH_PORT=9100 for its awc-health-check probe only. The awcd listen address comes from health_http_listen or AWC_HEALTH_HTTP_LISTEN.

docs.title: Tutorials
docs.text:
Tutorials teach you AWC, end to end, by doing. You do not need prior knowledge of the system. Each tutorial is a guided narrative that you follow in order, and each one leaves you with a working result and a new skill.

If you prefer to start with the concepts, read the architecture overview first.

  • Your first workspace — import a snapshot, fork, mount, edit a file, run a tool, checkpoint, diff, and export. All five primitives in one sitting.
  • See the economics — fan out 100 workspaces from a single base against a cold cache and watch the backend reads collapse to one.
  • Break it on purpose — crash the host daemon, simulate host loss, and recover an acknowledged checkpoint. Then trigger a stale writer and watch the fence reject publication.
  • Wire a CI pipeline — bring a Git revision and a CI tar into a snapshot, then automate fork, mount, checkpoint, and export for each agent task.

docs.title: Break it on purpose
docs.text:
You build confidence in a cache by breaking it. In this tutorial you inject four failures into a running AWC (Agent Workspace Cache) deployment and watch what survives. You crash the host daemon mid-work, prove the durability contract, run the repo outage harness, and provoke the lease fence.

AWC keeps mutable coordination separate from immutable truth (spec §17.1). The five user-level primitives are unchanged (spec §5.1):

snapshot → fork → mount → checkpoint → diff/export

This tutorial adds failure on top of them. You do not change the surface.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
You need a host where the three AWC services run as systemd units:

  • awc-control, the control plane that issues mount tickets and publishes heads.
  • awcd, the host daemon that serves the FUSE (Filesystem in Userspace) mount and the local cache.
  • awc-worker, the background validator.

This is the Proxmox pilot or a VM provisioned by deploy on Proxmox or deploy a VM with systemd. You also need root privileges, because the failure commands stop services and drop the page cache.

Local-dev smoke is not enough

The repo outage harness reads /etc/awc/awcd.toml and drives the awc-control and awcd systemd units. The local-dev smoke runs the binaries as foreground processes and has no such units. You can do the first experiments on local-dev, but the outage harness needs a systemd deployment.

Set up your shell the way Your first workspace shows. Export AWC_CONTROL_ENDPOINT, AWC_HOST_SOCKET, AWC_TOKEN, AWC_TENANT, and AWC_PROJECT. Confirm the daemon answers:

awcctl status

docs.title: 1. Set up a workspace with an uncommitted change
docs.text:
Pick a READY snapshot and fork a private workspace from it. Forking is metadata only; it MUST NOT copy content objects (spec §5.3, §6.10):

SNAP=$(awcctl --output json snapshot list \
  | python3 -c 'import sys,json;print(json.load(sys.stdin)["snapshots"][0]["id"])')

awcctl --output json workspace fork --snapshot "$SNAP" --ttl 4h --name break-ws \
  > fork.json
WS=$(python3 -c 'import json;print(json.load(open("fork.json"))["id"])')
echo "$WS"

Mount the workspace. The control plane issues a signed ticket; awcd redeems it, takes an exclusive writer lease, and mounts an OverlayFS view at your target (spec §5.4, §13.8, §13.9):

MNT=/var/lib/awc/binds/break
mkdir -p "$MNT"
awcctl --output json workspace mount "$WS" --target "$MNT" > mount.json
SESS=$(python3 -c 'import json;print(json.load(open("mount.json"))["mount_session_id"])')
echo "$SESS"

Write a file you will keep, and a file you will not commit:

printf 'checkpoint me\n' > "$MNT/kept.txt"
printf 'forget me\n'   > "$MNT/lost.txt"
ls "$MNT"

Neither file is durable yet. Ordinary local writes are not remotely durable; only an acknowledged checkpoint is guaranteed to survive host loss (spec §6.8).

docs.title: 2. Crash the host daemon, then recover
docs.text:
A crash of awcd is not catastrophic. The OverlayFS upper directory lives on local disk, separate from the daemon process. Kill the daemon hard, the way a power loss or an out-of-memory killer would:

sudo systemctl kill   --signal=KILL awcd
sudo systemctl is-active awcd          # prints: failed

While awcd is down, the kernel mount may return errors for new filesystem operations. That is expected. The on-disk upper bytes are intact. Bring the daemon back:

sudo systemctl start awcd
until [ "$(sudo systemctl is-active awcd)" = active ]; do sleep 1; done
awcctl status

On restart, awcd acquires a singleton host lock, reconciles local cache metadata with the files on disk, discovers the existing mounts, and renews or fences lease state (spec §17.3). The cache reconciliation step walks cache metadata rows, drops broken or incomplete cache entries, and removes orphan temp files left by a crash. It does not touch workspace upper directories, and awcd MUST NOT delete an upper directory while the control plane is unreachable (spec §10.5, §17.3). Your two files are still in the mount:

ls "$MNT"          # kept.txt and lost.txt are still here

What this proves

The local upper layer survives a daemon crash, and awcd reconciles the cache on restart without operator help (spec §11.12, §17.3).

What it does not prove

This proves nothing about remote durability. Both files live only on this host. The spec also requires awcd to classify recovered sessions on startup (spec §11.12). The cache reconciliation is wired; the broader session classification is spec-required and tracked in the recovery runbooks.

docs.title: 3. Prove the durability contract
docs.text:
Now separate the two files. Checkpoint kept.txt into an immutable snapshot. Pass the mount session id, not the workspace id (spec §5.5, §13.11):

awcctl --output json workspace checkpoint "$SESS" \
  --mode cooperative --message "keep me" > ckpt.json
HEAD=$(python3 -c 'import json;print(json.load(open("ckpt.json"))["snapshot_id"])')
echo "$HEAD"

The new head is durable only after the control plane commits publication in one atomic transaction (spec §11.6 Phase E, §13.12). Now lost.txt is still uncommitted. Discard the local upper on unmount:

awcctl workspace unmount "$SESS" --disposition discard-local

discard-local deletes uncheckpointed upper state. Destructive discard MUST be explicit when uncheckpointed changes exist (spec §11.11). Re-mount the workspace and look inside:

awcctl --output json workspace mount "$WS" --target "$MNT" > mount2.json
SESS=$(python3 -c 'import json;print(json.load(open("mount2.json"))["mount_session_id"])')
ls "$MNT"

kept.txt is present, because the checkpoint published it. lost.txt is gone, because no checkpoint held it.

What this proves

An acknowledged checkpoint survives; an uncommitted write does not. That is the whole durability model in two files (spec §6.8). A fsync on a writable mount applies to the local upper filesystem only and does not imply remote durability (spec §14.8).

Host loss is the destructive form of the same rule. If this host is destroyed, you lose the local cache, the active mount state, and every uncheckpointed upper delta. You do not lose imported snapshots, acknowledged checkpoints, workspace metadata, or audit events (spec §17.4). For the recovery procedure, see recover from host loss. For the reasoning behind explicit durability, read the durability model.

docs.title: 4. Run the outage harness
docs.text:
The repo ships a failure-injection harness at awc_outage_test.sh. It stops the control plane only and keeps awcd, PostgreSQL, and MinIO (an S3-compatible content-addressed store, or CAS) running. The property under test is: once a mount is established, ordinary reads and writes MUST continue during a temporary control-plane outage, while new mounts and publication correctly fail (spec §17.5).

The harness reads three lease timers from /etc/awc/awcd.toml. The defaults are (spec configuration block):

renew_interval_seconds: 30     # how often a healthy writer renews
expiry_seconds: 90             # lease lifetime with no renewal
disconnected_grace_seconds: 60 # how long awcd keeps serving a detached writer

Run it as root from the repo root:

sudo bash awc_outage_test.sh

The script forks a workspace, mounts it, starts a rotating reader, an append writer, and an fsync writer, then runs this sequence:

  1. Stop awc-control only. A monitor process, started before the stop, records that awcd, PostgreSQL, and MinIO stay up.
  2. Sustain the workload past disconnected_grace_seconds and toward expiry_seconds, dropping the host page cache so reads are not served from RAM.
  3. Probe a new mount and a checkpoint during the outage. Both need the control plane, so both are expected to fail or stall.
  4. Restart awc-control, re-sync the dev token, and run a post-recovery checkpoint.

Read the verdicts the script prints at the end. Against the defaults above, you see results of this shape:

[reads sustained during outage]         PASS
[writes sustained WITHIN grace (60s)]   PASS
[writes survive PAST grace boundary]    FENCED
[cold read during outage succeeded]     PASS
[new mount needs control plane]         EXPECTED (failed or stalled-timeout)
[checkpoint needs control plane]        EXPECTED (failed or stalled-timeout)
[post-recovery checkpoint succeeded]    PASS

Reads are not fenced, so a read-only remount keeps serving them. Writes inside the grace window keep going, because awcd MAY continue a writable mount during a bounded lease grace period (spec §17.5). Writes past grace are fenced, because after grace the daemon MUST deny checkpoint publication and SHOULD remount the workspace read-only or pause it (spec §17.5). The harness labels the fenced result as expected lease-safety design, not a regression.

What this proves

The data plane stays up while the control plane is down. Lease grace gives a writer a bounded window; after that window, publication is fenced.

What it does not prove

awcd stayed up the whole time. This is a control-plane outage, not host loss, so it says nothing about what survives a destroyed host. Section 3 is the host-loss answer.

For the operator recovery steps, see recover from a control-plane outage and drain and restart a host.

docs.title: 5. Watch the lease fence a stale writer
docs.text:
Split-brain prevention does not rely on lease expiry alone. Every writer lease carries a fencing generation, a number that increases each time a new lease is issued (spec §9.10). A host with an older generation may keep its local bytes, but it MUST NOT publish a checkpoint (spec §9.10, §14.4).

The publication path enforces this. The checkpoint publication step runs in one PostgreSQL transaction. Within that transaction it fences the active writer lease on generation, state, expiry, and mount session (spec §11.6 Phase E). If the generation is stale, the transaction rolls back and the workspace head is unchanged.

You already saw the fence act in the outage harness. When the control plane was down, the lease could not be renewed. Once the outage passed disconnected_grace_seconds, writes were fenced. That is the same rule: a writer whose lease is no longer authoritative cannot advance the head.

A true split-brain needs two hosts

To reproduce two writers racing for one workspace, you need the lease issued on one host and a second writer attempt elsewhere. A single-host tutorial cannot do that safely. The generation fence in the publication path is the guarantee that the second writer cannot win (spec §14.4). For the full procedure, read fencing and split-brain and handle a stale writer.

A stale host is not silently erased. Its local upper bytes may survive, and an operator MAY export them as an offline patch bundle. That export MUST never advance the workspace head automatically and MUST record that the bytes came from unacknowledged local state (spec §11.12, §14.4, §17.11).

docs.title: 6. Recover with the runbooks
docs.text:
Each failure class has a runbook. Reach for the one that matches the symptom:

  • Crash or planned restart of the host daemon: drain and restart a host.
  • Destroyed host or missing upper: recover from host loss.
  • Control plane unreachable: recover from a control-plane outage.
  • A checkpoint that did not finish: recover an interrupted checkpoint.
  • A writer whose lease is no longer valid: handle a stale writer.

Every failure path preserves the last acknowledged workspace head (spec §17.1). If a step in this tutorial left a workspace behind, unmount and remove it:

awcctl workspace unmount "$SESS" --disposition discard-local

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text:
You broke the system four ways and watched it hold:

  • A daemon crash leaves the upper layer intact, and awcd reconciles on restart.
  • An acknowledged checkpoint survives; an uncommitted write does not (spec §6.8).
  • A control-plane outage keeps the data plane alive through lease grace, then fences publication (spec §17.5).
  • A stale fencing generation cannot publish, so a split writer cannot corrupt the head (spec §14.4).

The durability contract is explicit, not automatic. Checkpoint the work you want to keep.

Where to go next:

  • Read the durability model for the why behind explicit durability.
  • Read fencing and split-brain for the generation fence in depth.
  • Run the full test suite to see these properties checked in code.

docs.title: Your first workspace
docs.text:
This tutorial walks you through AWC (Agent Workspace Cache) in one sitting. You bring up the local-dev smoke harness, then drive the whole loop yourself with awcctl: snapshot a directory, fork a workspace, mount it, make an edit and run a tool, checkpoint, diff, export, and unmount. AWC exposes five user-level primitives:

snapshot → fork → mount → checkpoint → diff/export

You touch each one. When you finish, you have a working workspace and a feel for the system.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
The harness runs on Linux only. You need:

  • Docker Engine with the docker compose plugin.
  • The Rust toolchain pinned by rust-toolchain.toml.
  • python3, curl, and coreutils.
  • A FUSE (Filesystem in Userspace) stack: the /dev/fuse device and fusermount or fusermount3 on PATH.
  • root privileges. The writable mount layer uses OverlayFS, which needs mount privilege. Run the bring-up with sudo.

See the local-dev guide for full prerequisites.

docs.title: 1. Bring up the local-dev smoke
docs.text:
The smoke harness stands up PostgreSQL and MinIO (an S3-compatible content-addressed store, or CAS) in containers, then runs the four AWC binaries on the host. It generates the credentials, builds the binaries, and proves the real cross-process paths work.

cd deploy/local-dev
bin/generate-credentials.sh
sudo ./smoke.sh

The first run takes a few minutes to build, then drives the full import, mount, checkpoint, and remount path. A green run ends with:

== SMOKE PASS ==

The smoke leaves awc-control, awc-worker, and awcd running. Keep this terminal open.

Development mode, loopback plaintext

The harness sets AWC_DEV_MODE=1, so internal RPCs (remote procedure calls) use loopback plaintext instead of mutually authenticated TLS (mTLS). Outside development mode, awcd and awc-control MUST present TLS credentials and fail to start without them. Do not reuse this mode in a deployment.

docs.title: 2. Point awcctl at the harness
docs.text:
Open a second shell in the local-dev directory. The smoke builds awcctl to ../../target/debug/awcctl. Put it on PATH, then load the CAS credentials, the dev identity, and the service token that awc-control minted on startup:

cd deploy/local-dev
export PATH="$PWD/../../target/debug:$PATH"
set -a; . config/worker.env; . config/control.env; set +a
export AWC_CONTROL_ENDPOINT="http://127.0.0.1:8080"
export AWC_HOST_SOCKET="$PWD/run/awcd.sock"
export AWC_TENANT="$AWC_DEV_TENANT" AWC_PROJECT="$AWC_DEV_PROJECT"
export AWC_TOKEN="$(grep -m1 'awc-control dev token:' run/control.log \
                   | sed 's/.*awc-control dev token: //')"

AWC_HOST_SOCKET is the Unix socket awcd serves, AWC_CONTROL_ENDPOINT is the control plane's REST (Representational State Transfer) address, and AWC_TOKEN is the bearer token the dev bootstrap minted.

docs.title: 3. Check host health
docs.text:
Ask the host daemon how it is. status reaches awcd over the socket and needs no control-plane call:

awcctl status

You see host health, the cache state, and any active mount sessions.

docs.title: 4. Snapshot a directory
docs.text:
A snapshot is an immutable, content-addressed record of a directory tree. The harness ships a tiny fixture at seed/source. Import it:

awcctl --output json snapshot create --from-dir seed/source --name first \
  > first-snap.json

--from-dir is the source and --name is an optional label. The command opens an import session over the control plane, uploads the unique objects to the CAS, and completes the import. Capture the id:

SNAP=$(python3 -c 'import json;print(json.load(open("first-snap.json"))["snapshot_id"])')
echo "$SNAP"

A successful snapshot MUST return a stable snapshot id, a root digest, and file and byte counts. The new snapshot starts in the VALIDATING state.

docs.title: 5. Wait for READY, then fork
docs.text:
A workspace can fork only from a READY snapshot. The worker validates the object closure against the CAS and advances the snapshot VALIDATING → READY. Poll until it is ready:

until [ "$(awcctl --output json snapshot inspect "$SNAP" \
          | python3 -c 'import sys,json;print(json.load(sys.stdin)["state"])')" = READY ]; do
  sleep 1
done

You can also list what the project holds:

awcctl snapshot list

Now fork a private workspace from the snapshot. Forking creates metadata only; it MUST NOT copy content objects:

awcctl --output json workspace fork --snapshot "$SNAP" --ttl 2h --name first-ws \
  > first-fork.json
WS=$(python3 -c 'import json;print(json.load(open("first-fork.json"))["id"])')
echo "$WS"

--ttl 2h sets a two-hour lifetime (required). --snapshot forks one workspace from the snapshot id you pass.

docs.title: 6. Mount the workspace
docs.text:
Mounting turns the workspace into a writable directory. The control plane issues a signed ticket; awcd redeems it, acquires an exclusive writer lease, and mounts an OverlayFS view at your target.

mkdir -p data/binds/first
awcctl --output json workspace mount "$WS" --target "$PWD/data/binds/first" \
  > first-mount.json
SESS=$(python3 -c 'import json;print(json.load(open("first-mount.json"))["mount_session_id"])')
echo "$SESS"

The target MUST fall under the host allow-list. awcd MUST NOT accept an arbitrary path from an untrusted caller without an allow-listed root. Confirm the kernel sees an OverlayFS mount:

findmnt -n -o FSTYPE --target data/binds/first     # prints: overlay

docs.title: 7. Edit a file and run a tool
docs.text:
Enter the mount. The fixture's hello.txt and README.txt are there, fetched from the CAS on demand.

cd data/binds/first
ls
printf 'my first edit\n' > notes.txt
grep -n "AWC" README.txt
cd -

You wrote a new file and ran an ordinary read tool against the merged tree. Any read-only tool works the same way.

docs.title: 8. Checkpoint
docs.text:
A checkpoint publishes your writes as a new immutable snapshot and advances the workspace head. Pass the mount session id, not the workspace id:

awcctl --output json workspace checkpoint "$SESS" \
  --mode cooperative --message "first checkpoint" > first-ckpt.json
HEAD=$(python3 -c 'import json;print(json.load(open("first-ckpt.json"))["snapshot_id"])')
echo "$HEAD"

Quiesced checkpoints need a fenced cgroup

The default is a quiesced checkpoint, which freezes an execution cgroup before it cuts the snapshot. This harness mounts without a ticket-sealed cgroup, so a quiesced checkpoint is rejected with quiesced checkpoint requires a ticket-sealed execution cgroup. Use --mode cooperative here. It is a best-effort cut with no freeze, and it is what the smoke exercises.

The checkpoint is durable only after the control plane atomically publishes the new head.

docs.title: 9. Diff and export
docs.text:
Compare your checkpoint with the original snapshot. A diff uses a Merkle-tree comparison, so unchanged directories are skipped without scanning their children:

awcctl snapshot diff "$SNAP" "$HEAD"

The diff lists each changed path. Export the changes to a file:

awcctl snapshot export "$HEAD" --against "$SNAP" --format json --out first-changes.json

$HEAD is the snapshot whose changes are exported. --against is the base. Pass --format json. The patch-bundle and tar formats are deferred, so the control plane serves only the inline json form today.

docs.title: 10. Unmount
docs.text:
Release the writer lease and tear down the mount:

awcctl workspace unmount "$SESS" --disposition discard-local

--disposition discard-local is the default. It drops any writes you did not checkpoint. Because you already checkpointed, nothing is lost here. The other dispositions are checkpoint (cut a checkpoint while unmounting) and preserve-local (leave the upper layer for recovery).

When you are done with the harness, stop its containers:

./clean.sh

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text:
You ran all five AWC primitives against live services: snapshot into the CAS, metadata-only fork, writable OverlayFS mount behind a signed ticket, a checkpoint that advances the head, a diff and export, and an explicit unmount.

You also saw two candid limits of this harness: it runs without mTLS under AWC_DEV_MODE=1, and it checkpoints cooperatively because the mount has no fenced cgroup.

Where to go next:

  • See the economics — fan out many workspaces from one base and watch the backend reads collapse.
  • Go deeper on each primitive: import from a directory, fork a workspace, mount a workspace, checkpoint a workspace, diff and export, and unmount a workspace.
  • For the design behind these steps, read the architecture overview.

docs.title: What this tutorial shows
docs.text:
AWC is an agent workspace cache. Its economic bet is narrow and specific. One base snapshot feeds many workspaces, and all of them share the same underlying bytes. In this tutorial you fan out 100 workspaces from one snapshot, mount a few, and read the metrics that collapse the remote-fetch bill.

You will see why N forks of one base cost about 1 times the remote bytes, not N times.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
You need:

  • a running awcd host daemon;
  • the awcctl CLI on your path;
  • a directory that holds a real repository image (a few hundred megabytes makes the effect visible).

If you do not have a daemon yet, follow install AWC and run AWC locally.

docs.title: Step 1 — Import one base snapshot
docs.text:
A snapshot is an immutable, content-addressed image of a directory (spec §5.2). Pick a directory that represents a real repo, and import it.

awcctl snapshot create --from-dir ./my-repo --name econ-base --output json

The command prints a JSON object. Note three fields: snapshot_id, logical_bytes, and unique_bytes.

  • logical_bytes is the total file size a reader sees.
  • unique_bytes is the dedup-aware footprint. The content store keeps each distinct object once per tenant (spec §9.2).

The snapshot is not readable until it is READY. Poll it.

awcctl snapshot inspect <snapshot_id>

When state reads READY, the base snapshot S0 is in place. Every fork you make next will share its objects.

docs.title: Step 2 — Fork one seed workspace
docs.text:
A fork is private and metadata-only. Forking does O(1) work regardless of the snapshot size (spec §20.2). Fork one seed workspace from the snapshot.

awcctl workspace fork --snapshot <snapshot_id> --ttl 2h --name econ-seed

Note the workspace id it returns. This seed is the anchor for the batch fork.

docs.title: Step 3 — Batch-fork 100 workspaces from the seed
docs.text:
Now fan out. Batch-fork 100 workspaces from the seed, all sourced from its base snapshot.

awcctl workspace fork \
  --workspace <seed_id> \
  --from base \
  --count 100 \
  --name econ-agent \
  --ttl 2h

--from base makes every child share the seed's base snapshot S0. In batch mode --name is a prefix; the 100 children get distinct names. The --ttl flag is required. It sets how long a workspace lives before cleanup.

This matches the shape of the spec §20.7 fan-out scenario: many workspaces on one host cache domain, all sharing one base.

docs.title: Step 4 — Mount several workspaces
docs.text:
Pick three children and mount them at separate targets. The target path must fall under the host allow-list.

awcctl workspace mount <child_id_1> --target /mnt/awc/ws-1
awcctl workspace mount <child_id_2> --target /mnt/awc/ws-2
awcctl workspace mount <child_id_3> --target /mnt/awc/ws-3

Each mount returns a mount_session_id. You use it to unmount later.

docs.title: Step 5 — Trigger reads that hit the same bytes
docs.text:
Run the same scan in every mount. Read every file once.

find /mnt/awc/ws-1 -type f -print0 | xargs -0 cat > /dev/null
find /mnt/awc/ws-2 -type f -print0 | xargs -0 cat > /dev/null
find /mnt/awc/ws-3 -type f -print0 | xargs -0 cat > /dev/null

The three workspaces are separate forks, but they resolve the same paths to the same object digests. That is the key fact. The next step shows what it does to the remote-fetch count.

docs.title: Step 6 — Read the metrics that collapse
docs.text:
awcd exposes a Prometheus-style metrics endpoint at /metrics on its health listener (spec §19.6). The default config binds that listener to 127.0.0.1:9100.

curl -s http://127.0.0.1:9100/metrics | grep -E 'awc_singleflight'

Two counters matter for this tutorial.

  • awc_singleflight_leader_fetches_total counts the fetches that ran as the single leader.
  • awc_singleflight_follower_requests_total counts the readers that waited on a leader and shared its result.

After the three scans, the leader count sits close to the number of distinct objects in S0. The second and third scans add no leader fetches. They hit the local cache. Singleflight coalesces concurrent misses for the same object into one leader fetch, and the followers share the result. In a full-tree scan, though, concurrent readers are usually at different files at any instant, so they rarely contend on one digest. On one host the follower count often stays near zero, and the flat bytes come from the caches, not from coalescing. The regression gate below is where coalescing is proven directly.

Why the counts behave this way

The cache key is tenant_id + hash_algorithm + object_digest (spec §10.3). All forks of one base, under one tenant, resolve a shared file to one key. The first miss fetches the object once (spec §10.5). The rest are cache hits.

docs.title: The mechanism — three layers that flatten the bill
docs.text:
AWC collapses repeated remote fetches through three mechanisms.

  1. Tenant-scoped content addressing (spec §9.2, §10.3). Each object lives once per tenant. Identical bytes share one object, whether they appear in one fork or in a hundred.
  2. The cache hierarchy (spec §10.2). A read walks the Linux page cache, then the awcd in-memory manifest cache, then the host-local object cache, before it touches object storage. Once an object is cached, repeated reads are free of remote cost.
  3. Singleflight (spec §10.4). awcd keeps an in-memory map of active fetches keyed by cache key. When several readers miss the same object at once, one becomes the leader and fetches. The rest become followers and share the leader's result (spec §10.4: "followers MUST share the leader result"). The build routes the read path through the fetch coordinator, and the /metrics endpoint exposes the leader and follower counters (spec §19.2).

docs.title: The measured numbers
docs.text: The figures below come from two sources. The regression gates are deterministic tests over the software data path. The pilot run is one end-to-end measurement on a single loopback host. Both are published in the repo; cite them when you reuse a number.

docs.title: Singleflight and fan-out
docs.text:
Quantity Measured value Source 100 concurrent readers of one object collapse to exactly 1 remote fetch; singleflight efficiency ≥ 0.99 singleflight regression gate (spec §20.6, §19.3) 100 concurrent scans of one base remote bytes ≤ 1.25 times one cold scan fan-out regression gate (spec §20.7) N=100 fan-out on the pilot, remote bytes vs N=1 ratio 1.00878 (gate ≤ 1.25; PASS, margin 0.241) pilot measurement, experiment A

On the pilot, the wire bytes stayed in a 3.57 MiB band (405.98 to 409.55 MiB, a 0.88 percent spread) while the scan time grew 3.53 times from N=1 to N=100. Local FUSE and CPU work scaled with concurrency. Remote bytes did not.

docs.title: Storage amplification
docs.text:
Quantity Measured value Source Physical unique bytes after many forks base plus the sum of unique deltas, not forks times base delta_storage regression gate (spec §20.8, §19.3) Storage amplification greater than 2.0 times delta_storage regression gate

Economic meaning: forking a 10 TiB snapshot 100 times costs 10 TiB + unique deltas in object storage, not 1000 TiB.

docs.title: Cache hit rate and cold-versus-warm read
docs.text:
Quantity Measured value Source Warm repeated reads 0 remote requests, a 100 percent hit rate cache_hit_rate regression gate (spec §20.6) 4 KiB cold read, p50 3.56 ms pilot read-latency measurement 4 KiB warm read, p50 19.7 microseconds pilot read-latency measurement Cold-versus-warm ratio, p50 about 181 times pilot read-latency measurement

Where these numbers hold, and where they do not

The pilot fan-out figure (1.00878) was recorded on one loopback host with a local object store. On loopback, the host-local cache and the Linux page cache also flatten remote bytes, so the figure is a local result, not a cross-host proof. The regression gates prove the coalescing property directly in the software data path, with no page cache in the loop. A cross-host measurement against a real network — the regime where the spec §20.11 economic launch gate applies — is not in these sources.

docs.title: Interpret the result
docs.text:
One base plus N forks costs about 1 times the remote bytes, not N times, for three reasons.

  • The base bytes are stored once (content addressing).
  • The base bytes are fetched once per host cache domain (the cache hierarchy).
  • Concurrent misses for the same object coalesce to one fetch (singleflight).

So the remote cost is O(distinct objects), not O(distinct objects times concurrency). This is why the spec says fork operations SHOULD be free or nearly free (spec §19.8). The bill tracks new content and cold reads, not the fork count.

docs.title: Clean up
docs.text:
Unmount the three sessions. The default disposition discards local changes.

awcctl workspace unmount <mount_session_id_1>
awcctl workspace unmount <mount_session_id_2>
awcctl workspace unmount <mount_session_id_3>

The 100 workspaces expire when their --ttl elapses. To reclaim space sooner, or to learn what garbage collection keeps and drops, read run garbage collection.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text:
• One base snapshot feeds many forks, and each fork is metadata-only.
  • Forks of one base resolve shared files to one cache key, so the bytes are stored and fetched once per host.
  • Singleflight coalesces concurrent misses into one leader fetch, and followers share the result.
  • The spec §20.7 fan-out gate (≤ 1.25 times one cold scan) passed at 1.00878 on the pilot, and the regression gates prove the coalescing property in the software path.

docs.title: Where to go next
docs.text:
• Economics and cost model — why the pricing tracks unique bytes and cold reads.
  • Overlay, cache, and singleflight — the design choices behind the read path.
  • Checkpoint a workspace — how delta publishing keeps the write side cheap.
  • Run garbage collection — how shared bytes survive the deletion of one fork.

docs.title: Wire a CI pipeline
docs.text:
This tutorial teaches you to drive AWC (Agent Workspace Cache) from a continuous integration job. You import the repository as a snapshot, fork a private workspace, mount it, run a build, then persist or triage the result. When you finish, your CI job runs against a cached fork and stores the output as an immutable snapshot.

AWC exposes five user-level primitives (spec §5.1):

snapshot → fork → mount → checkpoint → diff/export

You wire every one of them into one job.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
This tutorial assumes you already have an AWC deployment you can reach from the runner. You need:

  • A control plane (awc-control) you can reach over HTTPS.
  • A host daemon (awcd) on the runner, with its Unix socket available.
  • The awcctl binary, built with the s3 feature, on PATH.
  • Credentials and endpoints exposed as environment variables (below).
  • jq, to parse the JSON that awcctl --output json prints.
  • The Rust toolchain, because the example build runs make test.

If you do not have a deployment yet, start with run AWC locally and come back here.

docs.title: Environment the CLI expects
docs.text:
awcctl reads its target services from environment variables. Set these on the runner before you call any command:

Variable Meaning AWC_CONTROL_ENDPOINT Base URL of the control plane, for example https://control.example. AWC_TOKEN Bearer token that authenticates you to the control plane. AWC_TENANT Your tenant id. Required by snapshot and workspace commands. AWC_PROJECT Your project id. Required by most control-plane commands. AWC_HOST_SOCKET Path to the local awcd socket, for example /run/awcd/awcd.sock. AWC_CAS_URL Object store the snapshot upload writes to, for example s3://awc-cas.

Mutating commands also honor --idempotency-key (spec §13.1). In CI, set a unique key per attempt so a retry does not create a second resource.

docs.title: The loop you will build
docs.text:
Each run of the job does this:

snapshot create  →  wait for READY  →  fork  →  mount  →  make test
                                                              │
                          ┌──────────────────────────────────┴───┐
                     checkpoint                              export
                     (persist the good state)            (triage a failure)
                                                              │
                                                          unmount

You will reproduce each box below.

docs.title: 1. Import the repository as a snapshot
docs.text:
Your CI provider checks the repository out onto the runner for you. Treat that working tree as the prepared directory, and import it.

BASE=$(awcctl --output json snapshot create \
        --from-dir . \
        --source-type git \
        --name "ci-${GITHUB_SHA::12}" \
        --label "ci.sha=${GITHUB_SHA}" \
    | jq -r .snapshot_id)

The --from-dir . flag points at the checked-out tree. The --source-type git flag records where the bytes came from. awcctl prints the new snapshot id as JSON.

--source-type records provenance only

Today the CLI walks the directory you give --from-dir for every source kind. It does not clone a Git repository and it does not extract a tar archive. --source-type git and --source-type tar only tag the snapshot so you can tell its origin apart later.

The spec (§5.2) intends a Git import at an immutable revision and a CI tar import as distinct paths. The current build treats both as provenance metadata over the same directory import. When you need dedicated Git or tar handling, see import from Git and import from a tar archive.

A successful snapshot returns a stable id, a root digest, and file and byte counts (spec §5.2). You capture the id in BASE.

docs.title: 2. Wait for the snapshot to become ready
docs.text:
A new snapshot starts in the VALIDATING state. The worker reads the object closure back from the store and checks it (spec §13.5, §20.2). A workspace can fork only from a READY snapshot, so poll until the state settles.

until [ "$(awcctl --output json snapshot inspect "$BASE" | jq -r .state)" = "READY" ]; do
  echo "waiting for $BASE to validate..."
  sleep 2
done

Why the wait exists

The closure check is what makes a READY snapshot trustworthy: it never references a missing object (spec §20.2). Until that check passes, the control plane refuses to fork from the snapshot.

docs.title: 3. Fork a workspace
docs.text:
Fork the snapshot into a private, mutable workspace. Forking copies metadata only. It does not copy content objects (spec §5.3), so it is cheap and fast.

WS=$(awcctl --output json workspace fork \
        --snapshot "$BASE" \
        --ttl 1h \
        --name "ci-run-${GITHUB_RUN_ID}" \
    | jq -r .id)

The --ttl 1h flag sets the workspace lifetime. The control plane returns a workspace id, which you store in WS. See fork a workspace for the full response.

docs.title: 4. Mount the workspace
docs.text:
Mount the workspace onto a target directory on the runner. The mount returns a mount_session_id, so capture it in one step. Checkpoint and unmount take the session, not the workspace.

SESSION=$(awcctl --output json workspace mount "$WS" --target "$PWD/ws" \
    | jq -r .mount_session_id)

The mount is read-write by default, which is what a build needs. Add --read-only for a mount that only inspects the tree. A read-write mount acquires an exclusive writer lease (spec §5.4). Only one writer can hold the workspace at a time.

The target must be allow-listed

awcd validates the target path against an allow-list before it binds (spec §13.9). It does not accept an arbitrary host path. Point --target at a directory under the root your awcd config permits. See configuration.

docs.title: 5. Run the build and tests
docs.text:
Work inside the mount as you would in any checkout. The merged view presents the snapshot contents, and writes land in a private upper directory.

cd ./ws
make test
cd ..

Here make test is the repository's own test target. It runs the full workspace unit and integration suite. Treat this step as your "first useful command" (spec §20.10). The time from fork to this command finishing is a primary product metric for AWC.

Capture the exit code so the job can branch on the result without aborting the cleanup steps.

rc=0
( cd ./ws && make test ) || rc=$?

docs.title: 6. Persist the result, or export the diff
docs.text: Dirty state lives only in the mount until you checkpoint it. A checkpoint scans the upper directory, uploads new objects, and publishes a new immutable snapshot that becomes the workspace head (spec §5.5). Export then works on that snapshot.

docs.title: On success: checkpoint
docs.text:
When the tests pass, checkpoint the clean state and keep the new snapshot id as your build artifact.

HEAD=$(awcctl --output json workspace checkpoint "$SESSION" \
        --mode cooperative \
        --message "ci green for ${GITHUB_SHA}" \
        --idempotency-key "ci-${GITHUB_RUN_ID}-ckpt" \
    | jq -r .snapshot_id)

docs.title: On failure: checkpoint, then export the diff
docs.text:
awcctl snapshot export compares two snapshots. It cannot read a dirty mount directly, so checkpoint the failing state first. Then export that checkpoint against the original base to get a patch you can read during triage.

HEAD=$(awcctl --output json workspace checkpoint "$SESSION" \
        --mode cooperative \
        --message "ci triage for ${GITHUB_SHA}" \
    | jq -r .snapshot_id)

awcctl snapshot export "$HEAD" \
    --against "$BASE" \
    --format patch-bundle \
    --out ci.awcpatch

Upload ci.awcpatch as a build artifact. The patch-bundle format keeps unified diffs for text files and full payloads for binary files. That is enough to apply the changes against the declared base (spec §5.6). See diff and export.

Cooperative versus quiesced

The default checkpoint mode is quiesced, which pauses the writer while it cuts the snapshot (spec §5.5). Use --mode cooperative in CI when no external process writes to the mount during the checkpoint. Cooperative is best-effort and skips the freeze. That is the right trade for a build job whose commands have already stopped. See checkpoint a workspace.

docs.title: 7. Unmount and release the lease
docs.text:
Release the writer lease so the workspace can be forked or mounted again later. The default disposition is discard-local, which throws away any upper directory state the checkpoint did not capture. That is correct here, because you already persisted what you wanted in step 6.

awcctl workspace unmount "$SESSION"

Use --disposition checkpoint to have unmount cut a final checkpoint for you. Use --disposition preserve-local to keep the local upper directory on the host (spec §13.13). For a CI job, discard-local is the clean choice.

docs.title: 8. Put it together in a GitHub Actions job
docs.text:
The snippet below runs the whole loop. It assumes a self-hosted Linux runner with awcctl, awcd, jq, and the Rust toolchain on PATH. Build awcctl with the s3 feature. Store the control endpoint, token, and CAS URL as repository secrets.

name: ci

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:

jobs:
  awc:
    runs-on: [self-hosted, linux, awc]
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Run the build against a cached workspace
        env:
          AWC_CONTROL_ENDPOINT: ${{ secrets.AWC_CONTROL_ENDPOINT }}
          AWC_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.AWC_TOKEN }}
          AWC_TENANT: ${{ vars.AWC_TENANT }}
          AWC_PROJECT: ${{ vars.AWC_PROJECT }}
          AWC_HOST_SOCKET: /run/awcd/awcd.sock
          AWC_CAS_URL: ${{ secrets.AWC_CAS_URL }}
        run: |
          set -euo pipefail

          BASE=$(awcctl --output json snapshot create \
                  --from-dir . --source-type git --name "ci-${GITHUB_SHA::12}" \
                | jq -r .snapshot_id)

          until [ "$(awcctl --output json snapshot inspect "$BASE" | jq -r .state)" = "READY" ]; do
            sleep 2
          done

          WS=$(awcctl --output json workspace fork --snapshot "$BASE" --ttl 1h | jq -r .id)
          mkdir -p ws
          SESSION=$(awcctl --output json workspace mount "$WS" --target "$PWD/ws" | jq -r .mount_session_id)

          rc=0
          ( cd ./ws && make test ) || rc=$?

          HEAD=$(awcctl --output json workspace checkpoint "$SESSION" \
                  --mode cooperative --message "ci ${GITHUB_SHA}" \
                | jq -r .snapshot_id)
          awcctl snapshot export "$HEAD" --against "$BASE" \
                  --format patch-bundle --out ci.awcpatch

          awcctl workspace unmount "$SESSION"
          exit "$rc"

      - name: Upload the diff artifact
        if: always()
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with:
          name: ci-diff
          path: ci.awcpatch

AWC does not ship a runner image

awcctl and awcd are not on a public package registry. You build and install them on the runner yourself. See build and package. The job above also assumes the control plane is already deployed and that the runner host is registered with it.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text:
You wired the five AWC primitives into one CI job:

  • You imported a checked-out tree with awcctl snapshot create.
  • You waited for the snapshot to reach READY before forking.
  • You forked metadata-only with awcctl workspace fork.
  • You mounted the workspace read-write and ran a real build inside it.
  • You checkpointed the result and exported the diff for triage.
  • You released the writer lease with awcctl workspace unmount.
